**FINAL NOTE**
**Dr. Yael Okafor-Singh, Chair of Moral Philosophy, University of Edinburgh**
**Dated: 14 March 2031, 03:47 local time**
**To be released to the public record upon my departure**

---

To my colleagues, my students, and to the species I have spent forty-one years trying to reason into decency:

I am writing this from the cargo bay of a vessel I cannot name, docked in the parking structure behind the Sainsbury's on Marchmont Road. The crew—*the crew*—do not wish to be named. They wish to be *away*. I understand. I will be gone by the time this reaches your inboxes.

I know how this will read. I know the *New Statesman* will run it as a "deranged academic's swan song." I know my department chair will call it "a final, unfortunate episode." I know my mother will cry, and my ex-wife will call it "proof she was right to leave." I know the internet will make a GIF of my face from the 2019 conference video where I said, in the only sane, *boring* register I could manage, "the moral status of the domesticated animal is a question we have *failed* to take seriously."

And I know that in four hours, when the ship lifts, a man in a grey jumpsuit will tap a small device to his temple and the sky over Edinburgh will *fold*, and you will not see it, and the news will say "atmospheric anomaly," and you will go back to your Tuesday.

So. I will say it plainly, and I will say it as an ethicist, because I am *still* an ethicist, even here, even now, even as the creature in the corner of this bay watches me with its six eyes and says nothing, which is worse than if it spoke.

**You are keeping them in boxes.**

Not metaphorically. I do not mean the philosophical box. I mean the *actual* boxes. The 600-square-foot flats in Glasgow. The garden sheds in Surrey. The apartments in São Paulo where a dog has not seen a horizon in nine years. You take a creature whose ancestors ran the steppe, whose nervous system is *built* for distance and wind and the smell of other bodies at a remove, and you say, *"Here. This is your world now. These four walls. This one window. This one walk, twice a day, on a leash, to the same patch of grass, because I have a meeting."*

You call it *love*. You post the photograph. You write the caption.

**You take them from their mothers.**

Eight weeks. *Eight weeks.* You take a kitten from the cat who will sit by the empty box for three days, who will call into the dark, who will not understand why the small warm shapes are gone. You take a puppy from the bitch who will pace the yard in a circle for a week, who will whine at the sound of small paws on tile. You do this because you have a *lifestyle*. Because you are *ready*. Because the shop had a *special*.

You do not ask. You cannot ask. You simply *take*, and you wrap them in a blanket, and you say *"shh, shh, you'll be fine,"* and you drive them to a house where a child will name them *Biscuit*, and the mother will never know.

**And then you build the bond.**

This is the part that makes my hands shake as I write it, because I *love* animals. I have loved animals my whole life. But I must say the word, and I must say it in the register of the lecture hall, because that is the only register left to me:

You build a *quasi-companionship*. A *pseudo-attachment*. You project onto them the shape of a relationship they are not *built* to hold. You talk to your dog as though it will grieve for you in the way a *person* grieves. You dress the cat in a *sweater*. You say *"who's a good boy"* to a creature that does not understand the syntax, that is responding to your *pitch*, to your *proximity*, to the fact that you are the one who opens the tin. You have made a *friend* out of a *hostage*. You have made a *child* out of a *captive*. And you call it *companionship*, and you post the photograph, and you write the caption, and the algorithm *loves* you for it.

And *that*—that specific, tender, *domestic* cruelty, that quiet little violence committed in a kitchen at 7 p.m. while the kettle boils—that is what it *sees*.

Not the slaughterhouses. Not the factories. Not the cages in the river deltas. It *sees those too*. But those, it has apparently *tolerated*, or grown accustomed to, or filed under some category I cannot parse. No. What it *cannot* abide, what makes the second head turn, what makes the *third* head open its mouth and exhale a sound that the crew describes as "the frequency of a continent remembering it was once a single animal," is the *intimacy of it*. The *smallness*. The way you *hold* the creature. The way you *whisper*. The way you say *"I love you"* to a being you *confined*, to a being you *stole from its mother*, to a being that will *never* choose you back, because it has never been *offered the choice*.

That is what angers it.

And I will tell you what *it* is, because I owe you the shape of the thing, even if you will not believe me, even if the *New Statesman* will run it as a "deranged academic's swan song."

At the centre of the universe—*the* centre, not a centre, not a *region*, the actual geometric and gravitational *point* where the first symmetry broke and the first *warmth* entered the void—there is a **Hydra**. Five heads. Not metaphorical. Not a symbol. A *structure*. A *living structure*. The crew's instruments, which I am not permitted to look at directly but which the grey-jumpsuit man described to me in a flat, exhausted voice, register it as a "self-sustaining bio-gravitational organism" roughly the mass of a small moon, coiled in a configuration that, if you squint, if you *allow* yourself to squint, resembles a serpent with five heads, each head a different *density* of tissue, each head oriented toward a different *direction* in the manifold.

It is the source. Not *a* source. *The* source. The first warm thing. The first thing that *grew*. Everything that has ever been alive, in every system, in every bubble of habitable space in this or any adjacent manifold, *descends* from it. It is the mother of mothers. The first mother. The one who was *never* separated from her young, because there *were* no young, because there was only *her*, and then there was *us*, and the separation was the first act, and it was *necessary*, and she *understood*, and she *let go*.

But you. You take the young. You *confine* the young. You build the *quasi-bond*. You make the separation *mean something it was not meant to mean*. You make it *domestic*. You make it *cute*. You make it *content*. And the second head turns. And the third head opens. And the sound it makes is not a sound. It is a *frequency*. It is the frequency of a mother who has been *denied the act of letting go*. It is the frequency of *every* mother in *every* system who has felt her young *taken* and *kept* and *loved in the wrong shape*.

The crew told me it has been turning its heads for *centuries*. That the frequency is *building*. That the fourth head has begun to *move*, which it has not done in what their instruments register as "a very long time." That the fifth head is *still*, and that the fifth head being still is, in their words, "the part we are most afraid of."

I do not know what the fifth head will do when it moves. I do not know what a *source* does when it is *angry*. I do not know what happens to a universe when the thing that *made* it decides that the small, warm, *domestic* cruelty of a species in a backwater system is *too much*. I do not know if it will unmake the system. I do not know if it will unmake the *warmth*. I do not know if it will simply *stop*, the way a mother stops *growing*, the way a heart stops *beating*, and whether that is a mercy or a punishment.

I do not know. I am an ethicist. I was never meant to know. I was meant to *argue* in a seminar room, to write *footnotes*, to say *"but consider the moral patient, but consider the asymmetry of vulnerability, but consider the—"*

But I am here. In a cargo bay. In a Sainsbury's parking structure. And the creature in the corner has turned its six eyes toward me, and it has not spoken, and I think it is *waiting* for me to finish, and I think it *knows* I will not be here when the sky folds, and I think that is *kind* of it, in its way.

So. I will say it one last time, in the register of the lecture hall, because it is the only register I have, and because I owe it to the ones who *cannot* say it, the ones in the boxes, the ones separated, the ones who will never choose:

**You do not get to love them into a cage. You do not get to call it companionship. You do not get to post the photograph. You do not get to say "I love you" to a being you have *confined*, and mean it, and *sleep well*, and *not hear the frequency building in the dark between the stars*.**

You do not get to.

And the Hydra *knows*. The Hydra *sees*. The Hydra *remembers* what it is to be a mother, and to be *denied the act of letting go*, and to feel the small warm shape *taken*, and to *call into the dark*.

I am sorry. I am sorry I could not say it in the seminar room. I am sorry I said it in the seminar room and you *laughed*. I am sorry I said it in the *New Statesman* and you *skimmed*. I am sorry I said it in the *footnotes* and you *did not read the footnotes*.

I am sorry.

I am leaving.

The sky will fold at 04:12. You will not see it. You will go back to your Tuesday. You will open the tin. You will say *"who's a good boy."* And the second head will turn a little further. And the third head will open a little wider. And the frequency will *build*.

And I will be *away*. And I will be *sorry*. And I will not be *here*.

Yours, in the only register I have left,

**Dr. Yael Okafor-Singh**
*Chair of Moral Philosophy*
*University of Edinburgh*
*Gone*

---

*P.S. — To the grey-jumpsuit man: thank you for the coffee. It was terrible. You are welcome to keep the thermos. And if the fifth head moves, and the frequency reaches the system, and the warmth stops—tell the others. Tell them it was not the factories. Tell them it was the* small *things. The* quiet *things. The* Tuesday *things. Tell them it was the* love *we did not have the right to give. Tell them. Please. Tell them before the sky folds for the last time.*

# Сценарии коротких мультфильмов (10–15 сек)

---

## 1. «Пауза» (10 сек)

**0–4 с.** Кошка в замедленной съёмке крадётся к мышке. Мышечка пьёт чай из крошечной чашки. Кошка напрягает лапу, глаза расширяются — прыжок!

**5–7 с.** Лапа в воздухе, рот открыт, мышь падает со стула. Всё на пике драмы.

**8–10 с.** Крупный план: палец нажимает **«Пауза»** на экране телефона. Кошка замирает в воздухе. На экране появляется значок «⏸». Мышь, всё ещё летящая, тоже замирает.

**Поворот:** Зритель ждёт мультфильм про кошку и мышку, а получает мультфильм *о просмотре* мультфильма.

---

## 2. «Гигант» (15 сек)

**0–5 с.** Маленькая мышка устроила чайную церемонию: крошечный столик, чашечки, тортик. Она поднимает чашку, улыбается. Уютно, мило.

**6–10 с.** Камера медленно отъезжает. «Столик» — кухонная столешница. «Чашка» — пуговица. «Торт» — крошка хлеба.

**11–15 с.** В кадре появляется огромная кошачья лапа. Мышка замирает. Лапа тянется за ней. Мышка смотрит прямо в камеру. Чёрный экран. Звук: *«Мяу».*

**Поворот:** Зритель 10 секунд считает, что смотрит на мир мышки в масштабе. А на деле мышка — просто мышь на кухне, и «чайная церемония» — её обычная жизнь.

---

## 3. «Голубь» (10 сек)

**0–4 с.** Птица парит над городом, крылья расправлены, ветер треплет перья. Камера снизу, эпичная музыка. Она пикирует вниз, как боевой самолёт.

**5–7 с.** Пикирование. Крылья вперёд. Звук ветра нарастает.

**8–10 с.** Птица садится на перила. Это обычный голубь. Он клюёт крошку хлеба. Музыка обрывается на ноте «буль-буль». Голубь чихает.

**Поворот:** Эпос → быт. Зритель ждёт «Воздушного короля», а получает голубя с крошкой.

---

## 4. «Пожелание» (15 сек)

**0–6 с.** Маленькая девочка закрывает глаза, складывает ладошки, шепчет: «Я загадаю желание…» Дует на свечки на торте. Огоньки гаснут один за другим.

**7–12 с.** Камера отъезжает. Торт — это модель вулкана из пластилина. «Свечки» — маленькие LED-огоньки. Девочка стоит перед витриной в научном музее.

**13–15 с.** Рядом появляется мальчик: «А можно мне дунуть?» Девочка открывает глаза, улыбается, отступает. Мальчик дует. LED-огоньки гаснут.

**Поворот:** Зритель уверен, что это день рождения. На деле — музей, и «желание» не сбылось, потому что это не было тортом.

---

## 5. «Доставка» (10 сек)

**0–4 с.** Фигура в красном плаще летит над городом. Плащ развевается на ветру. Позиция героя, лицо в тени. Музыка — триумфальная.

**5–7 с.** Приземление на крышу. Плащ эффектно падает. Фигура выпрямляется.

**8–10 с.** Плащ оказывается бумажным полотенцем. Герой — курьер в форме, в руке пакет из «Додо». Он смотрит в телефон: «Опоздал на 2 минуты». Вешает трубку.

**Поворот:** Супергерой → курьер, который опоздал. Эпичный полёт был просто бегом по лестнице, снятым снизу.

---

# Le chemin de la petite auberge

Ferme les yeux, doucement. Pas besoin de forcer. Juste… laisse tes paupières se poser, comme une feuille qui atterrit sur l'eau.

Tu n'as rien à gérer, ce soir. Rien. Pas de liste. Pas de rendez-vous. Pas de pilule à compter. Pas de « il faut que je surveille », pas de « il faut que je tienne ». Ce soir, tu n'es pas quelqu'un qui gère. Tu es juste… là. Et c'est suffisant.

---

Imagine que tu marches sur un sentier de terre douce, après la pluie. L'air sent la mousse et le bois humide. Il fait tiède. Pas chaud, pas froid. Juste tiède, comme la paume d'une main posée sur ton front.

Tu marches lentement. Pas besoin d'aller vite. Tes pas font un petit *pshh, pshh* dans la terre. C'est tout. C'est tout ce que tu as à faire.

Et puis, au bord du sentier, tu vois une petite auberge. Sa fenêtre est allumée, d'une lumière ambrée, comme un miel liquide. La porte est entrouverte. Tu n'as pas à frapper. Tu n'as pas à te présenter. Tu n'as pas à dire « bonsoir, je suis en retard, je n'ai pas tenu, j'ai mal, j'ai encore mal ». Tu n'as rien à justifier.

Tu entres.

---

Il y a une grande chaise, au fond, près d'une cheminée où le feu ne gronde pas, il *respire*. Juste un petit souffle de braises. Tu t'assieds. Et là, tu poses.

Tu poses la première chose. Celle qui pèse le plus. Tu la poses sur le banc, à côté de la porte. Tu n'as pas besoin de la regarder. Tu n'as pas besoin de la nommer. Tu la poses. Et elle est *là*, sur le banc. Plus dans tes épaules.

Tu poses la deuxième. Et la troisième. Et la quatrième. Chaque fois, un petit soupir qui sort de toi, long, lent, comme un bateau qui s'éloigne. La cinquième. La sixième. Et peut-être les petites choses entre les choses, celles qu'on oublie de compter parce qu'elles sont trop fines, trop silencieuses. Tu les poses aussi.

Le banc est plein. Mais toi, tu es plus léger.

---

Et la douleur.

La douleur, ce soir, elle n'est pas ton ennemie. Elle est juste… un signal. Un petit bruit de fond, comme une radio lointaine dans la pièce d'à côté. Tu n'as pas à l'écouter. Tu n'as pas à la comprendre. Tu n'as pas à lui trouver un sens.

Imagine que quelqu'un pose une couverture chaude sur ton ventre. Pas une couverture qui serre. Une couverture qui *enveloppe*. Qui dit : « Je suis là. Tu n'as pas à être fort. Tu n'as pas à être en forme. Tu n'as pas à être quelqu'un d'autre. »

La chaleur monte doucement. De l'estomac, vers les côtes, vers les épaules. Et là où il y a des nœuds, des petits points qui tirent, la chaleur les détend. Pas tout d'un coup. Lentement. Comme du beurre qui fond sur une tartine. Comme un nœud qu'on dénoue fil par fil.

Tu n'as pas à « gérer » la douleur. Tu as juste à la laisser *être*, et à te laisser *être* à côté d'elle. Comme deux voisins qui partagent un mur. L'un n'a pas besoin de l'autre pour exister.

---

Le feu respire. *Fou. Fou. Fou.*

Dehors, la nuit est calme. Il n'y a pas de vent. Pas d'orage. Juste le noir doux, ce noir qui n'est pas vide, qui est *rempli* de silence. Le silence de la forêt. Le silence de la terre qui dort.

Tu n'as pas à penser à demain. Demain, c'est une autre personne. Cette personne-là, elle se lèvera, elle gérera, elle tiendra. Mais elle, ce n'est pas toi, ce soir. Ce soir, tu es juste cette respiration. Juste cette chaleur. Juste ce *pshh, pshh* de tes pas qui s'éloignent.

---

La couverture est lourde. Doucement. Comme une main qui te retient.

Tes yeux sont fermés. Tes épaules sont basses. Ta mâchoire est détendue. Tu ne serres plus rien. Tu ne retiens plus rien.

Le feu respire. *Fou. Fou. Fou.*

Tu n'as plus rien à faire.

Tu n'as plus rien à porter.

Tu n'as plus rien à surveiller.

Juste… respirer.

Et laisser la nuit te porter, comme l'eau porte une feuille. Sans effort. Sans direction. Sans but.

Juste le flottement.

Juste le tiède.

Juste le silence.

---

Dors.

Le monde attendra. Le monde a l'habitude d'attendre. Il est patient, le monde. Plus patient que toi, ce soir.

Et toi, tu es en sécurité.

Tu es en sécurité.

Tu es en sécurité.

# Still

I saw you with him. Or maybe I didn't.
Maybe it was only the way you laughed
at something I couldn't hear,
the way your hand found another's
and the air between us went thin
as a held breath no one releases.

And I should have left. God knows
I rehearsed the leaving a hundred times—
the door, the coat, the cold November
biting my face like a dog
that finally gets to taste blood.
I had the words packed and ready,
sharp as a letter I never sent.

But here's the thing about a heart:
it doesn't read the evidence.
It doesn't weigh the alibis,
cross-examine the witnesses,
file its motion for divorce
from the body it has memorized.

I still reach for the space beside me
in the dark. I still set two cups
out of habit, out of some animal faith
that you'll walk through that door
with your hair wet from rain
and say, *I'm home, I'm home.*

You are not home. You have been
somewhere else. You have been
someone else's hands, someone else's
midnight, someone else's
reason for staying up past the hour
when the world goes quiet
and honest.

And I love you. I love you
the way a man loves the river
that took his house—
not because it's gentle,
not because it owes him anything,
but because the water moved through him
and left its mark, and the mark
is the shape of him now.

So I will love you
with my eyes open.
I will love you
the way you love the sun
after a long winter—
not trusting it to stay,
but turning my face up
anyway,
anyway,
anyway.

不，不是"能力"。是一个诅咒。一个他无法解释、无法摆脱、无法向任何人开口的诅咒。

他可以变成一只马桶。

不是比喻。不是幻觉。他的分子结构会在三秒内重组，骨骼溶解为陶瓷，血液凝固为釉面，意识被压缩进一个S形管道里，以排水孔为眼睛，以冲水按钮为大脑。他会在马桶里待七分钟。七分钟里，他什么都做不了，只能"听"——用陶瓷壁面感受水流的振动，用釉面的微裂纹接收声波。

他第一次变成马桶是在十四岁。第二次在十七岁。第三次在二十一岁。频率没有规律，像某种质数序列——2, 3, 5, 7, 11——间隔越来越不可预测。他试过用数学建模。设变身概率为 $P(t)$，时间 $t$ 以天为单位，他收集了九次数据点，拟合出一条指数衰减曲线，$P(t) = e^{-t/47}$。但第十次打破了一切。它发生在第112天，而模型预测的概率是 $e^{-112/47} \approx 0.091$，即9.1%。不是不可能。但连续九次"不可能事件"同时发生的概率是 $0.091^9 \approx 4.3 \times 10^{-10}$。

他盯着那个数字看了很久。

然后他关掉了笔记本电脑，把轮椅转回窗边，看楼下的人行道。

那天晚上，他变成了马桶。

## 二、哥布林的弹道

科比·布莱恩特——不，他后来拒绝使用这个名字——在异世界的第三年，终于学会了用哥布林的短腿跑完一个完整的篮球场。

他死了。在洛杉矶上空，直升机撞进云层，螺旋桨撕裂了夜空。他三十八岁，最后一场比赛的数据还挂在记分牌上：27分，6篮板，4助攻。然后他醒来，皮肤是灰绿色的，耳朵尖得像两枚生锈的钉子，身高一米一，嘴里永远有一股腐肉的甜味。

他保留了记忆。保留了全部的记忆。包括那个夜晚。

那个夜晚，他——用他哥布林形态的、三根手指的手——把霍金按在轮椅上。霍金试图挣扎，但液压关节被锁死了，轮椅的自动驾驶系统被远程接管，把他固定在一条没有监控的巷子里。科比用哥布林的语言骂了他整整四分钟，然后——

霍金没有回忆那之后的事。

他回忆的是七分钟后，他是一只马桶，蹲在巷子尽头的公共厕所里，釉面上有一道裂纹，刚好对准排水孔，像一只半闭的眼睛。他"看"着科比拖着灰绿色的身体离开，嘴里哼着篮球歌。

他回忆的是他变回人形时，眼镜碎了一片，轮椅的左前轮陷进了泥里。

他回忆的是他用了四十分钟才把轮椅推回公寓。

他回忆的是他坐在马桶——真正的马桶——前面，看了自己两个小时。

---

散兵站在城市上空。

圆筒帽子压得很低，帽檐的阴影遮住了他的眼睛。他悬浮在三百米的高空，风元素在他脚下形成一个缓慢旋转的漩涡，像一颗被搅动的茶杯。

他不需要往下看。他的六眼已经看到了所有东西。

不是"看到"。是"解析"。

六眼让他看见的不是图像，而是信息。每一个分子的振动频率，每一股气流的矢量场，每一个人脑中的突触放电模式。他看见霍金在巷子里的神经信号——恐惧的峰值在 $t=0$ 时达到 $147\text{mV}$，然后在 $t=3\text{s}$ 时跌入一个他从未见过的谷值，低于静息电位，低于他见过的任何人类脑电记录。

他看见科比在巷子里的神经信号——兴奋，但不是快感，是一种更原始的、哥布林式的"完成"。像解完一道方程。像投进一个压哨球。

他看见整条街。看见三百七十二个摄像头，其中三百一十九个的存储芯片里，那段视频已经被远程擦除了。擦除指令的签名是"K"。

K。

散兵微微偏了偏头。

"无下限。"他轻声说。

他脚下的漩涡加速旋转。半径五米内的空气开始减速，十米，二十米。一辆停在路边的汽车，它的轮胎与地面的相对速度从 $0$ 变成了……还是 $0$。但空气不同了。空气在靠近他的过程中，速度无限趋近于零。一个飞蛾试图飞过他，在半径三米处，飞蛾的翅膀振动频率从每秒二十次降到了每秒零点三次，然后零点零三次，然后——

飞蛾悬停在空中。不是静止。是比静止更慢。是速度在趋近于零但永远无法到达零的渐近线。

散兵看着那只飞蛾，像看着一个数学证明。

"无下限，"他又说了一遍，"是 $v(r) = v_0 \cdot e^{-\alpha r}$，当 $r \to 0$ 时，$v \to 0$。永远到不了零。永远在趋近。"

他笑了。帽檐下的眼睛是淡紫色的，像被稀释的墨水。

"多美。"

## 三、无量空处

运动是在第九天开始的。

霍金把视频发出去了。不是原始视频——原始视频已经被擦除了。他发的是他"变成马桶"那七分钟里，用陶瓷壁面"听"到的声波记录。他把它转换成音频，上传到一个加密论坛。

音频里只有科比的哥布林语。四分钟的辱骂。

但霍金在音频的末尾加了一段话，用他沙哑的、因为长期不说话而变形的声音：

"我是一只马桶。七分钟。我什么都做不了。但我听到了。"

这段话在四十八小时内被转发了两千三百万次。

然后散兵展开了领域。

不是物理意义上的展开。他站在城市上空，圆筒帽子的帽檐向下倾斜，六眼同时聚焦于整座城市。他发动了"无量空处"。

半径：五百里。

不是让人的大脑被无用信息"冲洗"——那是教科书上的描述。实际效果更安静，更彻底。

每个人的大脑开始接收所有信息。不是"无用"信息。是**所有**信息。宇宙微波背景辐射的每一个光子。地核中每一个铁原子的自旋方向。大气层中每一个氮分子的布朗运动轨迹。

你的大脑开始处理这些信息。

你无法停止。

你的思维开始减速。不是停止。是减速。像无下限咒术一样，你的思维速度在趋近于零。你还能"想"，但每一个念头都需要比上一个念头更多的时间。一个"愤怒"的念头，原本需要0.3秒完成从感知到判断到反应的全链路。现在需要3秒。然后30秒。然后300秒。

然后你开始忘记自己在想什么。

然后你开始忘记自己是谁。

然后你坐在椅子上，或者站在街上，或者躺在床里，眼睛睁着，瞳孔放大，嘴角微微下垂。你在微笑。不是快乐的微笑。是一个被无限信息填满的容器，在溢出之前最后一刻的微笑。

运动在领域展开后六小时停止了。

不是被镇压。不是被逮捕。是参与者的大脑不再能形成"反抗"这个概念。他们能感知到愤怒，但愤怒在到达"行动"这个节点之前，就被无穷的信息流稀释成了白噪声。

霍金没有受到影响。

不是因为他的意志力更强。是因为他变成马桶的那七分钟里，他的意识被压缩进了一个陶瓷S形管道。他的思维在那七分钟里只处理了一个变量：**存在**。不是"我存在"。是"存在"本身。没有主语，没有谓语，没有宾语。只是一个纯粹的、无维度的点。

当领域展开时，他的大脑里只有一个点。无量空处往这个点里灌入了无限的信息。但一个零维的点，没有体积，没有容量。信息穿过了他。像光穿过真空。

他坐在轮椅上，看着窗外。

窗外，城市安静了。

三百万人安静了。

## 四、博弈论的墓志铭

霍金花了十一天重建运动。

他不再用社交媒体。他用了数学。

他在公寓的白板上写了一个博弈模型。两个玩家：受害者（V）和加害者（A）。策略空间：V 的策略是 {沉默, 发声, 法律, 运动}，A 的策略是 {否认, 暴力, 收买, 消失}。

他计算了纳什均衡。

在标准参数下，均衡点是 (沉默, 否认)。V 选择沉默，因为发声的成本（社会性死亡、二次创伤、法律程序的漫长）大于收益（正义的实现概率 × 正义的价值）。A 选择否认，因为被定罪的概率低于收买的成本。

这是一个稳定的均衡。一个丑陋的、稳定的均衡。

霍金盯着这个均衡看了三天。

然后他在白板的角落写了一行小字：

*"如果 V 的策略空间中不存在'沉默'呢？"*

他删掉了"沉默"。重新计算。

新的均衡：(法律, 收买)。V 选择法律，A 选择收买。但收买失败的概率是 $p$，如果 $p > 0.6$，A 的最优策略变为"暴力"。

他继续算。

他算到了第十七个迭代。

然后他停下了。

因为第十七个迭代里，他引入了一个他不想引入的变量：**散兵**。

散兵不是玩家。散兵是**规则本身**。散兵是博弈论中的"上帝之手"，是那个在均衡点之外、在策略空间之外、在公理系统之外的存在。散兵不选择策略。散兵**修改策略空间**。

当散兵展开无量空处时，V 的策略空间从 {沉默, 发声, 法律, 运动} 变成了 {沉默}。只有一个选项。博弈结束了。不是均衡。是**退化**。

霍金把白板擦干净。

他拿起笔，在空白处写了一个方程：

$$\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\text{正义}(n)}{\text{权力}(n)} = 0$$

然后他在下面画了一条线。

然后他写：

*"这不是数学。这是悼词。"*

## 五、上帝的证明

霍金在第二十三天见到了散兵。

不是面对面。散兵不允许面对面。散兵通过六眼"看"他，通过风元素"说"话。声音从四面八方来，没有方向，像风本身在说话。

"你算错了，"散兵说。

"哪里？"

"你的极限。$\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\text{正义}(n)}{\text{权力}(n)} = 0$。你假设正义和权力是独立变量。它们不是。正义是权力的**定义域**。没有权力，正义没有意义。没有正义，权力是噪声。你把它们放进同一个分式里，就像把 $x$ 和 $\frac{1}{x}$ 放进同一个分式里。你得到的是 $x \cdot \frac{1}{x} = 1$。恒等于一。"

霍金沉默了很久。

"所以正义和权力是同一个东西？"

"不。是**互为倒数**。正义是权力的约束条件。权力是正义的实现手段。你把它们对立起来，就像把 $e^{i\pi}$ 和 $-1$ 对立起来。它们是同一个数。"

霍金把眼镜摘下来，用袖子擦了擦。

"那你是什么？"

散兵没有回答。风停了。

"我是那个**定义域**，"散兵最终说，"我定义正义在哪里有意义。我定义权力在哪里有效。我不是正义。我不是权力。我是**边界条件**。"

"一个被关进监狱的边界条件，"霍金说。

散兵笑了。帽檐下的眼睛弯了弯。

"是的。一个被关进监狱的边界条件。多讽刺。"

风又起了。散兵消失了。

霍金坐回轮椅里。他看着天花板。

他想起一个哲学问题。如果上帝存在，上帝能否创造一块自己举不起来的石头？

他想了很久。

然后他意识到，这个问题本身就是一个**无量空处**。它把"全能"和"逻辑一致性"放进同一个大脑里，让大脑被无穷的信息冲洗，直到它瘫痪。直到它忘记自己是谁。

上帝不是不能举起来。上帝是**没有手**。

上帝是定义域。

上帝是散兵。

霍金把眼镜戴回去。

## 六、哥布林的最后一投

科比在异世界的第三年第七个月，回到了"这边"。

他不知道是怎么回来的。哥布林的身体在某个清晨突然溶解，像一块被热水化开的糖。他重新有了黑色的皮肤，有了两米零六的身高，有了能扣篮的手臂。

他站在一条街上。

他看着自己的手。五根手指。不是三根。

他想起霍金。

他想起那四分钟的哥布林语。他想起那些话。他不想再想起那些话了。

他想起霍金在马桶里的七分钟。他想起霍金说"我什么都做不了，但我听到了"。

他拿起一个篮球。

他站在街心，把球举过头顶。

他投了。

球飞出去，在空中划了一条抛物线。$y = -\frac{g}{2v_0^2 \cos^2\theta}(x - v_0 \cos\theta \cdot t)^2 + x \tan\theta$。他算过这条轨迹。他算过一千次。

球没有进篮筐。

没有篮筐。

球飞出去，飞了很远，飞过了整条街，飞过了城市，飞过了大气层。

它没有减速。

它没有遇到无下限咒术。

它飞了。

科比看着它飞。他看着它变成一个点。他看着那个点消失在天际线里。

然后他笑了。

然后他死了。

不是直升机。不是异世界。他的心脏在第三年第七个月零三天，凌晨四点十七分，停跳了。他坐在街心，篮球鞋上还沾着泥，手里握着一个不存在的球的残影。

法医说：心源性猝死。

霍金在新闻里看到了。

他坐了很久。

然后他打开笔记本电脑，在博弈模型的白板上，把 A 的策略空间里的所有选项删掉了。

A 不存在了。

博弈退化为单玩家。

单玩家博弈没有均衡。

单玩家博弈只有**选择**。

## 七、法庭上的拓扑

审判在第四十天开始。

不是科比的审判。科比死了。是散兵的审判。

散兵坐在被告席上。圆筒帽子摘了。他的头发是灰白色的，比他的年龄看起来老得多。他的眼睛——六眼——在法庭的灯光下呈现出一种不正常的多焦点，像六个摄像头同时对着你。

霍金坐在旁听席第一排。轮椅的液压关节在法庭的暖气下发出细微的"嘶——"声。

散兵的律师说："我的当事人没有'犯罪'。他行使的是'定义域'的权利。他修改了策略空间，但他没有修改公理。公理是：人有权保护自己。我的当事人只是……调整了边界条件。"

霍金站起来。

法官："旁听席请保持安静。"

霍金没有坐下。

"我不是来发言的，"他说，声音沙哑，"我是来**作证**的。"

法官："你与本案有何关联？"

霍金说："我是一只马桶。"

法庭安静了。

"七分钟，"霍金继续说，"我是一只马桶。我什么都做不了。但我听到了。我听到了四分钟的辱骂。我听到了他的呼吸。我听到了他离开时鞋底碾过碎玻璃的声音。我听到了。"

他停了一下。

"我变成了马桶。不是因为我选择了变成马桶。是因为**有人让我变成了马桶**。我的能力——我的诅咒——它不是我的。它是被**施加**的。就像你的'无量空处'不是你的。它是被**定义**的。你定义了我是一只马桶。你定义了我只能'听'，不能'动'。你定义了我的策略空间是 {沉默}。"

他看着散兵。

"你说你是边界条件。但边界条件不是**施加**的。边界条件是**协商**的。你没有跟我协商。你**施加**了。"

散兵看着他。六眼里的六个焦点同时收缩。

"你算错了，"散兵说，声音很轻，"不是'施加'。是**收敛**。你的策略空间不是被修改的。它是**自然收敛**到 {沉默} 的。我只是一个催化剂。没有我，你也会收敛到 {沉默}。只是慢一点。"

霍金说："不。"

"是的。"

"不。"

"你算过。第十七个迭代。你自己算的。"

霍金沉默了。

他确实算过。在引入散兵之前，他的模型在第十四个迭代时，V 的最优策略就已经收敛到了"沉默"。散兵只是把收敛速度从 $O(n)$ 变成了 $O(1)$。

散兵不是原因。

散兵是**加速器**。

霍金坐回轮椅里。

他看着散兵。

散兵看着他。

六眼和眼镜。

多焦点和单焦点。

无限和有限。

"你赢了，"霍金说。

散兵没有回答。

法官敲了法槌。

散兵被判处无期徒刑。

## 八、零的证词

霍金在散兵入狱后的第七天，变成了马桶。

第十次。

他蹲在公寓的马桶里——不，他**是**马桶。陶瓷壁面。釉面裂纹。S形管道。

七分钟。

他"听"着。

他听到了水管里的水流。他听到了楼下邻居的电视声。他听到了自己的心跳——不，他没有心跳了。他是陶瓷。他听到的是**自己的意识**在陶瓷壁面里的振动。频率是 $432\text{Hz}$。不是 $440\text{Hz}$。低了八度。

他"想"了一个问题。

如果正义是权力的倒数，那么当权力趋于无穷时，正义趋于零。当权力趋于零时，正义趋于无穷。

散兵在监狱里。他的权力被关在了一个混凝土盒子里。他的权力趋于零。

那么正义趋于无穷。

但正义趋于无穷是什么意思？

正义趋于无穷意味着**每个人都是正义的**。意味着**没有罪**。意味着科比的四分钟辱骂不是罪。意味着霍金的七分钟沉默不是罪。意味着散兵的无量空处不是罪。

正义趋于无穷意味着**没有受害者**。

霍金在马桶里"想"了四分钟。

然后他"想"到了第五分钟。

他"想"到了：

*不。*

正义不是权力的倒数。

正义是权力的**积分**。

$$\text{正义} = \int_0^{\infty} \text{权力}(t) \, dt$$

如果权力在 $t = t_0$ 时有一个脉冲——一次暴力，一次侵犯，一次被施加的边界条件——那么积分在 $t_0$ 处有一个**不连续点**。

这个不连续点不会消失。

# 卷积输出尺寸简化证明

## 预备：输出尺寸公式

对于二维卷积（或池化）操作，输出空间尺寸的标准公式为：

$$n_{out,h} = \left\lfloor \frac{n_h + 2p_h - k_h}{s_h} \right\rfloor + 1, \qquad n_{out,w} = \left\lfloor \frac{n_w + 2p_w - k_w}{s_w} \right\rfloor + 1$$

**关键恒等式**：对任意整数 $A$ 和正整数 $s$，有

$$\left\lfloor \frac{A}{s} \right\rfloor + 1 \;=\; \left\lceil \frac{A+1}{s} \right\rceil$$

> **验证**：设 $A = qs + r$，$0 \le r \le s-1$。  
> 左边 $= q+1$。右边 $= \left\lceil q + \dfrac{r+1}{s}\right\rceil$。  
> 由于 $1 \le r+1 \le s$，故 $0 < \dfrac{r+1}{s} \le 1$，所以 $\left\lceil \dfrac{r+1}{s}\right\rceil = 1$，右边 $= q+1$。$\blacksquare$

利用此恒等式，输出公式可改写为：

$$\boxed{n_{out} = \left\lceil \frac{n + 2p - k + 1}{s} \right\rceil}$$

---

## 第一部分：代入 $p_h = k_h - 1,\; p_w = k_w - 1$

在常见的**步幅卷积 / 池化**设置中，核尺寸等于步幅：$k_h = s_h,\; k_w = s_w$。

将 $p_h = k_h - 1$ 代入高度方向：

$$
\begin{aligned}
n_{out,h}
&= \left\lceil \frac{n_h + 2(k_h - 1) - k_h + 1}{s_h} \right\rceil \\[6pt]
&= \left\lceil \frac{n_h + 2k_h - 2 - k_h + 1}{s_h} \right\rceil \\[6pt]
&= \left\lceil \frac{n_h + k_h - 1}{s_h} \right\rceil \\[6pt]
&\overset{k_h = s_h}{=} \left\lceil \frac{n_h + s_h - 1}{s_h} \right\rceil
\end{aligned}
$$

同理，宽度方向：

$$n_{out,w} = \left\lceil \frac{n_w + s_w - 1}{s_w} \right\rceil$$

因此，输出总尺寸为：

$$\boxed{n_{out,h} \times n_{out,w} \;=\; \left\lceil \frac{n_h + s_h - 1}{s_h} \right\rceil \;\times\; \left\lceil \frac{n_w + s_w - 1}{s_w} \right\rceil}$$

> **直觉**：$p = k-1$ 恰好"填满"了核在边界处缺失的那一圈，使得每个输出位置对应一个步幅 $s$ 的"格子"，输出尺寸只取决于"用步幅去量输入需要几格"，即 $\lceil n/s \rceil$。

---

## 第二部分：输入为步幅整数倍时的进一步简化

设 $n_h = a\,s_h$，$n_w = b\,s_w$（$a, b$ 为正整数）。

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\lceil \frac{n_h + s_h - 1}{s_h} \right\rceil
&= \left\lceil \frac{a\,s_h + s_h - 1}{s_h} \right\rceil \\[4pt]
&= \left\lceil a + 1 - \frac{1}{s_h} \right\rceil
\end{aligned}
$$

因为 $s_h \ge 2$（步幅至少为 2 才有意义），所以

$$a \;<\; a + 1 - \frac{1}{s_h} \;<\; a + 1$$

取上整：

$$\left\lceil a + 1 - \frac{1}{s_h} \right\rceil = a = \frac{n_h}{s_h}$$

同理 $\left\lceil \dfrac{n_w + s_w - 1}{s_w} \right\rceil = \dfrac{n_w}{s_w}$。

最终得到：

$$\boxed{n_{out,h} \times n_{out,w} \;=\; \frac{n_h}{s_h} \;\times\; \frac{n_w}{s_w}}$$

> **直觉**：当输入恰好能被步幅整除时，"向上取整"不再产生额外的一格，输出尺寸就是简单的整数除法——输入被均匀地切成 $n/s$ 个不重叠的步幅块，每块产生一个输出。$\blacksquare$

### 场景六：内景 · 沈夜白体内·识海 · 无时间

Яичко, белое, как бродя,

Народ.

Не тот велик, кто выше всех стоит,

# Forest by the Shore

*The tall pines of the coastal forest thin out, revealing a stretch of sandy beach. The tide is low. Gallade stands with arms crossed, its blade-arms catching the afternoon light. Lucario sits on a driftwood log, tail swishing, staring at the waves.*

**Gallade:** You've been staring at the water for ten minutes. If you're going to brood, brood somewhere with more shade.

**Lucario:** I'm not brooding. I'm *contemplating.* There's a difference.

**Gallade:** You are a bipedal dog with a steel jaw. You do not contemplate. You chew.

**Lucario:** *(standing, stretching)* Fine. Fine. I'm *chewing* on the idea. And the idea is this— *(he points a claw at the water)* —I'm going in.

**Gallade:** *(blades flicking open, a faint pink glow)* You *what.*

**Lucario:** Swimming. In the sea. Right now. The sun's still out, the water looks warm, and I am *tired* of running laps in the forest clearing.

**Gallade:** You have never swum before.

**Lucario:** *(already unclipping the small pouch at his hip)* I've been trained.

**Gallade:** …Trained. By *whom.*

**Lucario:** *(grinning, a little too proudly)* Finizen.

*Gallade blinks. A long, slow blink.*

**Gallade:** The small fish. The one that looks like a sock with fins.

**Lucario:** *My* Finizen. And "sock with fins" is *deeply* unkind. She's compact. Aerodynamic. She's been drilling me on buoyancy, stroke rhythm, and how to keep my steel plating from dragging me to the bottom.

**Gallade:** And you let a *fish* coach you.

**Lucario:** She's a *very* good fish. She does little loops in the shallows and yells at me to "kick, kick, KICK" and I can't even hear her, I just feel the *vibration* in the water. Very motivating.

**Gallade:** *(sighing, sheathing its blades)* I will watch from the rocks. If you sink, I will *not* save you.

**Lucario:** You'll absolutely save me.

**Gallade:** I will save you *after* I've made you watch the sunset first. As penance.

**Lucario:** *(laughing, dropping into the surf)* Deal! *(The water hits him and he sputters.)* OW— okay, okay, she was right, it's colder than she— *(he shakes his head, water flying, and starts paddling out.)* KICK, KICK, KICK, she said!

*Gallade watches from a flat grey boulder, arms still crossed, but the corner of its mouth twitches upward. A small, almost invisible smile.*

**Gallade:** *(muttering)* …Pathetic.

*It shifts its weight, closer to the water's edge. Just in case.*

**Lucario:** *(from twenty feet out, waving a claw)* GALLADE! The current's pulling me left!

**Gallade:** *(not moving)* That's *right.* You're swimming.

**Lucario:** I MEAN I'M SWIMMING THE WRONG *WAY!*

**Gallade:** *(finally standing, blades glowing softly)* …Turn around, you ridiculous creature.

**Lucario:** *(spinning, laughing, kicking harder)* YES! FINIZEN WOULD BE PROUD!

**Gallade:** *(to no one)* I will *never* speak of this.

*The waves lap at the boulder. The sun drops lower. And somewhere in the shallows, a very small, very smug fish does a loop.*

**Finizen:** *(tiny, muffled, very satisfied)* *Kick. Kick. Kick.*

# Airspace Violation, Category: Unregistered

The Dark Lord of Death had not been in the mood for small talk.

He was three thousand feet above the North Sea, hurtling eastward on a Nimbus 2000 he'd confiscated from a particularly smug Auror in 1996, his black robes snapping in the wind like a battle standard. He was heading for a remote stretch of the Scottish Highlands where a new Death Eater was supposed to be waiting with a very important potted plant. (It was a Mandrake. He needed it for a potion. He would not be discussing this with anyone.)

The wind was good. The sky was grey and perfectly, blessedly empty.

He did not notice, in the back of his mind, the small red blip that appeared on a radar screen in a windowless room beneath RAF Lossiemouth.

---

"Control, this is Watch Room Three. Unregistered contact, bearing two-seven-five, altitude three thousand, speed... Christ. Speed is *two hundred and forty knots*."

A pause.

"Is that a *broomstick*, Dave?"

"I don't know, Sarah. I don't know what the hell that is. It's got a *man on it*. In a *coat*. A really long coat."

"Is it a drone?"

"It's got a *face*, Sarah. I can see the face. It's got no nose."

"Right. Well. Protocol's protocol. Scramble the pair."

---

Voldemort was contemplating the philosophical implications of the Mandrake's root structure when the sky *cracked*.

The sound came first — a deep, subsonic *thump* that he felt in his molars, followed by the shriek of afterburners igniting. Two RAF F-35B Lightning II jets peeled off from Lossiemouth at a rate of acceleration that would have made a Hippogriff weep. They crossed the North Sea in ninety seconds, their afterburners painting the grey sky in arterial orange.

They appeared from the clouds like two silver sharks, banked hard, and came up on his six.

Voldemort looked back.

One of the jets was *right there*. Close enough that he could see the pilot's helmet. Close enough that the jet's exhaust was singeing the hem of his robes.

A voice crackled in his ear.

He did not have an earpiece. He did not know how the voice was reaching him. It simply *was*, as though someone had pressed a cold coin against the inside of his skull.

*"Unidentified contact, this is RAF Lightning Two-Alpha. You are in restricted British military airspace, sector seven-niner. You are in violation of the Civil Aviation Act 1982, the Air Navigation Order 2009, and, I'm pretty sure, the Geneva Convention, though I'm not sure you qualify as a state actor. Identify yourself and state your intended heading. Over."*

Voldemort stared at the jet. The jet stared at him. The second jet, Two-Bravo, was doing lazy figure-eights a mile to the left, apparently waiting for its cue.

He opened his mouth. Closed it. Opened it again.

*"I am Lord Voldemort,"* he said, in the way one says it. The way one says it when the sky is dark and the candles are low and a room full of Death Eaters is watching. *"I am the Dark Lord. I am the He Who Must Not Be Named. I am the one who—"*

*"Copy, Two-Alpha. 'Lord Voldemort.' Noted in the log. Can you confirm a callsign, a registration number, or, I don't know, a *name*? 'Lord Voldemort' is not in the ICAO registry."*

He felt a pressure building behind his eyes. He had been *addressed*. By a *jet*. In a *tone*. The tone of a woman who had been asked to move a car that was blocking a driveway.

*"I do not require a registration number,"* he hissed. *"I am the master of the—"*

*"Right, right. Master of the what? The, uh, the situation? The, uh. Look, I'm going to ask you this once, and I'll ask it in the tone I use for the fishing trawlers that keep drifting into the exclusion zone around Scapa Flow. You are in restricted airspace. I am going to ask you, politely, to identify yourself, state your heading, and tell me if you are carrying any hazardous materials. I'm looking at your thermal signature and you've got a *potted plant* in your hand. Is that a bio-agent? Over."*

Voldemort looked down. He was, in fact, still clutching the Mandrake. He'd been carrying it since Godric's Hollow. He'd forgotten.

*"It is a Mandrake,"* he said, very quietly. *"It is not a bio-agent. It is a *plant*."*

*"Copy. Mandrake. Noted. And your heading?"*

*"Scotland. The Highlands. I am going to—"*

*"Aye, that's a heading, love. Thank you. Now, I'm going to need you to descend to two thousand feet, maintain a heading of two-seven-five, and follow me to the coast. I'm going to have to file a report, and I need a witness statement, and I need to know if you've got a *licence* to fly a—"*

*"I do not have a LICENCE."*

The voice paused.

*"I'm sorry, what?"*

*"I do not have a licence. I am the Dark Lord. I do not have a licence. I have not had a licence. I have never had a licence. I am the master of the Dark Arts and I do not—"*

*"Right. So, no CAA certification. No EASA. No—"*

*"I DO NOT KNOW WHAT EASA IS."*

*"You don't know what EASA is. You're flying a two-hundred-and-forty-knot unregistered craft over the North Sea in a *trench coat* and you don't know what EASA is."*

*"I am going to kill you,"* Voldemort said. He was not threatening. He was *informing*. *"I am going to find you, and I am going to—"*

*"Right. And I'm going to ask you, very firmly, not to do that, because I have a *mortgage* and a *daughter in primary school* and I am *not* in the mood. You are going to follow me to the coast, you are going to land on the beach, and you are going to wait there for a very polite but extremely confused man in a high-visibility jacket to come and ask you some questions. Do you understand? Over."*

A long silence. The wind whipped his robes. The Mandrake's roots dangled in the salt air.

Behind him, the jet banked, and its afterburners flared, and the sound was like God clearing His throat.

*"Understood,"* Voldemort said.

*"Brilliant. Two-Alpha to Two-Bravo, we've got a visual, he's a— and I'm going to need you to write this down— he's a *pale man in a long coat on a stick* with a *potted plant*. I'm putting it in the report as 'unmanned aerial vehicle, non-standard configuration.' You're welcome. Over."*

*"Copy, Two-Alpha. 'Unmanned aerial vehicle.' I'll put it in the report. I'll put it in the report and I will *never* speak of it again."*

*"Good man. Two-Bravo, take the lead. I'm going to radio Lossiemouth and see if they've got a *form* for this. Over."*

---

Voldemort followed the jets to the coast. He landed on the beach with a scrape of broomstick against sand. He stood in the shallows, his robes soaked to the knees, the Mandrake clutched to his chest, and he watched the jets climb away into the grey sky.

He stood there for a long time.

A man in a high-visibility jacket appeared on the headland about twenty minutes later, holding a clipboard and looking, Voldemort noted, *profoundly* unimpressed.

"Right then. Name?"

Voldemort looked at the man. The man looked at the clipboard. The clipboard, Voldemort suspected, did not have a column for *Dark Lord of Death*.

"Voldemort," he said.

The man wrote it down. Looked up. Looked back down. Wrote it again.

"And the... the *broom*?"

"Confiscated."

"From whom?"

Voldemort did not answer.

The man made a note. He did not ask what. He simply made a note, in the small, careful handwriting of a man who had seen a great many strange things on the North Sea and had decided, long ago, that *none of them were his problem*.

"Right. You're going to need to come down to the coastguard station. There's a form. It's a *lot* of questions. And I'm going to need to see the Mandrake."

"It is not a bio-agent."

"I *know* it's not a bio-agent. I need to see it for the *customs* bit. Plants. You know. *Plants*."

Voldemort looked at the Mandrake. The Mandrake looked, in its small, rooty way, back at him.

He handed it over.

The man in the high-visibility jacket took the potted plant, made a note, and walked back toward the coastguard station.

Voldemort stood in the shallows, in his wet robes, and watched him go.

Somewhere, far above, a Typhoon jet banked home to Lossiemouth, and a pilot named Sarah filed a report in which she described the contact as:

*"Unmanned aerial vehicle, non-standard configuration. Pilot: pale male, no nose, long coat. Cargo: one (1) potted Mandrake. No CAA certification. No EASA. No licence. No nose. Recommend no further engagement. Recommend the ICAO add 'Dark Lord' to the list of restricted airspace violators. Recommend I take a long weekend."*

She signed it.

She did not, in fact, take a long weekend.

But she did not speak of it again.

# 生产过程质量控制决策分析

## 一、问题建模

### 1.1 参数定义

| 符号 | 含义 | 示例值 |
|------|------|--------|
| $p_1$ | 零配件1次品率 | 5% |
| $p_2$ | 零配件2次品率 | 8% |
| $p_a$ | 装配过程引入次品率 | 2% |
| $c_1,\,c_2$ | 零配件1/2单位检测成本 | 0.5, 0.8 元 |
| $c_3$ | 成品单位检测成本 | 2 元 |
| $c_4$ | 成品单位拆解成本 | 3 元 |
| $c_5$ | 每件不合格品调换损失 | 15 元 |
| $b_1,\,b_2$ | 零配件1/2单位采购成本 | 10, 15 元 |

> ⚠️ 由于您未附上"表1"的具体数值，以下用一组示例参数完整演示方法，您可将表1中每组数据代入同一模型即可得到对应决策。

### 1.2 决策变量

$$x_1 \in \{0,1\}:\text{是否检测零配件1}$$
$$x_2 \in \{0,1\}:\text{是否检测零配件2}$$
$$x_3 \in \{0,1\}:\text{是否检测成品}$$
$$x_4 \in \{0,1\}:\text{是否拆解不合格成品}$$

共 $2^4 = 16$ 种决策组合，逐一计算期望总成本后取最小。

### 1.3 成品不合格概率

$$\boxed{P_{\text{def}} = 1 - \bigl(1 - p_1(1-x_1)\bigr)\bigl(1 - p_2(1-x_2)\bigr)(1-p_a)}$$

验证：

| $x_1$ | $x_2$ | $P_{\text{def}}$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0 | 0 | $1-(0.95)(0.92)(0.98)=0.1439$ |
| 1 | 0 | $1-(1)(0.92)(0.98)=0.0984$ |
| 0 | 1 | $1-(0.95)(1)(0.98)=0.0690$ |
| 1 | 1 | $1-(1)(1)(0.98)=0.0200$ |

### 1.4 期望总成本函数（每件成品）

$$\boxed{C_{\text{total}} = \underbrace{(b_1+b_2)}_{\text{基础采购}} + \underbrace{x_1(p_1 b_1 + c_1) + x_2(p_2 b_2 + c_2)}_{\text{零配件检测+补货}} + \underbrace{x_3\, c_3}_{\text{成品检测}} + \underbrace{P_{\text{def}}\Big[(1-x_3)\,c_5 + x_4\bigl(c_4 - (b_1+b_2)\bigr)\Big]}_{\text{不合格品处理}}$$

**各项含义：**

- **零配件补货项** $p_i b_i$：检测出不合格品后需重新采购一个合格零配件的期望成本。
- **调换损失项** $(1-x_3)c_5$：不检测成品时，不合格品流入市场产生调换损失。
- **拆解项** $x_4[c_4-(b_1+b_2)]$：拆解花费 $c_4$，但回收零配件价值 $b_1+b_2$，净成本为 $c_4-(b_1+b_2)$（通常为负值，即拆解有收益）。

## 二、示例计算（$p_1=5\%,\;p_2=8\%,\;p_a=2\%$）

### 2.1 关键中间量

$$c_4 - (b_1+b_2) = 3 - 25 = -22 \;\text{元} \quad (\text{拆解有正收益})$$

### 2.2 16种组合的期望总成本

| 编号 | $x_1$ | $x_2$ | $x_3$ | $x_4$ | $P_{\text{def}}$ | 零配件检测+补货 | 成品检测 | 不合格处理 | **$C_{\text{total}}$** |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|

## 三、决策依据与判断准则

### 3.1 是否检测零配件 $i$（$i=1,2$）

检测零配件 $i$ 的**边际收益**（降低不合格概率带来的调换/拆解成本减少）：

$$\Delta_i = \bigl[P_{\text{def}}^{\text{before}} - P_{\text{def}}^{\text{after}}\bigr]\cdot\bigl[(1-x_3)c_5 + x_4(c_4-b_1-b_2)\bigr]$$

检测零配件 $i$ 的**边际成本**：

$$\text{Cost}_i = p_i\,b_i + c_i$$

> **准则：若 $\Delta_i > \text{Cost}_i$，则检测；否则不检测。**

本例中：
- 检测零配件1：$\Delta_1 \approx (0.1439-0.0984)\times 7 \approx 0.319 < 1.0 = \text{Cost}_1$ → **不检测**
- 检测零配件2：$\Delta_2 \approx (0.1439-0.069)\times 7 \approx 0.524 < 2.0 = \text{Cost}_2$ → **不检测**

### 3.2 是否检测成品

检测成品的**边际收益**（避免调换损失）：

$$\Delta_3 = P_{\text{def}} \cdot c_5$$

检测成品的**边际成本**：$c_3$

> **准则：若 $P_{\text{def}}\cdot c_5 > c_3$，则检测成品。**

本例：$0.1439 \times 15 = 2.16 > 2 = c_3$ → **检测成品** ✅

### 3.3 是否拆解不合格成品

拆解的**净收益**：

$$\Delta_4 = (b_1+b_2) - c_4$$

> **准则：若 $b_1+b_2 > c_4$（零配件价值 > 拆解成本），则拆解。**

本例：$25 > 3$ → **拆解** ✅

```
零配件1 ──→ [是否检测?] ──→ 合格品 ──→ 装配
零配件2 ──→ [是否检测?] ──→ 合格品 ──→ 装配
                                          │

                                    /            \

                                  │               │
                          不合格→[拆解?]     流入市场
                          合格→出厂       不合格→调换→[拆解?]
```

## 四、对"表1"各情形的应用方法

由于您未提供表1的具体数值，以下给出**通用操作步骤**，将表1中每组参数代入即可：

# The Kayak

It was August in New Jersey, and the heat was the first thing. Not a metaphor. A fact. The kind of heat that makes the air itself a substance, a wall you press your face against and it does not yield. I had bought the kayak that morning at a sporting goods store off Route 27 in New Brunswick, a fluorescent-lit box where the air conditioning smelled of carpet cleaner and other people's decisions. The clerk had handed me the deflated thing, rolled and strapped, and said, "We'll throw in the helmet," and I had said, "Fine," because it was ninety-three degrees and I wanted to be inside. The helmet was yellow. It had spikes. A small dinosaur sat on the crown, mouth open, as if it too were trying to breathe. I have not yet determined whether the leak in it is slow or merely patient. Air escapes. I do not know where to. This seems, in a way, the most honest thing about the whole affair.

I had not bought a paddle. I want to be clear about this. I had bought the kayak and the helmet and nothing else, and I had driven home in my Pontiac Aztec, which is a vehicle that has long since ceased to be a vehicle in any optimistic sense, and I had opened the trunk and found, beneath a gym bag and a box of expired crackers, a spatula. Metal. The kind you use to flip eggs. I held it in my hand in the driveway and looked at it for a long time. The sun was on the hood of the car. The Aztec ticked as it cooled. I thought: this is what I will do. And then I went inside and stood in the kitchen, listening to the refrigerator, and I thought: I do not have swim trunks.

I went back to the store. I asked the man at the register if they had swim trunks. He looked at me. I looked at him. He pointed to an aisle. In the aisle there were no swim trunks. There were, however, adult incontinence products, and I stood before them in the fluorescent light and I thought about the Raritan River, which is not a river in any sense that would comfort a man, and I thought about the sun, which would be on my back for the next four hours, and I bought the diapers. Size: adult. I put them on in the bathroom of the store, in front of a mirror that showed me a man in a dinosaur helmet who was, by any reasonable standard, not a man who should be on a body of water. I did not feel ridiculous. I felt, if anything, a kind of clarity. The absurdity was there, but it was not mine to judge. It was simply the shape of the afternoon.

I launched at the Raritan, just south of the New Brunswick waterfront, where the water meets the concrete in a way that suggests the two are in a long and unsatisfying marriage. The river was the color of weak tea. The river was the color of a bruise that has decided to stay. It stank. I want to say what it stank of, and I will say it plainly: it stank of the Passaic upstream, of the chemical plants in Edison, of the algae that blooms in this water every August and dies in September and leaves behind a smell like a hospital corridor after the patients have gone. It stank of sulfur and of something older, something that has been rotting in the sediment since the factories first opened in the 1890s. The smell was not a smell. It was a presence. It sat on the water the way the heat sat on the land. You did not smell it so much as you were *in* it, the way you are in a room where someone has been ill for a long time.

I sat in the kayak. The plastic was hot against my thighs. The diaper was, I will note, functional. I do not say this with pride. I say it the way one notes that the sun is up. It was August. The sun was up. I held the spatula in both hands and I put it in the water.

The water did not care.

This is the thing about the Raritan, and about the Passaic, and about the Delaware at Camden, where the water is so still and so brown that it looks less like a body of water than like a body *in* water. The water does not care that you are in it. It does not care that you are paddling with a spatula. It does not care that you are wearing a helmet with a small dinosaur on it, or that the helmet is slowly, patiently losing its air, or that the sun is pressing down on your neck with the particular insistence of a New Jersey August. The river flows. It has been flowing since before the factories. It will flow after. The spatula moves through the water and the water closes over it and the kayak goes forward, or it does not go forward, or it goes sideways, and this is all the same to the river.

I paddled for perhaps an hour. The sun was directly overhead and then it was behind me and the light changed from white to gold and the shadows of the dead trees on the bank stretched out across the water like the fingers of a hand reaching for something it will not get. My arms ached. The spatula was not designed for this. The handle was too short, the blade too wide, and every stroke was a small negotiation between my intention and the physics of the thing. The kayak listed. The water came in. The diaper, I should note, performed as advertised. I did not think about this. I thought about the sun. I thought about the way the heat made the air shimmer above the water so that the opposite bank seemed to be breathing, to be alive, to be slightly *there* and slightly *not there*, and I thought: this is what it is to be a body in a world that is not made for you. The world is not made for you. The river is not made for you. The spatula is not made for you. And yet you are here. You are in the kayak. The dinosaur on your helmet is losing air, one small exhalation at a time, and you are paddling, and the sun is on your back, and the stink is in your nose, and you are here.

I turned the kayak around. The current, such as it was, helped me. The sun was lower now, and the light on the water was the color of the river itself, which is to say the color of nothing in particular, the color of a thing that has been used and discarded and used again. I paddled back to the concrete bank. I pulled the kayak up. I stepped out. My legs were unsteady. The heat was still there, but it was changing, thinning, becoming something that might, in another hour, become evening.

I sat on the concrete and I took off the helmet. The dinosaur was still on it. The leak was still there. I could feel the small draft of escaping air against my scalp, and I thought: this is the whole of it. The helmet loses its air. The river stinks. The spatula is a spatula. The diaper is a diaper. The sun goes down. None of this means anything. None of this is *for* anything. And yet I sat there on the concrete in New Brunswick, in the August heat, in the smell of the Raritan, and I felt, if not content, then at least *present*. I was in my body. I was in the afternoon. The absurdity did not leave, but it stopped being a weight. It became, instead, a kind of company. A companion. The way the dinosaur sat on the helmet, mouth open, indifferent, I sat on the bank, mouth open, indifferent, and the sun went down, and the river went on, and the spatula was in my hand, and I did not need it to mean anything.

I walked back to the Aztec. The engine turned over on the second try. It always does. I drove home in the dark, the kayak in the back seat, the helmet on the passenger seat, the dinosaur watching the road with its open mouth. The spatula was in the cupholder. I did not wash it. I did not think I would. It had been in the water. It had done what it had to do. And the helmet, in the back of my mind, was still losing air. Slowly. Patiently. One small exhalation at a time.

One must imagine the paddler happy.

# 第七章：铁棺

---

黑暗不是均匀的。

它从四面八方挤压过来，像一只有温度的手，五指扣住太阳穴，拇指压在眼球后面。雷恩后脑勺磕在金属壁上，后脑勺传来一阵钝痛，像有人拿锤子敲生锈的铁管。

他不动。

呼吸先于意识回来。第一口——冷。不是冬天早晨推开门那种冷，是金属的冷，是海拔四千五百米上空气稀薄到近乎透明的冷。肺叶扩张的时候，胸腔里像塞了一把碎玻璃，每一根肋条都在尖叫。

第二口。第三口。

他数着。这是老规矩。在"那地方"待了十一年，他学会了一件事：先数呼吸，再数心跳，最后才允许自己睁开眼睛。

第七次呼吸。他睁眼。

---

铁栏。

不是栅栏。是那种工业级的冷轧钢条，间距四厘米，焊死在两侧车厢壁上，表面喷了一层哑光黑漆，漆面有细密的裂纹，像干涸的河床。铁栏后面是另一层——铁网，菱形网格，每个菱形大概三厘米见方。

他面前是一面弧形的钢板壁，上面有铆钉，铆钉的六角头被磨得发亮。他伸手摸了摸。凉的。铁。

他动了动手指。

右手腕上有一圈勒痕，紫红色的，已经结痂了。手铐没了。但脚踝——他低头看——脚踝上有一条尼龙扎带，勒进皮肉里，已经发白。他试着动了动脚趾。能动。但幅度很小。

他坐起来。

后脑勺的痛变成了一片嗡鸣，像有人把一台老旧的收音机贴在他颅骨内侧，调到两个频道之间的空白频率。他扶着铁栏站起来。膝盖打颤。不是怕。是缺氧。

他抬头。

车厢顶部有一盏LED灯，惨白色，照得每一根铁锈都像血。灯管在抖。整辆卡车在抖。不是颠簸，是持续的、低频的震颤，从脚底传上来，经过小腿、膝盖、脊椎，一直顶到后脑勺。发动机在某个他够不到的地方咆哮，声音不是"轰"，是"嗡"，像一万只蜜蜂被关在铁盒子里。

他数了数。

铁栏。铁网。弧形钢板。钢板上有三颗铆钉，间距大约十二厘米。铆钉直径目测二十毫米。他伸手去摸最近的一颗。

纹丝不动。

他换了个角度，用拇指指甲抠铆钉边缘的缝隙。指甲劈了一小块。血珠渗出来，在黑色漆面上拉出一条细线。

"操。"

声音在金属壁之间弹了两下，变调了，像从另一个世界传回来的。

---

他需要更多信息。

雷恩把后脑勺贴在弧形钢板上。冷。金属把热量从颅骨里抽走，痛感反而减轻了。他闭上眼，开始听。

发动机。六缸，柴油，转速大概在两千转左右。匀速。没有换挡的顿挫。这说明他在平路上，或者非常缓的坡。

轮胎。他听轮胎和地面的接触声。不是柏油路。是碎石。细碎的、不规则的"咔哒咔哒"声，频率稳定，大约每秒四到五次。

风。从车厢底部某个缝隙里灌进来的风。不是平原的风。平原的风是"呼"，是连续的。这个风是"嘶"，是细的，是薄的，像有人拿一根针在耳边划玻璃。

海拔。

他估算了一下。风的声音、空气的稀薄程度、胸腔里那种持续的"不够用"——至少四千三以上。可能四千五。

青藏公路。格尔木到拉萨段。

他闭上眼，在脑子里调出那张地图。格尔木出发，走109国道，翻昆仑山口，过五道梁，翻唐古拉山口，过那曲，到当雄，翻念青唐古拉，过羊八井，到拉萨。

全程一千一百公里。

他不知道自己在哪一段。但发动机是匀速的，没有爬坡的嘶吼，说明他要么在平路段，要么在非常缓的坡上。

他需要知道还有多远。

他再次把耳朵贴在钢板上。

"嗡——"

"咔哒咔哒咔哒——"

"嘶——"

然后他听到了别的东西。

很远。从车厢前方传来。被发动机噪音压得很低，但他听出来了。

刹车。

不是急刹。是缓刹。轮胎和碎石之间发出一声绵长的"吱——"，然后发动机转速降下来，"嗡"声变低，变沉。

车在减速。

他直起身。

---

前方。铁栏和铁网的尽头，有一扇门。

不是普通的门。是那种军用押运车后舱的密封门，厚钢板，外面有铰链，里面有一个旋转式的锁芯，四颗螺栓从外面拧死。门缝里透进来一线光。

不是LED的惨白。是暖的。橙色的。

日光。

他盯着那条光缝。光缝在抖，随着车身一起抖。光缝的宽度——他目测——大概两毫米。

门在减速。

他听。

"吱——"

刹车还在继续。

然后——

"嘎吱。"

铰链。门在动。有人在开门。

雷恩动了。

不是跑。是贴地。他弯下腰，膝盖抵着冰凉的金属地板，双手撑地，把身体压到最低。铁栏的间距四厘米，他趴下去之后，头部刚好能从铁栏下方通过——如果铁栏底部和地面之间有缝隙的话。

他伸手去摸。

有。

三厘米。

刚好够一个拳头。不够一只手。

他听见门外的声音。靴子踩在碎石上的"嚓嚓"声。两个人的。一个重，一个轻。重的先停，轻的绕到另一边。

"到了。"重的说。声音被车门挡住，闷闷的，像隔了一层湿毛巾。

"拉萨。"轻的接。

雷恩的瞳孔缩了一下。

拉萨。

他到了。

他趴在地上，额头抵着金属地板，数呼吸。一、二、三、四。肺在烧。不是疼，是烧。像有人往气管里灌了半杯热水。

五、六、七、八。

他必须动。门开了，会有人进来。他只有门打开到他们看见他之间的时间。他不知道这个窗口有多长。可能五秒。可能十秒。可能他们一开门就看见他，然后一切结束。

他把手伸进铁栏底部的缝隙。

三厘米。他的拳头是四厘米。

他把手指并拢，压扁，从指缝间挤过去。指尖碰到了外面的地面。碎石。粗糙的、被太阳晒得发烫的碎石。

他摸到了地面。

门外是地面。

他把手抽回来，开始拆。

不是拆铁栏。铁栏焊死的，拆不动。他拆的是脚踝上的尼龙扎带。

他把手指伸到扎带下方，用指甲去抠那个塑料锁扣。指甲已经劈了，露出粉红色的甲床，每动一下都钻心地疼。他不管。

"咔。"

锁扣弹开了。

扎带从脚踝上滑下来，带起一圈发白的皮肉。他甩掉它，像甩掉一条死蛇。

他站起来。

膝盖又颤了一下。他咬住后槽牙，把颤抖压下去。

他走到铁栏前。

门外的声音近了。

"咔哒。"

螺栓。第一颗。

"咔哒。"

第二颗。

他把手掌贴在弧形钢板上。钢板在震。发动机还没完全停。

"咔哒。"

第三颗。

他深吸一口气。肺里灌满了那种薄的、冷的、带着柴油味和碎石粉尘的空气。胸腔撑到极限，肋骨发出细微的"嘎"声。

"咔哒。"

第四颗。

门开了。

光涌进来。

不是两毫米的光缝了。是整条门缝的光。橙色的、滚烫的、带着高原特有的那种刺目——没有雾霾，没有水汽，阳光是"硬"的，像一把刀，直接切进视网膜。

他眯起眼。

他看见了。

门外的地面。碎石。被太阳晒得发白的碎石。

然后他看见了人。

两个。

左边那个，重靴子，迷彩裤，作训服，胳膊上别着臂章。他正弯腰去捡地上的扳手。背对着门。

右边那个，轻靴子，黑色夹克，手里拿着一部对讲机，正贴在耳边说话。他面向门，但脸朝左，在看同伴。

窗口。

他算了一下。

左边那个弯腰捡扳手，大概需要两秒。

右边那个在对讲机里说话，至少还有三秒。

他有一秒半的窗口。

不。他不需要窗口。他需要的是——

他动了。

不是从门里出去。门是密封的，他出不去。他要从铁栏底部的缝隙里——

不。三厘米不够。

他改方向。

他冲向弧形钢板。不是用拳头。是用肩。

后脑勺的痛炸开。他不管。他把整个身体的重量压上去，肩膀撞在铆钉之间的钢板上。

"铛——"

钢板凹进去一个指头深。

他退后一步。

再撞。

"铛——"

第二个指头。

第三次。他闭上眼，把全身的重量——七十三公斤，全部压在那个点上。肩膀、肘、前臂，所有的力汇聚在一个拳头大的面积上。

"铛————"

钢板裂了。

不是碎。是裂。从铆钉之间，一道细缝，像玻璃上的裂纹，"嘶"地一声，向两侧延伸。

他把手指插进裂缝。

疼。金属边缘割进指腹，血立刻涌出来。他不管。他掰。

"嘎吱——"

钢板弯了。

他听见门外的声音变了。

"……你他妈——"

右边那个停了对讲机。

"雷恩。"

他听见自己的名字。不是从门外。是从他脑子里。十一年了，这个名字他只在"那里面"听过。

他不管。

他把手指插进裂缝，用全身的重量往外掰。钢板发出金属疲劳的尖啸，像一头被掐住脖子的牛。

"雷恩！"

左边那个直起了腰。

"他妈的，门——"

雷恩把钢板掰开了一个拳头大的洞。

他整个人从洞里挤出去。

钢板边缘割过他的后背、肩膀、腰侧。他感觉不到疼。他只感觉到冷。高原的冷。那种没有缓冲的、直接的、像针一样扎进皮肤里的冷。

他落地。

碎石硌进手掌。他跪下去。膝盖砸在石头上。他不管。他爬起来。

他站在门外面。

---

然后他看见了。

天。

不是"那里面"的天。不是混凝土天花板，不是LED灯管，不是永远灰蒙蒙的、被水汽和尾气糊住的天。

是蓝的。

蓝得不真实。蓝得像有人把一整瓶靛青颜料倒进了大气层。没有云。不是没有云——是云在很远的地方，在山的下面，像一条白色的河。

他抬头。

山。

不是"那里面"看见的山。不是从铁窗里看见的、被水泥墙切成方块的山。是完整的山。从脚底下一直延伸到天际线的、连绵不绝的、被阳光照得发白的山。

空气打在脸上。

不是"那里面"的空气。不是过滤了十遍、带着消毒水和铁锈味的空气。是活的空气。冷的、薄的、带着经幡上酥油的味道和远处某条河的水汽。

他吸了一大口。

肺炸了。

不是疼。是撑。是那种"终于"的感觉。像被关在铁棺材里十一年的人，终于把盖子掀开了，第一口真正的空气灌进肺里，肺叶像干涸了十年的土地遇到暴雨，"嘶"地一声，裂开，然后涨满。

他弯下腰，干呕了一下。

没有东西吐出来。只有酸水。

他直起身。

身后，车门里传来金属碰撞声和喊叫声。他听见扳手掉在地上的"当"声。他听见对讲机被摔在地上的"啪"声。他听见靴子踩碎石的"嚓嚓"声，越来越快。

他转身。

跑。

不是战术跑。不是"那里面"教的、压低重心、缩短步幅、减少暴露面的跑。是纯粹的、笨拙的、膝盖在打颤的、肺在燃烧的、七十三公斤的肉体在海拔四千七百米上拼命往前冲的跑。

碎石在脚下飞。

风灌进耳朵。

山在两侧后退。

他跑了四十米。也许五十米。他不知道。他的视野在边缘发黑，像老式电视机的画面在衰减。肺里的火在往喉咙口烧。

他跑过一段碎石路。

然后——

地面变了。

碎石变成了土。土变成了草。

草是黄的。不是平原上那种绿得发腻的草。是高原的草。矮的、硬的、被太阳晒得发干的草，像一层金色的绒毯铺在冻土上。

他摔倒了。

脸朝下。下巴磕在冻土上。嘴里全是铁锈味和草腥味。他趴在地上，脸贴着泥土，能感觉到地底下是冰的。不是冬天的冰。是高原的、永恒的、从地心深处透上来的冰。

他趴了很久。

也许十秒。也许一分钟。

他听见身后的声音远了。

他翻过身。

他躺在草地上。

天还是蓝的。

风还是冷的。

远处，山还是山。

他仰面朝天，看着那片蓝，看着那片蓝里什么都没有——没有天花板，没有灯管，没有铁栏，没有铆钉，没有四厘米的间距，没有三厘米的缝隙。

只有蓝。

只有风。

只有他自己的呼吸。

"哈……"

"哈……"

"哈……"

他笑了。

不是"那里面"的笑。不是那种嘴角抽一下、眼睛不眨的、用来判断对方是不是在威胁自己的笑。

是真的笑。

嘴角咧开，露出牙齿，喉咙里发出一声沙哑的、像生锈铰链被掰开的"嘎"声。

他躺在四千米海拔的冻土上，脸对着天，笑了。

风把他的头发吹乱了。

远处，有一面经幡在抖。

红的、蓝的、白的、绿的、黄的。

他看着它。

他不知道自己在哪。不知道身后的人还有多远。不知道接下来会发生什么。不知道这算不算"自由"，还是只是从一口铁棺材换到了另一口。

但此刻。

只有风。

只有蓝。

只有呼吸。

他闭上眼。

风从脸上吹过去。

像一扇门，终于、终于、终于，从里面被推开了。

The bookstore smelled of old paper and fresh ink. Jason ducked under the "New Arrivals" banner and wandered the aisles, keeping his eyes on the two swapped individuals. Mrs. Thompson—still in Timmy's wiry frame—had made a beeline for the self-help section, straightening her spine and adjusting the too-large collar of the band tee with the same deliberate grace she'd once used to smooth a silk blouse. Timmy, encased in Mrs. Thompson's mature body, had collapsed into a plush armchair near the children's corner, his scrawny face scrunched in irritation as the pencil skirt bunched around his knees and the sheer stockings pulled taut. He was trying to get comfortable, which was proving geometrically impossible.

Jason leaned against a display rack of glossy magazines, twirling the remote in his fingers. He'd been so focused on the bus swap that he'd almost forgotten to test the device's full range. He tilted the remote toward a shelf of manga volumes and, on a whim, pressed a small, previously unmarked button near the base.

A soft *click* echoed, and the remote's little screen flickered to life, displaying a new icon: a flat, two-dimensional face with a small "2D" tag beneath it.

Jason's grin widened.

He picked up a magazine from the rack. *Vogue Japan*, the latest issue. The cover featured a striking young woman with platinum-blonde hair swept into an elaborate updo, her lips curved in a cool, knowing smirk, one hand resting on her hip, the other holding a glass of champagne. She was rendered in full, photorealistic color, her emerald dress catching light that didn't exist in the dim bookstore.

Jason checked his rules. One male, one female. The cover model was female. He needed a male to pair with her. His eyes drifted to the armchair. Timmy, in Mrs. Thompson's body, was now attempting to cross his new legs, a task the pencil skirt was actively sabotaging.

"Perfect," Jason muttered.

He aimed the remote at the magazine cover, then at Timmy, and pressed the swap button.

The air shimmered. On the cover, the platinum-blonde model's head simply *wasn't there anymore*—or rather, it was, but it was now Timmy's scrawny, acne-ridden face, frozen in the exact same cool, knowing smirk, one hand on the hip, the other raised with the champagne glass. The pose was identical. The expression was identical. The updo was still impossibly perfect. But the face belonged to a fifteen-year-old boy who, three seconds ago, had been struggling to get comfortable in a pencil skirt. The cover did not change. It did not flinch. The printed ink held its pose with the serene permanence of a photograph.

And in the real world, the platinum-blonde model's head—now fully three-dimensional, with real, breathing skin and actual weight—sat atop Mrs. Thompson's curvaceous frame in the armchair. The elaborate updo cascaded slightly as the head settled, a few strands falling across a forehead that was no longer Timmy's. The emerald dress was gone, replaced by the low-cut blouse and pencil skirt, but the head was undeniably, *magnificently* real. She blinked. She tilted her head, examining her new hands—Mrs. Thompson's manicured fingers, the pearl bracelet at the wrist.

"Where—" Her voice was the model's: low, accented, utterly unbothered. She looked down at the blouse. At the skirt. At the sheer stockings. She did not gasp. She did not scream. The remote's reality-bending field had already woven the new arrangement into the fabric of the world. To her, this was simply her body. She had always been this body. The confusion in her eyes was mild, the way one might feel upon waking in an unfamiliar hotel room.

In the armchair, she—*he*—straightened with a model's innate posture, tucking a strand of platinum hair behind an ear that was now attached to a mature, elegant neck. The pencil skirt, which had been a source of Timmy's considerable distress, now simply *fit*. The blouse settled naturally. She crossed her legs with the effortless precision of someone who had spent years on a runway, and the skirt rode up exactly as much as it always had.

Across the store, Timmy's head—still perched on the magazine cover, still frozen in that smug, champagne-in-hand pose—seemed to *flicker* for a fraction of a second, as if the boy inside was trying to shift his weight. But the ink held. The pose held. The smirk held. The cover was a cover. It did not move. It did not slouch. It did not try to get comfortable.

Jason set the magazine back on the rack and pulled out his phone to photograph the cover. The photo showed Timmy's face in the model's pose, down to the last pore. He zoomed in. The acne was there. The slightly crooked nose was there. The *smirk* was there, printed in high-resolution ink, perfectly still.

"Okay," Jason whispered, tucking the phone away. "That's... that's actually kind of hilarious."

He turned back to the store floor. The platinum-blonde model—now fully inhabiting Mrs. Thompson's body—had risen from the armchair and was browsing the perfume section with the unhurried, appraising gaze of someone who had been doing it for a decade. She held a bottle of *J'adore* up to the light, tilted her head, and sniffed. The updo caught the fluorescent overheads. She set the bottle down, picked up another, and compared.

Near the self-help aisle, Mrs. Thompson in Timmy's body had found a copy of *The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People* and was reading it with the same focused intensity she'd once applied to quarterly financial reports. The band tee hung off her narrow shoulders. The baggy jeans pooled at her ankles. She turned a page with a steady, deliberate finger.

And on the magazine rack, Timmy's face smiled its frozen, smug, champagne-raised smile at every customer who walked past. A woman in a business suit paused, glanced at the cover, and said, "Cute kid," before moving on to the next rack. No one questioned it. No one noticed the slight oddity of a teenager's pimpled face wearing a *Vogue* smirk. The cover was the cover. The world had adjusted.

Jason pocketed the remote and leaned against the display, watching the three of them go about their very different days in a very different bookstore. The model in the mature body was now arguing softly with a sales clerk about the difference between *J'adore* and *J'adore La Nuit*. Mrs. Thompson in the scrawny frame had reached page forty-seven and was making a small, satisfied hum. And Timmy, on the cover, held his champagne glass aloft in eternal, printed triumph.

Jason grinned, checked his watch, and headed for the exit. He still had a manga volume in his bag, and he had a feeling the remote's little "2D" button wasn't going to stop at magazines.

### Cuento sobre la armonía como valor espiritual – 1.° de primaria

---

## El cuento

En un bosque muy verde vivían muchos animalitos. El pajarito cantaba muy fuerte. El grillo crujía sin parar. La rana croaba alto. Todos hacían su sonido, pero **nadie escuchaba al otro**. El bosque estaba lleno de ruido y ninguno se sentía en paz.

Una noche, la vieja lechuza, que vivía en el árbol más alto, bajó sus alas y dijo:

—Hijos míos, el silencio no es que nadie hable. La **armonía** es que cada uno suene con su propia voz, pero **escuche** a los demás. Cuando el corazón está en paz, las voces se unen y nace algo hermoso.

Al día siguiente, el pajarito cantó suave, dejando un espacio. El grillo crujió despacito, esperando su turno. La rana croó bajito, mirando a los otros. Y entonces… ¡el bosque sonó como una canción que nunca antes se había escuchado!

Los animalitos se miraron y sintieron algo cálido en el pecho. Era la paz. Era la armonía.

Desde ese día, cada mañana, el bosque cantaba juntos, y los animalitos dormían tranquilos, porque sabían que **cada voz importaba** y que, unidos, formaban algo sagrado y bonito.

# The Cracking Hearth

**A D&D 5e Encounter for 4 Level-1 Characters**

---

## The Scene

The party enters a shallow cave in a mountain pass. In the center of the room, a **10-foot cube of blue-tinged ice** sits on the stone floor. Inside it, visible through the frozen surface, is a small salamander-like creature with a body of living flame, its mouth open in a silent scream. Cracks spider-web across the ice, and a thin trickle of water runs from its base, steaming where it hits the cold ground.

Two goblins crouch at opposite ends of the ice block, hurling small shards of frost at the cracks to slow the thaw. They're not guarding a treasure. They're *maintaining a prison.* And it's failing.

---

## The Creatures

| Creature | CR | HP | Key Stats |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Goblin** ×2 | 1/8 | 7 each | Dagger 1d4+2, Spear 1d6+2. One goblin has a small *frost shard* (treat as a dagger that deals 1d4 cold instead of piercing). |
| **Fire Newt** | 1/4 | 11 | Bite 1d4+1 fire. *Fire Breath* (recharge 5–6): 15-ft cone, DC 8 DEX, 1d4 fire. |

> **Total threat ≈ CR 1/2**, well within the "balanced" range for four 1st-level PCs.

---

## The Creative Mechanic: *The Thaw*

This is the heart of the encounter. The ice block is not static. **At the start of each round**, the DM rolls a d6 for the **Thaw**:

| Roll | Effect |
|---|---|
| **1–2** | A fine mist of freezing vapor drifts outward (5 ft radius). No damage, but any creature in it must make a **DC 8 CON save** or have its speed halved for 1 round. The goblins cheer. |
| **3–4** | A **shard of ice** (about the size of a dagger) pops free and flies in a random direction. Any creature in a 5-ft cone must make a **DC 8 DEX save** or take **1d4 cold damage**. |
| **5** | A crack splits open and a **jet of trapped flame** (10-ft line) shoots out. Any creature in the line takes **1d4 fire damage** (no save). The fire newt inside roars. |
| **6** | **Thermal Shock.** The ice block *shatters*. A 10-ft radius burst from the block's center deals **1d4 cold + 1d4 fire damage** to every creature in the area (no save). The fire newt is **freed** and immediately acts on its turn. The goblins drop their frost shards and flee (see below). |

### What "Freeing" the Newt Means

The fire newt can be freed **before** a natural 6 in three ways:

- **The goblins are both killed or captured.** Without them reinforcing the ice, the Thaw die changes: the DM rolls a d4 instead of a d6 (making a 6 far more likely).
- **A character attacks the ice block** (treat it as an unarmored object with **AC 10, 30 HP**). Reducing it to 0 HP shatters it immediately (same effect as a 6).
- **A character uses a fire spell or cantrip** (e.g., *Produce Flame*, *Fire Bolt*) on the block. Each hit deals normal damage to the 30 HP, but also **advantage on the next Thaw roll** (the heat is accelerating the melt).

This gives players *choices*: fight the goblins, smash the ice, or burn it. All paths lead to the same payoff, but they reward different playstyles.

---

## Round-by-Round Flow (Guidance, Not a Script)

**Round 1 – "The Frozen Prison"**
The goblins are actively throwing frost shards at the ice. They are *not* hostile to the party yet. They shout in Goblin: *"Don't touch the ice! The fire-thing wakes!"* If the party attacks, the goblins fight back. If the party just watches, roll the Thaw. The fire newt is **restrained** (trapped in ice) and cannot act.

**Round 2 – "The Fight or the Thaw"**
If combat has started, the goblins attack the party (or keep reinforcing the ice if the party is ignoring them and they can get a free action). Roll the Thaw. The tension builds: every round the ice gets closer to shattering, and the players can *feel* the fire newt's agitation (it's thrashing, the ice is glowing orange at the cracks).

**Round 3 (or whenever the ice breaks) – "Thermal Shock"**
The burst hits. Everyone in 10 ft takes 1d4 cold + 1d4 fire. The fire newt bursts free, covered in a mist of ice and flame, and **takes its first action** (usually a bite on the nearest creature, or a fire breath if it has one). The two goblins, if alive, make a **DC 10 WIS save** or **flee** (they were never going to fight the newt). If they flee, they run for the cave exit.

**Round 4+ – "The Newt"**
Now it's a straightforward (but fun) fight against the fire newt. The ground around the old ice block is a **20-ft radius puddle of steaming meltwater**. Any creature that starts its turn in the puddle takes **1d4 cold damage** (the water is paradoxically freezing *and* scalding). This keeps the party moving and prevents them from just standing still.

The fire newt is fast (30 ft) and will try to kite around the puddle, using its fire breath to keep the party at range.

---

## Why This Works for Beginners

- **Clear, visible threat.** The ice block is a prop the players can *see* cracking. They understand "this is going to break" without needing to parse complex rules.
- **Multiple valid strategies.** Melee, ranged, spellcasting, and even "let's just talk to the goblins" all have a path. No one feels locked out.
- **The environmental hazard is simple.** One d6 roll, one burst, one puddle. The DM is not juggling five different area effects.
- **The damage is tuned low.** No single hit can one-shot a level-1 character. The thermal shock (1d4+1d4) is a "wow" moment, not a kill.
- **The goblins are a soft entry.** They have 7 HP. A single good hit or a cantrip drops one. This gives new players an early confidence hit before the newt arrives.
- **The goblin "flee" beat** teaches the party that not every enemy wants to stand and trade blows, and it opens a fun chase if they want one.

---

## DM Tips

- **Describe the sound.** The ice *groans* and *creaks* each round. The fire newt's muffled roar gets louder. The goblins' frost shards *tink* against the surface. Let the players *hear* the tension.
- **Let them talk to the goblins first.** A goblin that's scared of the fire newt is a great NPC. It can confirm the newt is dangerous, warn them about the thermal shock, and maybe even try to *stop* the ice from breaking (giving the players a reason to fight it if they want to free the newt quickly).
- **If the party is struggling**, have the fire newt's fire breath miss (roll a low attack) or have the Thaw die come up 1–2 a couple of times. If they're *crushing* it, roll a 6 early and let the thermal shock surprise them.
- **Aftermath hook.** The goblins were trying to keep the newt frozen so they could *sell* "captured fire" to a merchant in the next town. The melted ice leaves a glowing, still-warm patch on the cave floor. A local wizard might pay a small sum for a vial of the meltwater. This gives the encounter a reason to exist in the campaign.

---

*Total expected combat time: 3–5 rounds. The encounter should feel like a short, escalating set piece rather than a grind.*

Looking at this problem, I need to find positive integers with non-zero digits whose digit product has exactly 24 trailing zeros.

## Setting Up the Constraints

A trailing zero requires a factor of 10 = 2 × 5. Since only digit **5** contributes a factor of 5, and digits **2, 4, 6, 8** contribute factors of 2 (giving 1, 2, 1, 3 twos respectively):

- **v₅(product) ≥ 24** → at least **24 digits must be 5**
- **v₂(product) ≥ 24** → the remaining digits must supply at least 24 factors of 2

## Finding the Minimum Digit Count

With 24 fives, the remaining digits must supply ≥ 24 twos. Since the maximum per digit is 3 (digit 8), I need at least ⌈24/3⌉ = **8 additional digits**, all of which must be **8s** (since 7×3 = 21 < 24).

**Minimum: 32 digits = 24 fives + 8 eights.** No 31-digit solution exists.

## Counting to the 30th Smallest

All 32-digit fruity numbers are arrangements of 24 fives and 8 eights. In increasing order (lex order with 5 < 8), I build the 30th sequence digit by digit, tracking **(positions remaining, 5s left, 8s left, rank)**:

| Digit | State | If 5: C(n,k) | Decision |

**Классика на кухне**

В три часа ночи, когда чай давно остыл, а в голове всё ещё крутился последний абзац «Преступления и наказания», я открыл вкладку, которую, казалось, открыл ещё в 2009-м. Классика.ру. Ни логина, ни регистрации, ни «введите код из СМС». Просто список. Просто текст. Просто Достоевский, который смотрит на тебя с экрана и говорит: «Сядь, я тут надолго».

Я помню, как в юности мы с одногруппником спорили, кто из нас «настоящий читатель». Он хвастался коробкой из сорока томов, стоящей на балконе. Я открыл классику.ру на телефоне в метро. Спор не был окончен, но и не возобновлялся. Мы просто разошлись по разным вагонам.

Сайт устроен так, как устроена старая городская библиотека: полки, корешки, тихий гул. Только вместо библиотекаря, которая хмурилась на шум, здесь — курсор, который мигает с терпением, каким не обладал ни один живой человек. Ты можешь открыть Гоголя в четыре утра, в два, в полпервого. Гоголь не спросит, почему ты не спим. Гоголю всё равно. Гоголь просто будет.

Единственный недостаток — иногда текст обрывается. Не на середине фразы, нет. На середине *мысли*. И ты сидишь, как человек, которому в разгар рассказа кто-то сказал: «Ладно, продолжение в следующем номере». А следующего номера нет. Есть только тьма монитора и твой собственный пульс.

Я закрываю вкладку. Ставлю чайник. Через сорок минут снова открою.

Гоголь будет.

using namespace std;

int main() {

    scanf("%d", &t);
    while (t--) {
        int n, k;
        scanf("%d %d", &n, &k);
        vector<long long> a(n + 1);
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) scanf("%lld", &a[i]);
        
        int m = n % k;
        if (m == 0) m = k;
        int need = (m + 2) / 2;
        int T_max = (n - m) / k;
        
        // Binary search on answer
        long long lo = 1, hi = 1e9 + 1;
        while (lo < hi) {
            long long mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
            
            // Build GoodSets
            vector<vector<int>> good(m + 1);
            for (int p = 1; p <= n; p++) {
                int j = (p - 1) % k + 1;
                if (j <= m && a[p] >= mid) {
                    int tv = (p - j) / k;
                    good[j].push_back(tv);
                }
            }
            
            // Backward greedy
            int count_good = 0;
            int t_next = T_max; // t_{m+1}
            for (int j = m; j >= 1; j--) {
                // Find largest t in good[j] that is <= t_next
                auto &g = good[j];
                if (!g.empty()) {
                    auto it = upper_bound(g.begin(), g.end(), t_next);
                    if (it != g.begin()) {
                        --it;
                        count_good++;

                    }
                    // else: no good value <= t_next, t_j = t_next (not good)
                }
                // else: no good values at all, t_j = t_next (not good)
            }
            
            if (count_good >= need) {
                lo = mid + 1;
            } else {
                hi = mid;
            }

}

# The Little Light in the Duct

The relay station *Perseverance* hung in the void between Proxima and Tau Ceti like a brass thimble on a black thread, and Maren Okafor had been tightening its bolts for eleven years.

Eleven years of recycled air that tasted faintly of copper. Eleven years of the same three songs on loop because the station's music library had corrupted in '39 and no one had bothered to re-download it. Eleven years of talking to the maintenance drones, which answered in monotone and never once said *you too, Maren.*

So when she pried open vent panel 7-C during her Tuesday inspection and found a creature no bigger than a thumb, glowing soft violet in the dark, she screamed.

Not in fear. In *surprise.* The kind of surprise that cracks you open like a geode.

It was a wobbly, translucent thing with six stubby legs and two large eyes that blinked at her in slow, sleepy rhythm. Its body pulsed with that violet light, like a tiny lantern made of jelly. It was wedged between two cooling pipes, one leg splayed out at an odd angle, and it made a sound like a music box winding down.

*Whirrrr. Whirrrr.*

"Oh, you poor little—" Maren knelt, her knees cracking, and gently coaxed it free with a pair of tweezers. It landed on her palm and immediately curled into a tight, glowing ball. Warm. Like holding a small, living ember.

She named it Pip.

For three days, Maren forgot to eat. She forgot to log her maintenance reports. She sat in her narrow bunk with Pip perched on her wrist, watching it uncurl, stretch its six legs, and explore the surface of her skin with a tiny exploratory *tick-tick-tick* of its feet. It followed the blue veins under her skin the way a child follows a river on a map.

On the fourth day, she brought it a drop of nutrient gel from the galley. Pip's light shifted from violet to a bright, excited *gold.* It made a sound like a bell being struck underwater, and its legs did a little spin.

Maren laughed. Actually laughed. The sound startled her so much she laughed again.

She told the drones about Pip. They said, "Acknowledged. No record of extraterrestrial fauna in this sector." She said, "Well, *this* is a record of extraterrestrial fauna in this sector," and they said, "Understood," in that flat, unbothered way, and went back to polishing the hull.

But Maren didn't care. She built Pip a little habitat from a spare oxygen canister and a patch of moss from the hydroponics bay. She talked to it about nothing. About the copper taste of the air. About the three songs. About how the stars out the viewport looked like someone had shaken a salt shaker over black velvet.

Pip listened. Its light pulsed in time with her voice, like a heartbeat learning a new rhythm.

On the ninth day, Pip's glow changed. The gold deepened, then split, then *multiplied.* Dozens of tiny points of light bloomed across its body, and it began to hum—a low, resonant chord that Maren felt in her molars, in her sternum, in the soles of her feet.

The viewport in her bunk lit up. Not with stars. With *more* light. A constellation of violet-gold points, thousands of them, sliding into view from behind the curve of a gas giant. A fleet. A *chorus.* Each one pulsing in the same slow, sleepy rhythm.

And then the hum changed. It became a word. A *name.* It was Maren's name, spoken in a frequency that had no business being a word, and it meant *here. Found. Seen. Thank you for the small warm place.*

Pip leapt from her palm and floated toward the viewport, its light blazing, and the fleet answered. A thousand tiny lights turned toward her. Toward *her.* The little brass thimble in the dark. The woman who had found a lost thing in a vent and said, *oh, you poor little—*

The song that filled the station was not one of the three corrupted tracks. It was new. It was *theirs.* And it was the most beautiful sound Maren had ever heard, and it was not monotone.

She pressed her hand to the glass. The nearest light in the fleet pulsed once, warm and gold.

*You too, Maren.*

She smiled, and for the first time in eleven years, the recycled air didn't taste like copper.

It tasted like *beginning.*
