# The Night Shift at Freddy Fazbear's

## Part One: The Advertisement

The rain had been falling on the small, perpetually damp town of Greendale for three consecutive days. It drummed against the single-pane window of the cramped flat on the fourth floor of 12 Wetherby Road, a sound so constant that Mr. Bean had long since stopped hearing it. He sat in his armchair—the good one, the one with the slightly torn left armrest that he'd been meaning to repair for approximately six years—wearing his brown corduroy jacket, white shirt with the top button undone, and his signature bow tie, which was currently knotted at a jaunty, asymmetrical angle.

On the television, a nature documentary about penguins was playing. Bean watched with the rapt, slightly squinted attention of a man observing a particularly complex puzzle. A penguin slipped on ice. Bean's left eyebrow rose. He mimed the slip with his hand, a small, fluid gesture, and then returned his attention to the screen.

The doorbell rang.

Bean did not move. The doorbell rang again. And again. And again. A sustained, mechanical buzzing that seemed to vibrate the very fillings in his teeth. Bean's jaw tightened. He turned off the television with a sharp click of the remote, stood, and padded across the lino floor in his socks, his expression one of profound, existential irritation.

He opened the door.

Standing on the step, drenched, holding a soggy cardboard box, was a young woman in a yellow raincoat. She was perhaps twenty-two, with a clipboard tucked under one arm and a look of desperate, caffeinated urgency in her wide brown eyes.

"Mr. Bean?" she asked, shaking rain from her hair. "I'm from the Greendale Employment Bureau. I have a position for you."

Bean stared at her. He tilted his head. He looked past her shoulder, as if expecting a second person to emerge from the grey afternoon. Then he looked back at her. He pointed a single finger at himself.

"Yes, *me*," he seemed to say, with the particular emphasis on the word that suggested he was mildly offended that anyone might be confusing him with someone else.

The woman, whose name was Karen, thrust the clipboard forward. "You applied for the position at Freddy Fazbear's Family Diner on Route 9? The night shift? Security guard?"

Bean's eyes went wide. He blinked. Once. Twice. A slow, dawning smile spread across his face—the kind of smile that, in a different man, might have been called a grin. In Bean, it was more like a tectonic plate shifting. He grabbed the clipboard, scanned it with a speed that suggested he was not actually reading the words but rather *feeling* the shape of the information with his fingertips.

"Full room and board," he read aloud, in a voice so soft and precise it was almost a whisper. "Two thousand pounds a month. No experience necessary." He looked up at Karen. He pointed at the word *security*. He pointed at himself. He made a small, authoritative gesture with his hand, as if conducting an invisible orchestra.

He pointed at the word *night*. He made a "shhh" gesture with his finger to his lips.

Karen blinked. "Do you... do you want the job?"

Bean did not answer. Instead, he reached into his jacket pocket, produced a small, slightly deflated rubber rabbit—Mr. Bunny—and held it up to the light. He examined it. He gave it a gentle squeeze. Then he turned back to Karen, still holding Mr. Bunny, and gave a single, slow nod.

Karen sighed, pulled a pen from her hair, and scribbled something on the bottom of the clipboard. "Sign here. And here. And initial here. And here. And here. And *here*."

Bean signed each line with the careful, looping precision of a man signing a contract for the purchase of a very expensive and very specific brand of cheese. He initialled each line with a tiny, perfect *B*.

"Your first shift starts tonight. Ten o'clock. The back entrance on the loading dock. You'll be in the office on the east side of the dining area. There's a manual in the drawer. Don't open the doors after midnight. And for the love of God, *do not let the animatronics into the office.*"

Bean pocketed Mr. Bunny. He nodded. He pointed at Karen. He pointed at the sky. He made a small, "good luck" gesture with his hand.

Karen left. Bean closed the door. He stood in the hallway for a long moment, listening to the rain. Then he walked to the kitchenette, opened the cupboard, and retrieved a small, tin of beans—*his* beans, the ones he'd been saving for a special occasion. He opened the tin. He ate three beans, one at a time, with the solemnity of a man performing a small ritual.

He was going to Freddy Fazbear's.

---

## Part Two: The Arrival

The bus to Route 9 took forty-seven minutes. Bean sat in the back, by the window, his knees pressed against the seat in front of him. He held Mr. Bunny in his lap and talked to him in a series of low, grumbling murmurs that no one else could quite make out. He was explaining, he felt, the situation. The job. The animatronics. He used his hands to illustrate the size of the animatronics, spreading them wide, then bringing them together. Mr. Bunny's button eyes stared forward, unblinking.

The bus lurched. Bean's head bounced. He caught himself with a hand on the window, his expression one of mild indignation. He looked at the elderly woman in the seat ahead of him, who was knitting a scarf. She glanced back. Bean gave her a small, apologetic nod and returned to his explanation.

When the bus finally groaned to a halt outside Freddy Fazbear's Family Diner, the building was a monument to 1980s excess. Neon signs buzzed and flickered: a giant yellow "F" for Freddy, a pink "C" for Chica, a purple "B" for Bonnie. The windows were dark. The parking lot was empty save for a single, rusted delivery truck and a shopping cart that had been blown by the wind into a decorative planter. The smell of old grease and artificial strawberry hit Bean the moment he stepped off the bus. He wrinkled his nose. He pulled his jacket collar up.

He found the back entrance: a steel door with a peephole and a sign that read **EMPLOYEES ONLY – NO ANIMATRONIC REPAIRS IN PROGRESS**. He knocked. No answer. He knocked again. He pressed his eye to the peephole. Nothing. He knocked a third time, harder, and then, when still no one appeared, he simply pushed the door open. It was unlocked.

The interior of the loading dock was a cathedral of shadows. Cardboard boxes stacked to the ceiling. The smell of machine oil and old carpet. A single fluorescent tube flickered overhead, casting everything in a sickly, intermittent glow. Bean's shadow stretched and contracted with each flicker.

"Hello?" he called. His voice was small in the vast, empty space. "Is anyone—"

A door at the far end of the dock swung open, and a man appeared. He was tall, thin, with a receding hairline and a mustache that looked like it had been drawn on with a shaky hand. He wore a grease-stained apron over a polo shirt, and his eyes had the particular hollow, exhausted look of a man who had not slept properly in approximately three years.

This was Henry. Or rather, this was the night supervisor, whose name tag read **GARY – NIGHT SUPERVISOR – DON'T ASK ABOUT THE ANIMATRONICS**.

"You're the new security guard," Gary said. It was not a question.

Bean nodded. He held up Mr. Bunny. "This is Mr. Bunny. He is here for support."

Gary stared at the rubber rabbit. He stared at Bean. He stared at the rabbit again. "Right. Well. Come on. I'll give you the tour. And before you ask—yes, they are real. No, I don't know what they are. No, I will not explain. Yes, you will be in that office for eight hours. No, you cannot leave. Yes, the cameras are there for a reason. No, I will not elaborate."

He turned and walked. Bean followed, his socks squeaking on the concrete floor.

---

## Part Three: The Tour

The dining area of Freddy Fazbear's was a vast, circular room with a stage at the far end. Tables and chairs, all in primary colors, were arranged in a pattern that suggested they had been set up by someone who had been drinking. The carpet was a deep, institutional red, and it had the particular matted, lifeless quality of a carpet that had been walked on by thousands of small, sticky feet over many years. The air smelled of old pizza, artificial strawberry, and something else—something metallic and faintly sweet, like old pennies left in a glass of water.

On the stage, in the shadows, stood four figures.

Bean stopped walking.

He looked up.

Freddy Fazbear was the tallest—a bear, roughly seven feet, in a brown suit with a top hat and a red bow tie. He stood at the center of the stage, his head tilted at an angle that suggested he was listening to something no one else could hear. His eyes were black, glassy, and utterly still. His mouth was a wide, painted smile that did not reach those eyes.

To Freddy's left stood Bonnie, a purple rabbit in a green shirt, his long ears drooping at slightly different angles. To Freddy's right stood Chica, a yellow chicken in a green dress, a bib around her neck that read **LET'S EAT!!!** in red letters. And behind them, slightly to the side, was Foxy, a red fox in a torn eye patch and a tattered pirate coat, standing in a curtained-off section of the stage that was half in shadow.

Bean stood very still. He looked at Freddy. Freddy did not move. Bean looked at Bonnie. Bonnie did not move. Bean looked at Chica. Chica did not move. Bean looked at Foxy. Foxy did not move.

He exhaled. He pointed at Freddy. He pointed at himself. He made a small, "hello" gesture.

Nothing happened.

"Right," Gary said, appearing at Bean's elbow. He had been standing there, Bean realized, for approximately ninety seconds. Bean had not noticed. "They're powered down for the day. They only activate at night. Ten o'clock to six a.m. That's your shift. You sit in the office, you watch the cameras, you make sure none of them get in. That's the job."

"And if they do get in?" Bean asked.

Gary's mustache twitched. "Then you have a problem."

He led Bean through the dining area, past a row of vending machines that hummed and flickered with a faint, electric blue light, past a bathroom that was locked with a padlock and a sign that read **DO NOT ENTER – BIOHAZARD**, and into a corridor. The corridor was narrow, the walls lined with a faded mural of cartoon stars and moons. The floor was a different color of carpet—blue, this time, and it was *worse*. Bean stepped over a small puddle of something dark and viscous without looking at it.

At the end of the corridor was the office.

It was a small, rectangular room, perhaps ten feet by twelve. A desk. A chair. A computer monitor with a grid of camera feeds. Two doors—one to the left, one to the right—each with a small window and a button above it that could close a metal security shutter. A fan on the desk, its blades slightly bent. A phone, its cord coiled like a sleeping snake. A small, framed picture of a man in a bear suit, smiling, pinned to the wall above the desk. The man's eyes in the photograph seemed to follow you.

"This is where you sit," Gary said. "Eight hours. You watch the cameras. You manage the power. You close the doors if you hear them. You do *not* open the doors. You do *not* leave the office. You do *not* go into the dining area after ten. You do *not* go into the back corridors. You do *not*—"

"I understand," Bean said.

Gary looked at him. "Do you?"

Bean pointed at the desk. He pointed at the chair. He pointed at the camera monitor. He pointed at the two doors. He made a series of small, precise gestures: *sit, watch, button, close, repeat*. He gave a thumbs-up.

Gary stared at him for a long moment. Then he nodded. "Right. Well. The manual is in the drawer. I'd read it. I'd actually read it. The whole thing. Not just skim it."

He left. The corridor door closed. The lock clicked.

Bean was alone.

He sat in the chair. He placed Mr. Bunny on the desk, propped up against the monitor so the rubber rabbit could see the camera feeds. He adjusted his bow tie. He straightened his jacket. He looked at the two doors. He looked at the monitor. He looked at the fan, which was ticking and wobbling.

He reached into his jacket pocket and produced a small, silver watch. He set it on the desk. 9:47 PM. Thirteen minutes to ten.

He leaned back. He closed his eyes. He breathed.

---

## Part Four: Ten O'Clock

At 9:58, the lights in the dining area flickered.

Bean opened his eyes. He looked at the monitor. The camera feeds showed the dining area, the stage, the corridors, the kitchen, the restrooms. All empty. All still.

At 9:59, the lights flickered again.

At 10:00, a sound came from the dining area. A deep, mechanical *clunk*, like a large joint being forced into alignment. Then another. Then a series of them, a rhythmic, grinding, *whirring* sound, like a very large, very old clock being wound.

Bean leaned forward. He pressed his eye to the left door's window.

Nothing.

He pressed his eye to the right door's window.

Nothing.

He turned back to the monitor. The camera in the dining area showed the stage. The four figures were still. But—

He squinted.

Freddy's head had moved. Just a fraction. Just enough that the angle of the top hat was different. Just enough that the painted smile seemed, in the blue glow of the monitor, to be a *millimeter* wider.

Bean blinked. He looked again. The head was still. The angle was the same.

He exhaled. He picked up Mr. Bunny and gave him a squeeze. "It's fine," he murmured. "It's just... settling. Like a new sofa. You know. The springs. They need to... *adjust*."

He put Mr. Bunny back. He leaned back. He closed his eyes.

At 10:14, the fan on the desk made a sound. Not the usual ticking and wobbling. A *thud*. A small, solid, *impact* sound, as if something had landed on the desk.

Bean opened his eyes.

On the desk, to the left of Mr. Bunny, was a single, small, yellow feather.

He stared at it. He reached out with one finger and touched it. It was soft. It was warm. It was *real*.

He looked at the monitor. Camera 1A: Dining Area. The stage was empty. All four figures were gone.

His blood went cold.

He looked at the left door. The window was dark. He could see, just barely, in the blue glow from the corridor, the shape of a long, purple form standing in the hallway.

Bonnie.

Bean did not scream. Bean did not panic. Bean did something far more unsettling.

He stood up. He walked to the left door. He pressed his eye to the window. Bonnie was there, his long ears drooping, his black eyes staring directly at the glass. His painted mouth was open. His jaw was *moving*. He was *singing*. A low, mechanical, grinding sound, like a music box with a broken spring, but shaped into something that might, in a generous interpretation, have been a melody.

Bean watched. He tilted his head. He listened.

Then, with the calm, methodical precision of a man who has spent his entire life solving problems through physical manipulation of objects, he reached up and pressed the button above the left door.

The metal shutter slammed down. *CLANG.*

Bonnie's singing stopped.

On the other side of the door, there was a sound. A *knocking*. Three slow, heavy knocks. *Thud. Thud. Thud.* Then silence.

Bean stood very still. He listened. The knocking did not come again.

He turned back to the monitor. The power meter in the corner of the screen read **87%**. The shutter had used 13%.

He sat back down. He picked up Mr. Bunny. He held the rabbit up to the monitor, as if introducing him to the camera feeds. "Hello, Mr. Bunny. We are being... *visited*."

---

## Part Five: The First Hour

The next forty minutes were a study in controlled, methodical tension.

Bean sat in the chair, his back straight, his hands on the desk, his eyes moving from camera to camera with the slow, deliberate focus of a man watching a very long, very boring piece of television. He did not fidget. He did not pace. He did not check the doors every thirty seconds. He watched the cameras. He watched the power meter. He watched the clock on the desk.

At 10:42, the camera in the West Hall (2A) showed a movement. A shadow. A shape. The long, purple silhouette of Bonnie, moving slowly down the corridor.

Bean watched. He did not press the button. He watched.

Bonnie reached the end of the West Hall. He stopped. He stood there, in the blue glow of the monitor, his head tilted. He was *looking* at the camera. At the office. At *Bean*.

Bean looked back.

He pointed at the camera. He pointed at himself. He made a small, "you there?" gesture.

On the monitor, Bonnie's head tilted the other way.

Bean frowned. He pointed at the left door. He made a "go away" gesture, a small, firm wave of his hand.

On the monitor, Bonnie's jaw moved. The grinding, music-box sound came through the speaker in the office, tinny and distorted. It was not singing. It was *talking*. Or trying to. The words were unrecognizable, a series of mechanical clicks and groans that might, in a very generous interpretation, have been a sentence.

Bean listened. He tilted his head. He pointed at the speaker. He made a "what?" gesture.

The sound stopped.

On the monitor, Bonnie turned and walked back down the West Hall. He disappeared around the corner.

Bean exhaled. He picked up Mr. Bunny. He held the rabbit up to the camera. "You see, Mr. Bunny? He is *shy*. Like a penguin. You remember the penguin? The one who slipped on the ice? He is like that. He walks up to you, and then he *slips*."

He put Mr. Bunny down. He leaned back. He closed his eyes.

At 10:58, the power meter read **79%**.

---

## Part Six: Chica

At 11:23, Bean was examining the vending machines on Camera 4 (the side corridor near the kitchen) when he heard a sound from the dining area.

A *clatter*. Like a plate being set down on a table. Then another. Then a series of them, a rapid, clattering, *clinking* sound, as if someone were setting a table for a very large, very hungry dinner.

Bean turned to the dining area camera. The stage was empty. But in the dining area, at table seven, a figure was moving. Chica. She was *sitting down*. She had lowered her large, yellow body into a child's chair, and the chair was *groaning* under her weight. She was holding a plate. She was *eating*.

Bean watched. He leaned forward. He pressed his eye closer to the monitor.

Chica was eating a slice of pizza. She was eating it with her hands. She was eating it *fast*. The pizza was disappearing into her painted mouth in large, mechanical bites. Her jaw moved up and down. Her bib—**LET'S EAT!!!**—was stained with something red.

Bean's stomach did a small, involuntary flip. He looked away. He looked back.

Chica was now eating a *second* pizza. She had pulled it from the air. There was no box. No wrapper. It simply *appeared* in her hands, and she ate it.

Bean pointed at the monitor. He pointed at himself. He made a "I am not hungry" gesture.

On the monitor, Chica stopped eating. She turned her head. She looked at the camera. At the office. At *Bean*.

Her painted eyes were wide. Her mouth was open. A piece of pizza was hanging from her jaw.

Bean pointed at the pizza. He made a "that's not... *hygienic*..." gesture.

Chica's jaw moved. The grinding, music-box sound came through the speaker. This time, it was more rhythmic. More *insistent*. It sounded like a question.

Bean frowned. He pointed at the left door. He pointed at the right door. He made a "you can come in, but you must use the *table* and the *chair* and you must *wipe your hands*" gesture. He produced, from his jacket pocket, a small, folded napkin. He held it up to the monitor.

On the monitor, Chica's head tilted. She looked at the napkin. She looked at the camera. She *smiled*. Or rather, her painted mouth widened by a fraction of a millimeter.

Then she stood up. The chair *cracked*. She walked toward the office door.

Bean's eyes widened. He looked at the left door. He looked at the right door. He looked at the monitor. Chica was walking toward the *right* door.

He lunged for the button.

He pressed it.

The shutter slammed down. *CLANG.*

On the other side, a sound. Not a knock this time. A *thud*. A heavy, full-body *thud*, as if Chica had pressed her entire chest against the metal door. Then a *scrape*, as if she were dragging her feet. Then silence.

Bean sat back down. His hands were shaking. He put them flat on the desk. He breathed in. He breathed out. He picked up Mr. Bunny. He held the rabbit in both hands and squeezed.

"It's fine," he murmured. "It's just... a chicken. A big chicken. She is *hungry*. You know how it is. You are hungry, and you see a pizza, and you think, 'I shall eat the pizza.' It is *natural*. It is *understandable*."

He put Mr. Bunny down. He looked at the power meter. **64%**.

---

## Part Seven: The Manual

At 11:51, Bean opened the drawer.

The manual was a thick, water-stained booklet, its cover peeling. The title page read: **FREDDY FAZBEAR'S FAMILY DINER – ANIMATRONIC MANAGEMENT HANDBOOK – 3rd EDITION (REVISED 1987) – FOR EMPLOYEE USE ONLY – DO NOT REMOVE FROM PREMISES**.

Bean opened it. The first page was a diagram of the building, with the animatronics' patrol routes marked in red. The second page was a list of the animatronics' behaviors, their schedules, their *preferences*.

Bean read. He read slowly, carefully, his finger tracing each line. He read the section on Freddy: *Freddy is the most predictable. He moves slowly. He prefers the stage and the dining area. He will not enter the office unless directly confronted. He is, in most cases, docile.*

He read the section on Bonnie: *Bonnie is the most aggressive. He moves quickly. He prefers the West Hall and the Backstage. He will attempt to enter the office if he senses the guard is distracted. He is drawn to the sound of music. He is, in most cases, irritable.*

He read the section on Chica: *Chica is the most erratic. She moves unpredictably. She prefers the dining area and the kitchen. She will attempt to enter the office if she senses food. She is drawn to the smell of grease. She is, in most cases, ravenous.*

He read the section on Foxy: *Foxy is the most dangerous. He moves in a straight line. He prefers the Pirate Cove and the East Hall. He will attempt to enter the office if the curtain is opened. He is drawn to the sound of running. He is, in most cases,* ***unpredictable.***

Bean closed the manual. He looked at the monitor. He looked at the two doors. He looked at Mr. Bunny.

"Right," he said. "We have a *plan*."

He stood up. He walked to the left door. He opened it a crack—just enough to see the corridor. The West Hall was empty. The blue glow from the emergency lights was steady. He closed the door.

He walked to the right door. He opened it a crack. The East Hall was empty. The blue glow was steady. He closed the door.

He sat back down. He opened the manual again. He read the section on power management. *The power is used by the doors, the lights, and the cameras. If the power reaches 0%, the lights go out, the doors open, and the animatronics will enter the office. The animatronics will then... perform.*

He read the word *perform* three times.

He closed the manual. He put it in the drawer. He locked the drawer. He put the key in his pocket.

He looked at the clock. 11:58 PM.

Four hours to go.

---

## Part Eight: Foxy

At 12:34 AM, the camera in the Pirate Cove (5A) showed a movement.

The curtain was drawn. Behind it, in the dark, a shape was shifting. A red shape. A *torn* red shape.

Bean watched. He leaned forward. He pressed his eye to the monitor.

The curtain twitched.

Bean's hand went to the camera switch. He could turn off the camera. The manual said that if you turned off the camera for too long, Foxy would move. If you turned it back on, you could see how far he'd gotten. Stage 1: behind the curtain. Stage 2: curtain half-open. Stage 3: curtain fully open. Stage 4: Foxy is in the East Hall. Stage 5: Foxy is at the East Hall door.

Bean turned off Camera 5A.

He waited.

Ten seconds. Twenty. Thirty.

He turned it back on.

The curtain was half-open. Stage 2.

He turned it off again.

Ten seconds. Twenty. Thirty.

He turned it back on.

The curtain was fully open. Stage 3. And behind it, in the dark, two yellow eyes were glowing. Foxy was *looking* at the camera.

Bean turned it off.

He waited. He counted to sixty in his head. He counted to sixty again.

He turned it back on.

The Pirate Cove was empty. The curtain was fully open. Foxy was gone.

Bean looked at Camera 6A: East Hall.

Foxy was in the East Hall. He was *running*. His long, red body was a blur, his torn coat flapping, his eye patch askew. He was running *toward the office*.

Bean's hand went to the right door button.

He pressed it.

The shutter slammed down. *CLANG.*

On the other side, a sound. A *screech*. A high, metallic, *shrieking* sound, like a nail dragged across a chalkboard, amplified a thousand times. Then a *crash*. A heavy, full-body *crash*, as if Foxy had thrown himself against the metal door. Then a *scrape*. Then a *thud*. Then silence.

Bean sat back down. His hands were not shaking this time. They were *clenched*. His knuckles were white.

He looked at the power meter. **51%**.

He looked at the clock. 12:37 AM.

Three and a half hours to go.

He picked up Mr. Bunny. He held the rabbit up to the monitor. "He is *running*, Mr. Bunny. He is running very *fast*. Like a penguin on ice. But the penguin slips. This one does not slip. This one *runs*."

He put Mr. Bunny down. He leaned back. He closed his eyes.

At 12:41, the screeching came again. From the right door. From *inside* the door. As if Foxy were still there, still pressing, still *screeching*.

Bean opened his eyes. He looked at the right door. The metal shutter was dented. A small, crescent-shaped dent, as if something with a very sharp, very pointed claw had pressed against it.

He stared at the dent.

He reached into his jacket pocket. He produced a small, silver coin. He held it up to the light. He examined it. He put it back in his pocket.

He looked at the door. He pointed at it. He made a "you will not get in" gesture.

The screeching stopped.

## Part Nine: The Vending Machine

At 1:15 AM, Bean was watching Camera 4 (the side corridor near the kitchen) when he noticed something.

The vending machine. The one on the left. The one with the blue light. The one that hummed.

It was *moving*.

Not much. Just a small, slow, lateral shift. An inch. Two inches. The machine was *walking*. Its four small wheels were turning. It was moving toward the office door.

Bean stared. He blinked. He looked again. The machine was still moving. Slowly. Deliberately. Its blue light pulsed.

He looked at the other vending machines. They were still. Only the left one was moving.

He looked at the monitor. Camera 4 showed the machine from the side. It was in the corridor, perhaps twenty feet from the office door. It was moving toward him.

Bean stood up. He walked to the left door. He opened it a crack.

The corridor was empty. The vending machine was not there.

He closed the door. He looked at the monitor. Camera 4. The machine was still in the corridor. Still moving.

He looked at Camera 3: the back corridor. The machine was not there.

He looked at Camera 2A: the West Hall. The machine was not there.

He looked at Camera 1A: the dining area.

The machine was in the dining area. It had *walked* around the building. It was now at table three, in the center of the dining room. Its blue light pulsed. Its wheels were still.

Bean stared at the monitor. He pointed at the machine. He made a "how?" gesture.

On the monitor, the machine's display flickered. The words **OUT OF ORDER** changed to **OUT OF BEANS**.

Bean's eyes went wide.

He looked at the machine. He looked at the monitor. He looked at the machine.

He stood up. He walked to the left door. He opened it.

The corridor was empty. The blue glow was steady. He stepped out.

The dining area was vast and dark. The stage was empty. The tables were empty. The air smelled of old grease and artificial strawberry. And there, at table three, was the vending machine. Its blue light pulsed. Its display read **OUT OF BEANS**.

Bean walked toward it. His socks squeaked on the carpet. He reached the machine. He looked up at it. It was taller than him. Its blue light washed over his face.

He reached into his jacket pocket. He produced a small, silver coin. He held it up. He looked at the machine. He looked at the coin. He looked at the machine.

He inserted the coin.

The machine *shuddered*. Its wheels turned. It *leaned* toward him, as if in anticipation.

The display changed. **OUT OF BEANS** became **INSERT COIN**. Then **PROCESSING**. Then **ERROR**. Then **OUT OF BEANS**.

Bean frowned. He reached into his pocket. He produced a second coin. He inserted it.

**ERROR**. **OUT OF BEANS**.

He produced a third coin. He inserted it.

The machine *shuddered* again. Its blue light pulsed faster. Its display flickered. And then, from the dispensing slot at the bottom, a small, tin of beans rolled out.

Bean caught it. He held it up. He examined it. He opened it. He ate one bean. He closed it. He put it in his pocket.

He turned to leave.

And he saw Freddy.

Freddy was standing at the edge of the stage. Seven feet tall. His top hat was slightly askew. His bow tie was crooked. His black, glassy eyes were fixed on Bean. His painted smile was wide.

They stared at each other.

Bean raised the tin of beans. He held it up. He pointed at the tin. He pointed at Freddy. He made a "you want some?" gesture.

Freddy did not move.

Bean took a step back. Freddy did not move. He took another step. Freddy did not move. He turned. He walked back to the office. He entered. He closed the door.

He sat down. He put the tin of beans on the desk. He picked up Mr. Bunny. He held the rabbit up to the tin. "A *gift*, Mr. Bunny. For the bear. A small *gift*."

He looked at the monitor. Camera 1A. The stage was empty. Freddy was gone.

He looked at the power meter. **43%**.

## Part Ten: The Phone

At 2:07 AM, the phone rang.

Bean looked at it. The cord was coiled like a sleeping snake. The receiver was black, its surface sticky with something he chose not to identify. The phone rang. And rang. And rang.

He picked it up. He held it to his ear.

A voice. A man's voice. Calm. Measured. Slightly distorted, as if it were coming from a great distance.

"Hello? Is this the new guard?"

Bean held the phone. He nodded. He pointed at himself.

"Right. Well. Listen. I'm calling from the front office. The *real* front office. The one on the other side of the building. You can't see it from where you are. I'm calling to let you know that the animatronics are *not* what you think they are. They are not machines. They are not robots. They are *people*. Or they were. The suits... the suits are *housed* in something. Something that *remembers*. Something that *wants*."

Bean held the phone. He tilted his head. He pointed at the receiver. He made a "who?" gesture.

"You don't need to know who I am. You just need to know that if you hear a *music box*, do not follow it. If you see a *shadow* that moves when you're not looking, do not look at it. If you hear *breathing* in the walls, do not investigate. And if you see a *child* in the dining area, do not speak to them. Do not *acknowledge* them. Just... walk past."

Bean held the phone. He looked at the monitor. Camera 1A. The dining area was empty. No child. No shadow. No music box.

He looked back at the phone. He pointed at the receiver. He made a "thank you" gesture.

The voice said, "You're welcome. And... good luck. You're going to need it. It's only two in the morning."

The line went dead.

Bean put the phone down. He sat very still. He looked at the monitor. He looked at the doors. He looked at Mr. Bunny.

"It's *people*," he murmured. "They are *people* in the suits. Like... like a very large, very expensive *costume*. You know. Like a penguin in a tuxedo. A very *angry* penguin in a tuxedo."

He put Mr. Bunny down. He leaned back. He closed his eyes.

At 2:11, he heard it.

A music box. Faint. Distant. Coming from the West Hall. A small, tinkling melody, like a child's toy, but *wrong*. The notes were slightly flat. The rhythm was slightly off. And it was *getting closer*.

Bean opened his eyes. He did not look at the left door. He did not look at the monitor. He sat very still. He breathed. He waited.

The music box got closer. Closer. Closer.

It stopped.

Silence.

Bean exhaled. He looked at the left door. The window was dark. The metal shutter was closed.

He looked at the power meter. **38%**.

## Part Eleven: The Shadow

At 2:43 AM, Bean was watching Camera 2A (West Hall) when he saw it.

A shadow. On the wall. At the far end of the corridor. A tall, thin shadow, with long ears and a wide, flat head. It was *moving*. Not walking. *Sliding*. Like a shadow cast by a very large, very slow object moving across a very bright light.

Bean watched. He did not look away. He did not blink.

The shadow moved. It slid down the corridor, toward the office. It was *fast*. Faster than Bonnie should have been able to move. Faster than any animatronic should have been able to move.

Bean's hand went to the left door button.

He did not press it.

He watched.

The shadow reached the end of the corridor. It stopped. It *turned*. The shadow's head tilted, as if it were looking at the camera. At the office. At *Bean*.

And then it *dissolved*. Like smoke. Like a shadow being pulled back into the dark. It was gone.

Bean sat very still. He breathed in. He breathed out. He looked at the left door. The window was dark. The metal shutter was closed.

He looked at the monitor. Camera 2A. The West Hall was empty. No shadow. No Bonnie. No movement.

He looked at the power meter. **34%**.

He picked up Mr. Bunny. He held the rabbit in both hands. He squeezed. He squeezed *hard*.

"It's fine," he murmured. "It's just a *shadow*. You know how it is. You are in a dark room, and you see a shadow, and you think, 'That is a monster.' But it is just... a *shadow*. A shadow of a coat on a hook. A shadow of a *penguin*. A shadow of a *penguin in a tuxedo*."

He put Mr. Bunny down. He leaned back. He closed his eyes.

At 2:47, the breathing started.

In the walls. A low, wet, *rhythmic* sound. Like a large animal breathing in its sleep. In and out. In and out. It was coming from *everywhere*. From the walls. From the floor. From the ceiling. From the desk. From the chair. From *inside the monitor*.

Bean opened his eyes. He did not investigate. He did not look at the walls. He sat very still. He breathed. He waited.

The breathing stopped.

He exhaled. He looked at the power meter. **31%**.

## Part Twelve: The Child

At 3:15 AM, Bean was watching Camera 1A (Dining Area) when he saw the child.

A small figure. A boy, perhaps seven or eight. Wearing a yellow shirt and blue shorts. He was standing at table five, in the center of the dining room. He was *holding a balloon*. A red balloon. He was looking at the camera. At the office. At *Bean*.

Bean stared.

The child looked at the camera. He smiled. He raised the balloon. He pointed it at the camera.

Bean did not speak. He did not acknowledge. He looked away. He switched to Camera 2A.

He switched back to Camera 1A.

The child was still there. Still smiling. Still holding the balloon. But he was *closer*. He was at table three now. He had moved. He had *walked*.

Bean looked away. He switched to Camera 3.

He switched back.

The child was at table one. He was *very* close to the office door.

Bean's hand went to the left door button.

He did not press it.

He looked at the child. The child looked at the camera. The child raised the balloon. He *popped* it.

The sound was *deafening*. Not through the speaker. Through the *air*. Through the *walls*. Through the *floor*. The balloon popped *inside the office*. The red rubber fragments landed on the desk, on the monitor, on Mr. Bunny's head.

He looked at the monitor. Camera 1A. The dining area was empty. The child was gone. The balloon was gone.

He picked up a red rubber fragment. He held it up to the light. He examined it. He put it in his pocket.

He looked at the power meter. **27%**.

He looked at the clock. 3:16 AM.

Two and a half hours to go.

## Part Thirteen: The Power

At 3:45 AM, the power meter read **19%**.

Bean was watching Camera 5A (Pirate Cove). The curtain was drawn. The dark behind it was *deep*. He could not see the eyes. He could not see the shape. He could only see the *absence* of light.

He turned off Camera 5A.

He waited. He counted to sixty. He counted to sixty again.

He turned it back on.

The curtain was fully open. The Pirate Cove was empty.

He looked at Camera 6A (East Hall).

Foxy was in the East Hall. He was *running*.

Bean pressed the right door button. *CLANG.*

The screeching came. The crashing. The scraping. The thudding.

He sat back down. He looked at the power meter. **14%**.

He looked at the clock. 3:47 AM.

Two and a quarter hours to go.

He looked at the manual in the drawer. He did not open it. He did not need to. He knew what would happen when the power reached zero. The lights would go out. The doors would open. The animatronics would come. And they would *perform*.

He looked at Mr. Bunny. He held the rabbit up. "We have a *problem*, Mr. Bunny. The *power* is going out. And when the power goes out, the *bears* come in. And the bears do not *dance*. The bears *eat*."

He put Mr. Bunny down. He leaned back. He closed his eyes.

## Part Fourteen: The Performance

At 4:15 AM, the power meter read **4%**.

Bean was watching Camera 1A. The dining area was empty. The stage was empty. The tables were empty. The air was still.

He looked at the left door. The window was dark. The metal shutter was closed.

He looked at the right door. The window was dark. The metal shutter was closed.

He looked at the power meter. **3%**.

He stood up. He walked to the left door. He opened it.

The corridor was dark. The blue glow from the emergency lights was *flickering*. He could see, at the far end of the West Hall, a shape. A large, brown shape. A *bear*.

Freddy.

He was standing at the end of the hall. He was *waiting*. His top hat was straight. His bow tie was straight. His painted smile was wide. His black, glassy eyes were fixed on Bean.

Bean looked at Freddy. Freddy looked at Bean.

Bean pointed at the door. He made a "you will not come in" gesture.

Freddy did not move.

Bean pointed at the tin of beans in his pocket. He made a "I will give you the beans" gesture.

Freddy did not move.

Bean closed the door. He walked to the right door. He opened it.

The East Hall was dark. The blue glow was flickering. And at the end of the hall, a shape. A red shape. A *fox*.

Foxy.

He was standing at the end of the hall. He was *waiting*. His eye patch was askew. His torn coat was flapping. His yellow eyes were fixed on Bean.

Bean looked at Foxy. Foxy looked at Bean.

Bean pointed at the door. He made a "you will not come in" gesture.

Foxy did not move.

Bean closed the door. He sat back down. He looked at the power meter. **2%**.

He looked at the clock. 4:18 AM.

One and a half hours to go.

He picked up Mr. Bunny. He held the rabbit in both hands. He squeezed. He squeezed *hard*.

"It's *almost* over, Mr. Bunny. We are *almost* there. You know how it is. You are at the end of a very long, very boring *film*. And you think, 'When is it going to *end*?' And then it *ends*. And you go *home*. And you eat your *beans*."

He put Mr. Bunny down. He leaned back. He closed his eyes.

At 4:22, the power meter read **1%**.

The lights in the office flickered. The fan on the desk slowed. The monitor dimmed.

At 4:23, the power meter read **0%**.

The lights went out.

The doors opened.

The monitor went dark.

And in the darkness, in the silence, in the *smell* of old grease and artificial strawberry and something *metallic* and *sweet*, the animatronics *moved*.

## Part Fifteen: The Dark

Bean sat in the dark.

He could not see. He could not hear. Or rather, he could hear *everything*. The *clanking* of metal joints. The *whirring* of servos. The *grinding* of gears. The *sliding* of feet on carpet. Four sets of feet. Four sets of *heavy*, *metallic* feet, moving through the dining area, moving through the corridors, moving *toward the office*.

He sat very still. He breathed. He counted.

One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight. Nine. Ten.

The clanking stopped.

Silence.

He counted again. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight. Nine. Ten.

The clanking started again. *Closer*.

He sat very still. He breathed. He did not move.

The clanking stopped.

Silence.

He counted. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight. Nine. Ten.

And then, in the dark, a sound. A *music box*. Faint. Distant. A small, tinkling melody. A child's toy. *Wrong*. The notes were flat. The rhythm was off.

And then, a *voice*. Not a mechanical voice. Not a grinding, music-box voice. A *real* voice. A *child's* voice. Small. Fragile. *Afraid*.

"Please. I've been in here for so long. Please. I just want to go home."

Bean sat very still. He did not move. He did not breathe.

The voice stopped.

The music box stopped.

The clanking started again. *Farther away*. Moving *away*.

Bean sat very still. He breathed. He counted.

One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight. Nine. Ten.

The clanking stopped.

Silence.

He counted. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight. Nine. Ten.

And then, in the dark, a sound. A *thud*. A small, soft *thud*, as if a small, heavy object had landed on the floor. Then another. Then a series of them, a rapid, clattering, *clinking* sound, as if someone were setting a table for a very large, very hungry dinner.

Bean sat very still. He breathed. He counted.

And then, in the dark, a light. A small, blue light. The vending machine. Its blue light pulsed. And in the blue light, he could see a shape. A small, yellow shape. A *chicken*.

Chica.

She was standing in the doorway. In the blue light. Her painted eyes were wide. Her mouth was open. A piece of pizza was hanging from her jaw.

Bean looked at her. She looked at him.

He raised the tin of beans. He held it up. He pointed at the tin. He pointed at her. He made a "you want some?" gesture.

Chica's head tilted. Her painted mouth widened. The piece of pizza fell from her jaw. It hit the floor. *Thud*.

And then she *walked past him*. Into the office. She walked to the desk. She looked at Mr. Bunny. She looked at the tin of beans. She looked at the red rubber fragment on the desk.

She *smiled*. Or rather, her painted mouth widened by a fraction of a millimeter.

And then she walked out. Into the dark. Into the dining area. Into the night.

Bean sat very still. He breathed. He counted.

One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight. Nine. Ten.

The lights came back on.

The power meter read **100%**.

The monitor was on. The camera feeds were live. The dining area was empty. The stage was empty. The corridors were empty.

Bean sat in the chair. He looked at the desk. The tin of beans was gone. The red rubber fragment was gone. Mr. Bunny was still there, but his left ear was *torn*. A small, clean tear, as if something with a very sharp, very precise claw had *pinched* it.

Bean picked up Mr. Bunny. He examined the tear. He frowned. He put the rabbit down.

He looked at the clock. 4:31 AM.

One and a half hours to go.

## Part Sixteen: The Morning

At 5:47 AM, the sun was coming up. The grey light from the windows was turning, slowly, from grey to a pale, watery gold. The neon signs outside were still buzzing, but they were dimmer now. The parking lot was still empty. The delivery truck was still there. The shopping cart was still in the planter.

Bean sat in the chair. He was still in his jacket. His bow tie was still knotted at its jaunty, asymmetrical angle. His socks were still squeaking. Mr. Bunny was on the desk, his torn ear held together with a small piece of tape that Bean had produced from his jacket pocket.

The power meter read **100%**. The clock read 5:47 AM.

He stood up. He walked to the left door. He opened it.

The corridor was empty. The blue glow was steady. The carpet was blue. The walls were lined with the faded mural of cartoon stars and moons.

He walked out. He walked down the corridor. He walked into the dining area.

The dining area was empty. The stage was empty. The tables were empty. The air smelled of old grease and artificial strawberry. And on the stage, in the center, in the pale gold light from the windows, stood Freddy.

Freddy was *still*. His top hat was straight. His bow tie was straight. His painted smile was wide. His black, glassy eyes were fixed on the stage. On the audience. On *no one*.

Bean walked to the stage. He stood in front of Freddy. He looked up.

Freddy looked down.

Bean raised the tin of beans. He held it up. He pointed at the tin. He pointed at Freddy. He made a "you want some?" gesture.

Freddy did not move.

Bean put the tin in Freddy's paw. He patted the paw. He patted the head. He straightened the top hat. He adjusted the bow tie.

He turned. He walked to the exit.

The door opened. The morning light poured in. The rain had stopped. The sky was pale and grey and *clean*.

Bean stepped out. He stood in the parking lot. He looked at the building. He looked at the neon signs. He looked at the sky.

He took a deep breath. He exhaled.

He walked to the bus stop.

---

## Part Seventeen: The Return

The bus to Greendale took forty-seven minutes. Bean sat in the back, by the window, his knees pressed against the seat in front of him. He held Mr. Bunny in his lap. The rabbit's torn ear was held together with tape. The rabbit's button eyes stared forward, unblinking.

Bean talked to him. In a series of low, grumbling murmurs. He was explaining, he felt, the situation. The job. The animatronics. The *child*. The *music box*. The *vending machine*. He used his hands to illustrate the size of the animatronics, spreading them wide, then bringing them together. He used his fingers to illustrate the shape of the balloon, pinching them together, then letting them go. *Pop*.

The bus lurched. Bean's head bounced. He caught himself with a hand on the window. He looked at the elderly woman in the seat ahead of him, who was still knitting her scarf. She glanced back. Bean gave her a small, apologetic nod and returned to his explanation.

When the bus finally groaned to a halt outside 12 Wetherby Road, Bean stepped off. The rain had stopped. The sky was pale and grey and *clean*. The street was wet. The pavement glistened.

He walked up the four flights of stairs. He opened the door to his flat. He closed the door. He stood in the hallway. He listened to the silence.

He walked to the kitchenette. He opened the cupboard. He retrieved the small, tin of beans. He opened the tin. He ate three beans, one at a time, with the solemnity of a man performing a small ritual.

He walked to the armchair. The good one. The one with the slightly torn left armrest. He sat down. He put Mr. Bunny in his lap. He turned on the television.

A nature documentary about penguins was playing. A penguin slipped on ice. Bean's left eyebrow rose. He mimed the slip with his hand, a small, fluid gesture.

He looked at Mr. Bunny. He squeezed the rabbit's torn ear. He held it together with the tape.

"It's fine," he murmured. "It's *fine*."

He turned back to the television. The penguin got up. It waddled away. The documentary continued.

Bean watched.

And for the first time in eight hours, he did not think about the animatronics. He did not think about the music box. He did not think about the child. He did not think about the vending machine, or the balloon, or the tin of beans, or the shadow in the West Hall, or the breathing in the walls, or the screeching at the right door, or the clanking in the dark.

He thought about penguins.

He thought about beans.

He thought about the small, torn ear of a rubber rabbit, held together with tape.

And he slept.

---

## Epilogue: The Next Night

At 9:47 PM, the doorbell rang.

Bean opened the door. Karen was there. Drenched. Holding a soggy cardboard box.

"Mr. Bean. I have a position for you. Freddy Fazbear's. Night shift. Security guard. Full room and board. Two thousand pounds a month. No experience necessary."

Bean stared at her. He tilted his head. He looked past her shoulder. He looked back.

He pointed at himself.

He pointed at the sky.

He made a small, "good luck" gesture with his hand.

And then, with the calm, methodical precision of a man who has spent his entire life solving problems through physical manipulation of objects, he reached into his jacket pocket, produced a small, silver coin, and held it up to the light.

He examined it.

He put it back in his pocket.

He closed the door.

He sat in the armchair.

He turned on the television.

A nature documentary about penguins was playing.

A penguin slipped on ice.

Bean's left eyebrow rose.

And he mimed the slip with his hand, a small, fluid gesture, and returned his attention to the screen.

---

*In the parking lot of Freddy Fazbear's Family Diner, the neon signs buzzed and flickered. The delivery truck was still there. The shopping cart was still in the planter. And in the dining area, in the dark, in the silence, in the smell of old grease and artificial strawberry, the animatronics stood. Still. Waiting. Patient.*

*Freddy's head tilted. Just a fraction. Just enough that the angle of the top hat was different.*

*Just enough that the painted smile seemed, in the blue glow of the emergency lights, to be a millimeter wider.*

*And in the Pirate Cove, behind the drawn curtain, in the deep, deep dark, two yellow eyes glowed.*

*And in the West Hall, in the blue glow, a shadow slid.*

*And in the dining area, at table five, a small, red balloon floated.*

*And in the office, on the desk, a small, tin of beans sat.*

*And in the tin, three beans remained.*

*And in the dark, in the silence, in the smell of old grease and artificial strawberry, the music box played.*

*And the notes were flat.*

*And it was getting closer.*

*And it was getting closer.*

*And it was getting* ***closer.***

---

**THE END**

*(Or rather. The beginning. Because the next night, the doorbell will ring. And Karen will be there. And the coin will be in the pocket. And the penguin will slip on the ice. And the penguin will get up. And the penguin will waddle away. And the documentary will continue. And the night will come. And the animatronics will move. And the music box will play. # The Locked Room

The stone was cold against Margaret's cheek. She opened her eyes to a ceiling of damp, blackened brick and the amber glow of a single oil lamp on a wooden table. The room was perhaps twelve feet square. One door, iron-banded, its keyhole sealed with what appeared to be fresh wax. No window. The air tasted of chalk and something faintly sweet, like lilies left too long in a vase.

She sat up. Her grey dress was wrinkled, her hat gone. Beside her, on a second chair, a man was stirring—tweed jacket, spectacles askew, a silver chain catching the lamplight. He blinked, touched his temple, and saw her.

"Where—"

"Don't." Margaret held up a hand. "I don't know. And I'd rather not shout."

He straightened his spectacles. "Thomas Wren. Pathologist. St. Bartholomew's." He said it the way a man states a fact he's not entirely sure of.

"Margaret Hale. Clerk. Finsbury office." She looked at the door, the sealed keyhole, the bare walls. "We're in a cellar."

"Apparently." He rose, moved to the door, tested the handle. Solid. He pressed his ear to it. "No footsteps. No draft. We're below street level, at least two floors."

They stood in silence. The lamp hissed.

It was Margaret who saw it first: pinned to the table with a heavy iron nail, a newspaper clipping. The *Evening Standard*, March 14th, 1936. A small obituary. *Eleanor Voss, 41, of Harrow, passed peacefully in her sleep.* Beneath it, in a cramped hand, someone had written a single word in red ink: *Liar.*

Thomas went pale. Margaret felt the floor tilt.

"You know her," he said. Not a question.

"I typed the certificate." Margaret's voice was very small. "The death certificate. Heart failure. I typed it because I was told to."

# Deep Space Rivalry

## Day 1 — Late Morning

The observation lounge of the *Meridian Accord* stretched in a sweeping arc of polished obsidian and warm amber lighting, a cathedral of luxury suspended in the void. Beyond the triple-layered viewport, the docking corridor glowed a sterile white, and somewhere out in that glow, a royal vessel was decelerating.

Caelen Voss stood at the railing with a glass of untouched champagne, watching the approach vector scroll across the holo-display. His father, Ambassador Dorian Voss, was already three decks down in the negotiation chamber, running final briefings with the diplomatic staff. His mother, Lady Elara, was somewhere in the upper suites, making sure every silverware placement on the welcome tray met her exacting standards.

Caelen had been given one job: be presentable at the dock. Smile. Nod. Don't spill anything on anyone's shoes.

Simple.

He was twenty-three, lean, with the kind of sharp, slightly restless energy that made his mother sigh and his father shake his head. Dark hair, perpetually a little too long. A tailored charcoal suit that cost more than most people's monthly rations. He looked, by all accounts, like a young diplomat.

He did *not* look like a man dreading his own arrival.

"Voss." A voice behind him. Lieutenant Kade, the yacht's operations officer, falling into step with a datapad. "Royal vessel *Crown of Ashworth* is on final approach. ETA to docking in twelve minutes. The full Ashworth delegation is aboard. Forty-three souls."

Caelen's jaw tightened. He set the champagne down.

"Of course the *full* delegation," he muttered.

"Princess Seraphine is listed as lead cultural envoy. She'll be in the forward suite." Kade paused, glancing at him with the careful neutrality of a man who had worked on this yacht for nine years and had learned not to comment. "She's... grown up, sir. You might want to prepare yourself for a different dynamic than, say, the Voss-Ashworth children's incident of '41."

Caelen's eye twitched. *The incident.* The one where he'd "accidentally" rerouted the gravity in the royal children's playroom and she'd "accidentally" locked his father in the ventilation shaft for six hours. The one where he'd called her *'your majesty's little dictator'* and she'd called him *'the ambassador's embarrassing afterthought.'*

Five years. They were adults now. It didn't matter.

"Twelve minutes," Caelen repeated flatly.

"Eleven," Kade corrected, and walked away.

---

The docking clamps engaged with a deep, resonant *thrum* that Caelen felt in his molars. The corridor lights shifted from white to the soft gold of the Ashworth greeting protocol. The airlock cycled.

And then the doors opened.

The Ashworth delegation poured in like a river of silk and authority. Courtiers. Aides. A small honor guard in deep burgundy. And at the center, flanked by two elderly advisors, a woman.

Seraphine Ashworth.

She was—

Caelen's brain short-circuited for approximately 1.3 seconds.

She was *tall*. Taller than him, which was—no. She'd always been the taller one. But the *proportions* were different now. The angular, sharp-featured girl who'd once thrown a grape at his head in the mess hall was gone. In her place: a woman in a structured ivory coat with a high collar, her auburn hair pulled back in a severe, elegant knot. Her face was all clean lines and sharp cheekbones, her eyes a pale, almost silver grey that caught the amber light of the corridor and *held* it. She moved with the unhurried, proprietary grace of someone who had never once in her life been told *no* and had never once accepted it.

Their eyes met across the corridor.

Seraphine's expression did not change. Did not flicker. Did not soften. But the corner of her mouth did something *almost* like a smile. Almost.

"Voss," she said. Her voice was lower than he remembered. Smoother. Still carrying that faint, aristocratic lilt. "You look *exactly* the same. Still like a disgruntled cat in a too-fine suit."

Caelen straightened his spine. "Your Highness. You look *exactly* the same. Still like a tyrant in a too-fine coat."

A beat of silence. The courtiers behind them shifted uncomfortably.

Seraphine's smile *almost* completed. "Delighted to see you, Caelen. I trust the yacht is in as *deplorable* condition as I remember."

"Only the *slightest* bit of mold in the east corridor. The rest is pristine."

"Good. I'll be sure to avoid it." She turned, her ivory coat sweeping, and began walking toward the forward suites. Then, without looking back: "Try to be *interesting* this time, Ambassador's Son. I've had a very long flight and I refuse to be *bored* for a week."

She disappeared down the corridor.

Caelen stood very still.

His heart was doing something *inappropriate*.

"Kade," he said, very quietly.

"Sir?"

"Make sure the east corridor mold is *actually* fixed before she gets there. And get me a drink. A real one. Not the champagne."

"Yes, sir."

---

The observation lounge was empty now. Caelen poured himself a measure of amber whiskey and stared at the viewport, where the *Crown of Ashworth* was already undocking, retreating into the dark.

Seven days. Seven days on a ship the size of a city block, with *her* in the forward suite, his parents in the negotiation chamber, and absolutely nowhere to hide.

He took a long drink.

# 铁与沙

## 一、高卢的雨

她叫阿斯特拉。不，那是后来罗马人给她起的名字，取自"星"。在高卢，她叫**布兰温**——"白鹰"。

她出生在塞纳河以北一片灰绿色的森林里，属于一个没有名字的小部落。公元前87年的冬天，她四岁。那年冬天很长，长到她记不清母亲的脸，只记得母亲的手。那双手指节粗大，指甲缝里永远嵌着洗不掉的泥和铁锈，因为她的母亲是部落里唯一的女铁匠。

父亲是猎人，死在她五岁那年。一头熊。不是那种故事里温顺的熊，是饿了三天的、眼睛发黄的熊。父亲用矛捅了它七下，第八下捅穿了自己的肋骨。

从那以后，布兰温跟着母亲在锻炉前长大。

她六岁学会拉风箱。七岁能抡起两磅重的锤子，一下一下把烧红的铁条敲成刀坯。九岁那年，她第一次独自完成一把短剑——剑身歪了，刃口也不齐，但部落里的老铁匠（一个瘸了腿的男人）看了之后说："这丫头的手，比男人稳。"

她十岁。高卢的冬天像一把钝刀，不割肉，只磨骨头。她每天天不亮就起来生炉子，把母亲留下的铁料重新烧、重新锤。她的肩膀比同龄男孩宽，小臂上青筋像藤蔓一样爬着。她跑起来很快，不是那种轻盈的快，是带着重量的、压着地面的快，像一头小兽。

她喜欢打架。

不是那种女孩之间揪头发的打架。是和男孩打。和比她大两岁的男孩打。用拳头，用肘，用牙齿。她打赢了大多数。输的时候不哭，把嘴角的血吐在地上，说"再来"。

部落里的人开始用一种奇怪的眼神看她。不是厌恶，是一种……不安。好像她身上有什么东西不属于这个季节，不属于这片土地。

## 二、火与链

公元前85年，她七岁。

罗马人来了。

不是苏拉——苏拉还在意大利半岛的泥潭里跟自己的将军们打内战。来的是他的一个军团，一个在苏拉命令下北征的军团，统帅是个叫昆图斯·穆基亚努斯的百夫长。他带了两千个士兵，穿过高卢的森林，像一把烧红的刀切进黄油。

布兰温记得那天的火。

不是锻造的火。锻造的火是橙色的，有节奏的，风箱一拉一推，铁在锤下唱歌。那天的火是黑色的。是整片森林在烧。是邻居的茅屋在烧。是母亲在锻炉前被一个罗马士兵用剑柄砸碎了后脑勺时，溅在铁砧上的血，被炉火烤出一种甜腻的、令人作呕的气味。

她跑了。

她跑进树林里，跑了一整夜。赤脚。十一月的泥地冻得像铁板。她的脚底被碎石割开，血和泥混在一起，每一步都在雪地上印出一个模糊的掌印。

她跑了三天。

第三天，她倒在一棵倒下的橡树下面。一个罗马斥候找到了她。他大概十五岁，比她大不了几岁，脸上还有没长开的绒毛。他看了她一眼，又看了看她身后那片还在冒烟的森林，把一条绳子扔在她面前。

"走。"他说。拉丁语。她听不懂。

但她听懂了绳子。

## 三、罗马的阶梯

她被卖到了罗马。

不是直接到的。中间经过了两个奴隶贩子、一条船、一次在迦太基港口的转手。她八岁到九岁那年的大部分时间都在船上度过。船底。和其他奴隶挤在一起。空气是臭的，是汗、是尿、是呕吐物、是铁锈。她学会了在船底打拳。对着空气打。对着木板的缝隙打。拳头打在木头上，指骨肿起来，消了，再打。

她到罗马的时候是九岁。

第一个主人是一个叫马库斯·弗拉维乌斯的元老院议员。他买她不是为了让她洗衣服或者做饭。他买她是因为在奴隶市场上，一个奴隶贩子把她推到他面前说："看看这丫头的手臂。"

弗拉维乌斯确实看了。他捏了捏她的小臂，像捏一块生肉。然后他笑了，付了钱。

他把她带到了他的**铁匠铺**。

不是真正的铁匠铺。是元老院议员用来"管理"自己铸币和武器订单的作坊。但活儿是一样的。风箱。锤子。烧红的铁。

她九岁到十二岁，三年。

三年里，她每天工作十四个小时。从日出到日落，从日落再干到月亮升起来。拉风箱。锻打。淬火。打磨。她的身高在长，但她的肩膀没有再变宽——它们已经宽了。她的背脊被风箱的把手磨出了一层硬茧，又厚又黄，像树皮。

她学会了拉丁语。不是从书本上学的，是从骂人声里学的。弗拉维乌斯的助手们骂她"小母牛""高卢野狗""铁砧上的蛆"，她把这些词一个一个捡起来，塞进脑子里，像捡铁屑。

她也会挨打。弗拉维乌斯心情不好的时候——通常是政治上的事，苏拉死了，新的人上台，旧的秩序在摇晃——他会拿鞭子抽她。抽在背上。抽在手臂上。她从来不叫。她只是把锤子握得更紧，指节发白，然后继续打铁。

# 轻奇幻浪漫小说构思：《回声修复所》

## 一、核心奇幻设定（非穿越）

世界上不到千分之一的人能看见 **"物的回声"**——任何有年头的物件（老怀表、旧瓷碗、一栋老楼的门把手）身上，会浮现出它经历过的**最浓烈的一段记忆**，像半透明的光影、声音、气味，飘在物体周围。

主角**控制不好**这个能力：在旧书店会"走神"盯着一个杯子发呆，在地铁里被一个老皮箱的回声刺到眼眶发红，社交中显得"怪"。

> 关键原则：这个能力**不改变世界**，不能预知、不能回溯、不能操控。它只是"看见"。故事的力量来自**选择如何回应**自己看见的东西。

---

## 二、行业背景（对应《穿Prada的女王》）

一家传奇的 **"回声修复所"**，专门修复那些"回声即将消散"的珍贵老物件，并将回声转化为可保存的档案/展览。

所里的"工种"：
| 角色 | 说明 |
|------|------|
| **回声师** | 能看见回声的人（极稀有），负责"读取" |
| **修复师** | 不能看见，但凭触觉、材料学、工艺把物件修好 |
| **记录师** | 把回声转成影像/文字/声音档案 |
| **策展人** | 决定哪些故事值得被公开展示 |

这是一个**有严格等级、有审美标准、有行业黑话**的世界，和时尚圈一样"残酷又迷人"。

---

## 三、主要角色

**林晚（女主，26岁）**
- 回声师，但"野路子"，没受过训练，看回声像"被泼了一脸颜料"，粗糙、混乱、过载。
- 性格：社恐但内心热烈，审美直觉极好，极度缺乏自信，习惯用"我没事"掩饰"我被吓到了"。
- 口头禅式的内心独白，幽默、自嘲。

**沈渡（男主，31岁）**
- 首席修复师。**看不见回声**，但能用手指摸出釉面0.1毫米的裂纹走向，用鼻子闻出哪段木料被火烧过。
- 性格：温和、专注、话少，笨拙的浪漫——不会说漂亮话，但会默默把林晚看回声时"过载"后需要的那杯温水放在手边。
- 他和林晚是**互补**：她看见故事，他修复载体。

**顾先生（导师，55岁，对应Miranda）**
- 修复所创始人，毒舌、要求近乎变态、极度护短。
- 经典台词风格：*"你管这叫'看见了'？你看见的是一坨颜色。重新来。"* / *"我花了三十年让这所里的人学会'安静'，你进来第一天就把我的茶杯吓裂了？"*
- 但会在林晚被客户刁难时，一句话把对方怼回去，然后面无表情走开。

---

## 四、情节结构

### 第一幕：被"看见"

- 林晚在一家小图书馆做管理员，日子灰扑扑。她总盯着旧物发呆，被同事当怪人，被领导暗示"你要么调岗要么辞职"。
- 一次意外：一个即将被丢弃的旧怀表在她手里"响"了——她看见了1943年一个年轻女人在战壕外等信的画面，持续了整整七秒。她慌忙把怀表放回箱子，但手指在木箱上按下了一个很轻的"修复"（她不知道自己能做这件事）。
- 第二天，顾先生坐在她对面。*"你昨晚碰了那枚怀表。它现在能走了。"*
- 顾先生没有"邀请"，是**命令**：*"周一来上班。迟到一分钟我扣你三个月工资。"*

### 第二幕：入行与成长（最核心的篇幅）

**行业"入坑"线（对应Andy的成长）：**
- 林晚第一次进修复所，满屋子老物件的回声**同时涌来**——她当场"过载"，蹲在地上干呕。顾先生面无表情递给她一条毛巾：*"……你连我的茶杯都看不住？"*
- 顾先生给她定规矩：*"不许主动看。只有客户委托、你被指定、你'需要'的时候，才能看。否则你看到的不是故事，是噪音。"*
- 她开始学习"控制"：如何只打开一个物件的回声、如何不"走进去"、如何在看完之后**把门关好**。
- 从"外行"到"被认可"：第一次独立读取一件宋代瓷碗的回声，顾先生沉默了很久，说了句：*"……还行。别得意。"*（全所都知道这是最高评价。）

**爱情线（对应《时空恋旅人》的"日常感"）：**
- 沈渡是她的搭档。他看不见回声，但每次她看完一件物件，他会问：*"你看到了什么？"* 然后**真的听**。不笑，不打断，不评价。
- 他们的浪漫是**极日常的**：
  - 一起蹲在工作台前修一个旧座钟，谁也不说话，只有齿轮声。
  - 林晚看完一个物件后情绪崩溃（回声太痛了），沈渡什么也没说，只是把自己的外套搭在她肩上，然后继续修手里的东西。
  - 他给她讲一件木料"为什么这样裂"，讲得极认真，像在讲一个很无聊但很重要的事。她觉得这是他最动人的样子。
- **没有**"突然告白"、"雨中奔跑"、"机场追人"。他们的关系是：某天她发现他桌上多了一小瓶她随口提过想试的松节油；某天他加班到很晚，她"刚好"也还在，两个人分了一盒已经凉掉的饺子。

**幽默/轻喜感：**
- 林晚第一次看顾先生的私人收藏室，一百多件老物同时"响"，她像被交响乐砸了一脸，扶着门框说：*"顾先生，您的茶杯在哭。"* 顾先生：*"……那是1987年的。它不哭。它只是釉面有微裂纹。"*
- 所里新来的记录师是个二十出头的年轻人，把一件老旗袍的回声录成了"ASMR"，顾先生看了三秒，把硬盘摔了。

### 第三幕：核心冲突与选择

一个**极重要的委托**：一位已故老画家的最后一幅画，回声即将完全消散（画作本身也在劣化）。顾先生亲自带队，林晚是唯一的回声师。

- 修复过程中，她看见了画中的回声——不是"美丽的"，是一个**遗憾**：画家在画完最后一笔后，对着画看了很久，然后把它翻过去了。他**不想再看**。那段回声里有一种极安静的、"我放下了"的疲惫。
- 林晚卡住了。她习惯了"看见故事→修复→保存"，但这段回声的"意思"是：**"我不需要被记住。"**
- 她开始动摇：*"如果我只是个'偷看别人故事'的人，我把它保存下来，是对它好，还是对它残忍？"*
- 她跟沈渡吵了第一次架（很轻的、很安静的吵）：*"你修好了画，但我把它的回声录下来了。它本来想'走'的。"*

*Медведь поднимается на валун у старого дуба, кладёт лапу на его ствол и молчит. Ветер стихает. Даже кукушка замолкает. Тогда он говорит, и голос его идёт по лесу, как гул под землёй:*

---

Сыны и дочери моих лесов. Волки, рыщущие по границам. Олени, несущие рога, как короны. Птицы, что шьёте небо перьями. Рыбы, что плетёте реку в живую нить. Муравьи, что строите без единого слова, но строите прочнее, чем я.

Я говорю с вами не с высоты. Я говорю *из* земли, из корня, из того самого тёмного места, где зимовал и вы, и я, и камень под вами. Мы все — одного дыхания.

Я вижу, как суетится лиса, как торопится заяц, как спорят вороны на ветке, будто мир кончается завтра. Не кончается. Солнце встанет. Лёд треснет. Берёза выпустит лист, и вы снова будете шуметь, ругаться, влюбляться, терять, находить.

Но я скажу вам одну вещь, и запомните её крепче, чем я запоминаю запах мёда в августе:

**Вы не одни.**

Волк, ты не один, когда идёшь в стае. Рысь, ты не одна, когда сидишь на ветке и ждёшь. Даже я, в своей берлоге, в тридцатиградусный мороз, когда за стеной воет ветер и кажется, что мир — это только темнота и холод, — я не один. Потому что за стеной дышат вы. И когда я выйду весной, вы будете здесь. Шумные, живые, злые, прекрасные.

Не губите друг друга из суеты. Не берите больше, чем нужно. Река не ваша собственность, хоть и пьёте из неё. Дуб не ваш, хоть и прячетесь в его тени. Мы — гости в этом лесу. Все. Даже я. Даже корень, даже камень.

А теперь — тишина.

Я ухожу в берлогу. Не потому что мне страшно. А потому что лесу нужен покой, как вам нужен сон. И пока я сплю, вы живите. Ссорьтесь, танцуйте, охотьтесь, пойте. Только помните: когда я открою глаза весной, я хочу увидеть, что лес стоит. Что вы — здесь.

Спитесь, мои подданные. Зима длинна, а утро — коротко.

# THE OTHER MAN

### A Feature Film Synopsis

---

## FADE IN:

**COLD OPEN — BLACK. Then sound: a boot on concrete. Breathing. A voice, low and calm, speaking in a language we don't recognize. A flash of white light. A man's face, contorted, screaming silently. CUT TO BLACK.**

**TITLE CARD: "NINETY-THREE DAYS."**

---

## ACT ONE — THE GHOST COMES HOME

**DANIEL COLE** (38, gaunt, eyes that look like they haven't slept in years) works the overnight shift at a logistics warehouse in Tucson, Arizona. He's a former 75th Ranger who served two tours in Afghanistan before being captured alongside a small unit in a remote compound outside Kandahar. He was held for ninety-three days. He came home to a handshake, a plaque, and a benefits application that's been "under review" for four years.

His wife, **SARAH**, left eight months ago. His sixteen-year-old daughter, **LILY**, now lives with her mother in Flagstaff and answers Daniel's calls with monosyllables. His apartment is a mausoleum of unopened mail and cold coffee. He talks to no one. He goes to a VA support group twice a month and sits in the back row, saying nothing.

The film opens in a quiet, aching register. Daniel is a man being slowly erased. He blames the war for everything — the marriage, the job, the silence in his own head. *"They sent me in there to die for a flag, and when I came back, the flag didn't even know my name."*

At the support group, a new face is introduced: **MARCUS WREN**, a former Special Forces operator who was held in the same compound, in the same cage block, for the same ninety-three days. They were cellmates. They haven't spoken since the debriefing.

The reunion is electric. Marcus is everything Daniel is not: warm, magnetic, sharp-tongued, *alive*. He laughs too loud. He orders two whiskeys and slides one across the table without asking. He puts a hand on Daniel's shoulder and says, *"Ninety-three days, brother. I remember every one. You don't have to carry it alone anymore."*

Daniel, for the first time in years, feels *seen*.

Over the next several weeks, Marcus becomes a constant presence. He shows up at the warehouse. He drives Daniel to Flagstaff to see Lily (a tense, painful visit where Daniel can't get a word out of his daughter). He talks Daniel off the ledge — literally, one night, when Daniel stands on the overpass above the Santa Cruz River, and Marcus's hand closes on his wrist and his voice is steady: *"You don't get to do this. Not for them. Not for the people who forgot you exist."*

Marcus validates every bitter thought Daniel has. The government abandoned them. The VA is a scam. The country took his best years and gave him a cardboard certificate. *"You bled for them. They don't get to act like you owe them your silence."*

And Marcus has a quality that unsettles Daniel in ways he can't name: he has **no moral compass**. He talks about people the way you talk about weather. He once, over beers, described a man he'd known in the compound — a translator who'd tried to help them — and said, flatly, *"I'd do it again. Wouldn't think twice."* Daniel is disturbed but doesn't push it. Marcus is the only person who *gets it*. And Daniel is so lonely, so hollowed out, that he doesn't want to lose him.

The tone is intimate, slow-burning, aching. A man rebuilding a life around the only person who remembers what he went through.

---

The film's register begins to shift. Marcus starts talking about **the compound**. Not the vague, sanitized version from the debriefing. The *real* version. The things they did to them. The program didn't implant a ghost into Daniel Cole. **Daniel Cole was the ghost.** Daniel Cole was the *construction*. A new identity, built from fragments, designed to be the "surface" — the forgotten veteran, the bitter warehouse worker, the man who could be triggered, manipulated, and sent to do the program's work. ## TONE & STYLE NOTES

The film is structured in two distinct registers. **Acts One and Two** play as a slow, intimate character drama in the mode of *Manchester by the Sea* or *A Ghost Story* — quiet, aching, grounded in the specific textures of a man's small, broken life. The cinematography is warm, handheld, close. The sound design is sparse. Daniel's world is small and muffled, as if he's underwater.

**Act Three** shifts into the tight, cold, procedural tension of *The Sixth Sense* and *The Manchurian Candidate*. The camera goes static. The color palette drains to steel and blue. The sound design opens up — we hear the hum of servers, the tick of a clock, the *absence* of a second breathing in the room. The thriller elements (the heist, the paranoia, the pursuit) are played with the methodical dread of a locked-room mystery.

The **Manchurian Candidate** parallel is structural: the "hero" is the programmed one, the real person is buried beneath, and the "possession" is not an external force but the self, fighting to resurface. The **Sixth Sense** parallel is in the reveal mechanics: the audience is made to *re-contextualize* everything they've seen. Every scene with Marcus is rewatchable. Every "conversation" was a monologue. Every "shared" moment was a man, alone, talking to the ghost of his own buried identity.

The military element is never played for patriotism or action. The war is a *wound*, a *fracture*, a thing that happened to a person and made him into a *product*. The compound is not a battlefield. It's a *factory*. And the film's central horror is not that a man was tortured, but that a man was *replaced* — and that the thing doing the replacing was his own mind, doing what it was told to do.

# Сценарий свадебного фильма «Ты — мой самый верный маршрут»

**Хронометраж:** 6–7 минут
**Формат:** 4K, тёплая цветокоррекция, лёгкое зерно
**Голос за кадром (ГЗК):** мужчина, мягкий, чуть хриплый, говорит как будто рассказывает другу

---

## АКТ I. ТИШИНА ПЕРЕД (0:00 – 1:10)

**ВИДЕО:** Чёрный экран. Тикают часы. Потом — крупный план: рука невесты поправляет манжету. Рука жениха затягивает галстук. Два отдельных кадра, два разных пространства.

**ЗВУК:** Только дыхание. Тихий тиканье.

**ГЗК:**
> «Знаете, я долго думал, с чего начать. С того дня, когда мы впервые увиделись? С того, как я перепутал имя? С того, как ты сказала: „Ты опять забыл ключи?" — и я понял, что уже не могу представить утро без этого голоса?
>
> Нет. Начну с тишины. С того момента, когда в комнате стало тихо — и я понял, что тишина стала *нашей* тишиной. Такой, в которой можно не говорить. И это — лучший разговор.»

**ВИДЕО:** Переход — два чашки кофе на подоконнике. Пар от них. Утренний свет.

**МУЗЫКА:** Вступает тихий пианино. Медленно, с паузами.

---

## АКТ II. ПЕРВЫЕ ШАГИ (1:10 – 2:40)

**ВИДЕО:** Коллаж из «сырых» кадров (на телефон, чуть трясётся):
- Они стоят в незнакомом городе, смотрят карту.
- Он что-то объясняет, она смеётся.
- Первый совместный поход на рынок — она выбирает сыр, он держит сумку.
- Вечер на крыше, бокалы, город за спиной.
- Они бегут от дождя, прикрываясь одним зонтом.

**ГЗК:**
> «Мы не знали, что будет дальше. Ни маршрута, ни карты. Просто — шаг за шагом. И каждый шаг был чуть смелее предыдущего.
>
> Помнишь тот первый дождь? Мы оба промокли до нитки, и ты сказала: „Вот это и есть приключение". А я подумал: да, с тобой — любое приключение. Даже мокрое. Даже глупое.»

**ЗВУК:** Под микс — смех, шорох зонтов, далёкий гул города.

**МУЗЫКА:** Пианино добавляет лёгкую гитару. Темп чуть быстрее.

---

## АКТ III. ОБЩИЙ ДОМ (2:40 – 4:10)

**ВИДЕО:** Более «домашние» кадры:
- Они вместе собирают полку. Он держит дрель, она прижимает полку. Оба ругаются на кривой уровень.
- Вечер на кухне: она готовит, он стоит рядом и «помогает» (на самом деле ест сырое тесто).
- Ночной кадр: она спит, он читает книгу рядом, поправляет ей одеяло.
- Они сидят на полу среди коробок после переезда, оба в пыли, смеются.
- Кот (если есть) проходит между ними по кадру.

**ГЗК:**
> «А потом стало *наше*. Не «моё» и «твоё». А *наше*. Наше утро. Наша полка, которую мы вешали три часа. Наша кухня, где пахнет луком и твоим любимым чаем.
>
> Я не помню, как именно мы перестали быть двумя людьми в одной квартире и стали… одним. Но это произошло. Тихо. Как рассвет. Ты даже не заметила, как стало светлее.
>
> А я заметил. Я всегда замечал.»

**МУЗЫКА:** Вступает струнный квартет. Тепло, с нарастанием.

---

## АКТ IV. ТО, ЧТО НЕ ВИДНО (4:10 – 5:10)

**ВИДЕО:** Короткие, почти статичные кадры:
- Её руки, когда она гладит его по щеке.
- Его руки, когда он держит её ладонь.
- Они стоят у окна, смотрят в одну точку. Не разговаривают.
- Она плачет (радостно или от усталости), он просто обнимает. Без слов.
- Крупный план: их пальцы переплетены.

**ГЗК:**
> «Есть моменты, которые не влезут ни в один кадр. Когда ты молча ставишь мне чай, потому что видишь, что я устал. Когда я просто стою за твоей спиной и чувствую, что всё в порядке.
>
> Это не кино. Это не сюжет. Это — то, что держит. То, что я хочу, чтобы ты видела сегодня. Не только праздник. А *меня*. Настоящего. С того самого утра, когда ты сказала: „Ты опять забыл ключи?"»

**ЗВУК:** Музыка уходит почти на ноль. Только дыхание.

**ПАУЗА:** 3 секунды тишины.

---

## АКТ V. СЕГОДНЯ (5:10 – 6:20)

**ВИДЕО:** Смена ритма. Кадры свадебного дня:
- Она выходит из комнаты в платье. Он замирает.
- Их глаза встречаются через зал.
- Обмен кольцами — крупный план пальцев.
- Они идут по залу, гости аплодируют.
- Они танцуют первый танец — камера медленно отъезжает, видны все лица гостей.

**ГЗК (темп чуть быстрее, с улыбкой в голосе):**
> «А сегодня — ты. И я. И все, кого мы любим. И да, я опять забыл ключи. Но ты уже не ругаешься. Ты просто берёшь их из сумки и говоришь: „Иди, я подожду".
>
> И я иду. Потому что знаю: ты будешь там. Всегда. На любом маршруте. В любом дожде. В любой тишине.»

**МУЗЫКА:** Полный оркестр. Финальный аккорд — тёплый, открытый.

---

## АКТ VI. ФИНАЛ (6:20 – 6:50)

**ВИДЕО:** Они стоят спиной к камере, держатся за руки. Перед ними — зал, свет, люди. Камера медленно поднимается вверх (дрон или кран).

**ГЗК (тихо, почти шёпотом):**
> «Спасибо, что ты — мой самый верный маршрут.
>
> Даже когда мы теряемся. Даже когда дождь. Даже когда я забываю ключи.
>
> Мы всегда находим друг друга.»

**ВИДЕО:** Кадр растворяется. На чёрном экране — надпись белым:

> *«[Имя невесты] + [Имя жениха]*
> *[Дата]*
> *Наш маршрут только начинается.»*

**ЗВУК:** Последний аккорд. Тишина.

---

## ТЕХНИЧЕСКИЕ ПОМЕТКИ ДЛЯ ОПЕРАТОРА / МОНТАЖЁРА

| Элемент | Примечание |
|---|---|
| **Цветокоррекция** | Тёплая, золотистая. Акт IV — чуть холоднее, «ночной». Акт V — яркий, праздничный. |
| **Ритм монтажа** | Акт I — длинные планы (8–12 с). Акт II–III — средний темп (3–5 с). Акт IV — почти статика. Акт V — ускорение, динамичные склейки. |
| **Звук** | ГЗК записывать в отдельной студии, «сухо». Фоновые звуки (смех, дождь, музыка) — на 20–30 % под голос. |
| **Музыка** | Подбирать оригинальную инструментальную композицию (пианино → гитара → струнные → оркестр). Избегать популярных хитов. |
| **Кадры для съёмки в день свадьбы** | Выход невесты, встреча пар, кольца, первый танец, общий зал — снимать на 2 камеры, один оператор — «на эмоции», второй — «на пространство». |
| **Кадры для предварительной съёмки** | Утро, кухня, полка, переезд, дождь, крыша — снять за 2–4 недели до свадьбы в естественном свете, без постановки. |

---

## АЛЬТЕРНАТИВНЫЕ ФИНАЛЬНЫЕ КАДРЫ (на выбор)

- **Вариант А:** Они поворачиваются к камере и улыбаются. Зал хлопает. Кадры «вживую» без ГЗК.
- **Вариант Б:** Экран гаснет. Зал молчит 2 секунды. Потом — аплодисменты.
- **Вариант В:** На чёрном экране появляются «открытки» от гостей (по 3–4 секунды каждая): *«Мы любим вас, ребята. Счастливого пути!»*

---

Сценарий рассчитан на то, что **конкретные детали** (имя, город, история знакомства, кот, ключи, дождь) заменяются на реальные истории пары. Структура и эмоциональная дуга остаются — меняется только «наполнение». # The Dirt

For three months after Thomas died, Margot did not go to the community garden.

She told herself it was the cold. Then it was the schedule. Then it was simply that the plot in the back corner, the one they'd shared for eleven years, was *his* plot, and to walk in there would be to walk into a room where a chair still held the shape of a man.

The tomatoes grew wild and unpruned. The zucchini took over the beans. By July, the whole square was a tangle of green chaos, and the neighbors walked around it like you walk around a puddle.

In August, Margot's granddaughter, Lily, came to stay. Seven years old, with dirt already under her fingernails by the time she'd been awake an hour. She found a half-eaten peach in the yard and ate it standing up, juice running down her chin, and said, "Can we go to the garden? I want to see the zucchini."

Margot said no. Then she said, "It's a mess." Then, quieter: "Okay."

They walked the path. Margot kept her eyes on the ground, on her shoes, on the gravel. She did not look at the back corner.

But Lily looked. Lily always looked at everything.

"Grandma," she said, pointing at the tangle. "There's a little one hiding in there. A tiny one. It's so small it can't even see the sun."

Margot crouched. And there, buried under a collapsed zucchini vine, was a single pepper plant. Barely six inches tall. Stunted. One yellow leaf. Alive, but barely.

She pulled the vine away with her fingers. The dirt was cool and wet and real under her nails. She hadn't touched soil in three months. Her hands remembered the motion before her mind caught up.

"It's still here," Margot said. She wasn't sure if she was talking to Lily or to the plant or to the eleven years in the back corner.

Lily sat cross-legged in the dirt and said, very seriously, "I can help you pull the weeds. You pull the big ones, I'll pull the little ones."

Margot laughed. It came out rusty, a little broken, but it was a laugh. She knelt fully. She pulled.

They worked for an hour. The zucchini vines came away in long, snapping ropes. The pepper plant stood in a small clearing of its own, ridiculous and stubborn and green.

On the way home, Lily's hand was in Margot's, and her thumb was dirty, and she said, "We should come back tomorrow."

Margot looked at the sky, which was doing nothing in particular, just being a sky. And she said, "Yeah. We should."

It wasn't a cure. The chair in the back corner was still empty. The plot was still *his* plot, and it would be hers, and that was a different kind of grief, the kind you learn to carry the way you learn to carry a cup of water without spilling.

But the pepper plant was still here. And so was she. And tomorrow, she would go back, and her hands would go into the dirt, and a small girl would be beside her, pulling at the weeds.

And that was enough. That was the whole, quiet, ordinary miracle.
