# YAKKO, WAKKO & DOT vs. DISCORD

## CHARACTER ANALYSIS

**The Warner Siblings (Animaniacs):**
Yakko, Wakko, and Dot are cartoon entities existing within a meta-reality that transcends conventional physics. According to the Animaniacs Fandom wiki, they possess the ability to break the fourth wall, manipulate their environment through "cartoon logic," pull any object into existence from a pocket or hat, survive any and all forms of destruction (flattening, disintegration, explosion) and reassemble, freeze or reverse time, shrink to subatomic size or grow to cosmic scale, write directly onto the "screen" of reality, sing songs with tangible magical effects, and exist simultaneously in two-dimensional and three-dimensional space. They are, by the fundamental rules of their existence, *unkillable* in any permanent sense. Their arsenal is literally infinite: any object, any weapon, any tool can be produced at will. They can also step outside the "frame" of their reality, rendering them intangible to forces that operate within a single dimensional plane.

**Discord (My Little Pony: Friendship is Magic):**
Discord is a primordial Chaos Creature, one of the oldest and most powerful entities in Equestria. Per the My Little Pony Fandom wiki, his abilities include: full matter manipulation (turning any substance into any other), reality warping on a local to regional scale, gravity manipulation, time manipulation (limited), shapeshifting, portal creation to other dimensions, sound and light manipulation, probability distortion, the creation of "chaos energy" blasts capable of leveling cities, the generation of duplicate constructs, the ability to turn his body into intangible chaos matter, the creation of black holes, the corruption of the fabric of spacetime, and a "chaos shield" that renders him nearly impervious to conventional physical and magical attacks. He was sealed in a crystal for one thousand years and was ultimately subdued only by the combined power of six Elements of Harmony wielded by a united group. His weakness is that he operates *within* the rules of his universe's physics, however distorted they may be.

---

## PART 1: THE CONVERGENCE

The sky above a grey, featureless plain split open like a wound. [A rift in the fabric of spacetime] tore across the heavens in a jagged line of violet and black, and from it tumbled a creature that defied geometry: a serpentine body of white fur and pink scales, a mane of flowing chaos-energy, and eyes that shifted between yellow, green, and a color that had no name. Discord stretched his long, lanky frame and yawned, his tongue tasting the air. "Hmph. Another dimension. How *tedious*," he drawled, his voice carrying the weight of centuries. He had been flung here by some interdimensional accident, and he was in no mood for company.

Three hundred yards to the east, a flat, circular patch of ground simply *ceased to exist* and was replaced by a hole in the air through which three figures dropped, landed, and stood up as if they had merely stepped off a curb. Yakko adjusted an invisible bow tie. Wakko's enormous mouth stretched into a grin that showed every tooth. Dot twirled a strand of pink hair and tilted her head.

"Yakko, I don't like this place," Dot said, her voice small but sharp. "There's no music. No color. No *anything*."

Yakko whistled. "Dot, sweetheart, there's no *here*. We fell out of the screen again. [Fourth-wall breach, third time this week.] But hey—" he spread his arms wide, "—at least the scenery is *minimalist*."

Wakko burped. "I'm hungry. Is there a snack machine? A vending machine? A *really* big sandwich?"

Before Yakko could answer, the ground beneath Discord's feet *liquefied*. He looked down. His shadow was no longer his shadow. It was a giant, grinning mouth with teeth like piano keys.

"Hello, Mr. Weird Snake!" Yakko called out, waving. "Name's Yakko. This is my brother Wakko, and this is my sister Dot. We're the Warner Brothers. Well, *Siblings*. We changed the name. Legal reasons."

Discord's eye narrowed. His chaos energy flared, and the grey ground around him turned to bubbling tar. "I am *Discord*, the Chaos Creature. I do not do *introductions*." He raised one long-fingered hand, and a sphere of crackling violet energy formed between his claws. "And I do not do *company*."

Dot stepped in front of her brothers. "He's being rude, Yakko."

"I noticed, Dot. I *noticed*."

---

## PART 2: FIRST BLOWS

Discord did not wait for a second greeting. The sphere of chaos energy *detonated*—not outward, but *inward*, collapsing into a point of infinite density and then expanding in a ring of anti-matter that tore a trench two hundred yards wide through the plain. The shockwave hit the Warners at full force.

Yakko, Wakko, and Dot were *flattened*. Not metaphorically. They became three-dimensional pancakes, pressed into the dirt like meat in a skillet. For one full second, they were nothing but flat, two-dimensional shapes. Then—*pop*—they inflated back to their original forms, shaking dirt from their fur and clothes.

"Ow," Wakko said, rubbing his head. "That *ow*."

"Right," Yakko said, his smile not wavering. "So. He's not a fan of small talk."

Discord had already moved. He was *everywhere*—a smear of white and pink across the sky, a shadow under the ground, a whisper in the wind. His body had become intangible chaos-matter, and he was *reaching* for them, tendrils of his form extending from every direction like a three-dimensional spider. "Let me see what you're made of, little *cartoon*," he hissed, and the tendrils *closed*.

They wrapped around Yakko's torso. The pressure was immense—enough to crush a mountain. Yakko's ribs cracked. His spine bent. He was being *compressed* into a space the size of a marble.

But then his face *smiled*.

"Hey, Wakko?" Yakko said, his voice muffled. "You remember that thing about being *flat*?"

Wakko, who was being wrapped in a separate tendril, grinned. "Flattening? Yeah."

"Good. Because I'm about to *be* it."

Yakko's body *stopped resisting*. He let the chaos tendrils compress him. He let them squeeze. And then—*snap*—he went *two-dimensional*. He became a flat, painted image, a *drawing* on the inside of Discord's tendril. The chaos matter, which operated in three dimensions, could not *grip* a two-dimensional surface. The tendrils slipped off him like water off glass.

Yakko peeled himself off the tendril, now a flat, smiling cartoon, and *tossed* himself back into three dimensions with a little *boing*.

Discord *stopped*. For the first time in a thousand years, something in his ancient, chaotic mind registered *confusion*. "What *are* you?"

"A cartoon, buddy," Yakko said. "And you're about to learn why that's a *problem*."

---

## PART 3: THE ARSENAL

Wakko did not wait for the conversation to continue. He reached into his mouth—*his actual mouth*—and *pulled* out a trombone. Not a small one. A *full-sized* brass trombone, three feet of gleaming metal. He extended the slide to its maximum length and *thwacked* Discord across the jaw.

The sound was *deafening*. A shockwave of pure acoustic force rippled outward, and the ground for a mile in every direction cracked and shattered. Discord's head snapped sideways. His chaos-matter body *rippled* where the trombone had struck, and for a brief moment, his form *solidified*—he was briefly, painfully, *tangible*.

"MY *FACE*!" Discord roared. His eyes had turned into spinning pinwheels of chaos. "You *insolent*—"

"Hey, Wakko, nice swing!" Dot called out. She had already produced a *gun*. Not a toy. A full-sized, silver-plated revolver with a barrel that glowed faintly blue. She aimed it at Discord's chest and *pulled the trigger*.

The bullet was not lead. It was a *word*—the word "STOP" rendered in physical form, a glowing blue glyph that screamed as it flew through the air. It struck Discord in the sternum and *exploded* in a shower of blue light. Discord staggered back, his chest *cracking* like porcelain.

"Ow ow ow ow *OW*," Discord sputtered, clutching his chest. His chaos shield flickered, dimmed, and *held*. Barely. The word-bullet had not penetrated, but it had *stung*. "You little *mice*—"

"We're not mice," Dot corrected, reloading. "We're *Warner Brothers*."

Yakko was already moving. He had pulled a *lever* out of thin air—a red, industrial lever on a little pedestal that simply *appeared* in his hand—and he *yanked* it. The sky above them *froze*. Not metaphorically. The clouds stopped moving. The wind died. The light from the non-existent sun *locked* in place. Time, in a radius of five miles, had *stopped*.

Discord's mouth was still open. His eyes were still spinning. He was *frozen* in a single frame of reality, a statue of chaos.

"Freeze," Yakko said, walking up to him. He examined Discord's face with the casual curiosity of a man inspecting a fruit at a market. "Huh. Scales. Sna-thing. Very *on-brand* for a guy named Discord." He poked Discord's nose. It was solid. "You're *real*. In here. In this frozen frame."

Wakko waddled up, trombone under his arm. "Can I hit him again?"

"Later, Wakko. Later."

Dot pointed her gun at Discord's frozen face. "Do we *kill* him, Yakko?"

Yakko considered this. He looked at Discord's frozen, furious face. He looked at the frozen sky. He looked at his siblings.

"No," he said. "We *finish* him. There's a difference. Killing is *boring*."

---

## PART 4: THE CHAOS UNLEASHED

Yakko released the time-freeze.

The sky *resumed*. The wind *howled*. And Discord *moved*.

But he was not the same Discord. The word-bullet, the trombone strike, the time-freeze—these had *angered* him. His chaos energy, which had been a simmer, was now a *flood*. His body *expanded*. He grew from his normal serpentine height to *two hundred feet*, his form *unraveling* at the edges into raw, screaming chaos. His eyes were no longer eyes. They were *portals*—swirling vortices that looked *into* other dimensions. His mouth was a *wound* in reality, and from it poured a sound that was not a sound but a *frequency*, a vibration that made the atoms in the ground *vibrate apart*.

"I will *unmake* you," Discord said, and his voice was the sound of a galaxy *dying*. "I will pull you apart *atom by atom* and scatter your *essence* across every dimension that *exists* and every dimension that *doesn't*. You will not *die*, little cartoons. You will *un-exist*. There will be *nothing* where you were. No memory. No trace. No *cartoon*."

He raised both hands, and the ground *dissolved*. Not cracked. Not shattered. *Dissolved*. The plain beneath them turned to a fine grey mist and *vanished*. The Warners were falling, dropping through a hole in the world, and below them was *nothing*—a void of absolute, lightless, soundless *absence*.

"Yakko!" Dot screamed.

Yakko *laughed*. He was falling, and he was *laughing*. "Wakko! DOT! Don't forget the *important* thing about cartoons!"

Wakko, tumbling end over end, trombone clutched to his chest, shouted back: "What?! What's the important thing?!"

"WE *DON'T* FALL! WE *BOING*!"

And they *boinged*. All three of them, mid-fall, hit an invisible floor that was not a floor but a *concept*—the concept of "the ground is here"—and they *bounced* upward, rocketing back through the hole in the world and into the sky.

Discord stared up at them, his chaos-energy blazing. "That's *impossible*."

"Nothing's impossible in a cartoon, big guy," Yakko called down. "You just gotta *believe* in the *gag*."

---

## PART 5: DISCORD'S COUNTER

Discord was not a fool. He had survived a thousand years of imprisonment. He had outwitted the most powerful mages in Equestria. He would not be *boinged* by three flat, ridiculous *mice*.

He *reached*. Not with his hands. With his *mind*. He extended his consciousness into the fabric of the local reality and *gripped* it. The air around the Warners *solidified*. Not into ice. Not into stone. Into *chaos*—a substance that was simultaneously solid and liquid, hot and cold, heavy and weightless. It wrapped around them like a cocoon, and it *squeezed*.

Dot's gun *cracked*. The metal twisted, the barrel bent, the trigger *melted* into a puddle of silver. She dropped it. "Yakko! The gun's *gone*!"

Yakko was *struggling*. The chaos-cocoon was *compressing* him, and for the first time, his cartoon-physics were *fighting back*. He was being squeezed, and he was *flat*, and he was *flat*, and he was *flat*—

"Yakko!" Wakko's voice was *distant*. He was in a separate cocoon, three feet away, and he was *screaming*. His trombone was *bending*, the brass warping under the pressure.

Discord *leaned in*. His face was inches from Yakko's cocoon, and his eyes were *calm*. "You are *interesting*," he said, and his voice was almost *gentle*. "You break the rules of *physics*. You break the rules of *dimension*. You break the rules of *narrative*. And yet—" he pressed his palm against the cocoon, and it *thickened*, "—you are still *bound*. You are still *in a story*. And every story has an *ending*."

He *squeezed*.

Yakko's flat form *cracked*. A line of white light split across his painted face. He *screamed*—a high, thin, *cartoon* scream that was less a sound and more a *vibration in the ink*.

But then—

"YAKKO!"

Dot was *singing*. Not a song. A *note*. A single, pure, *impossible* note that came from somewhere *outside* the cocoon, *outside* the chaos, *outside* the rules. It was the note that a cartoon character sings when they are about to *do the thing that breaks the show*. It was the note that says *I am not in your story. I am in MINE*.

The note *hit* the chaos-cocoon, and the cocoon *shattered*. Not broke. *Shattered*. Like glass. Like a *screen*. Like a *frame*.

Yakko, Wakko, and Dot tumbled free, gasping, *three-dimensional*, *whole*.

Discord *recoiled*. His hand was *smoking*. The chaos energy around his fingers was *flickering*, *dying*. "What... *what* was that?"

Dot wiped her mouth. "That was a *Dot*," she said. "And you *ow*."

---

## PART 6: THE SONG

Yakko was *bleeding*. Not cartoon blood. Not red. *White*—the white of blank paper, of empty space, of *unwritten*. The crack in his face was *wider*, and through it, he could see *nothing*. Not darkness. *Nothing*. The absence of the page.

"He's *damaged* us," Wakko said, and for the first time, his voice was not a joke. His eyes were *wide*. "Yakko, your *face*—"

"I know, Wakko." Yakko touched the crack. It *itched*. "I know."

Discord was *rebuilding*. His two-hundred-foot form was *shrinking*, condensing, *focusing*. The chaos energy that had been a flood was now a *laser*. He was *aiming*. His eyes had become two *suns*, and from them, he was *drawing* a beam of pure, concentrated *unmaking*.

"Last chance," Discord said. His voice was *flat*. "Last chance to *disappear* quietly."

Yakko looked at his siblings. Dot was *shaking*. Wakko's trombone was *bent beyond repair*. Yakko's face was *cracked*.

"Dot," Yakko said. "You remember the song?"

Dot's eyes *widened*. "The... the *one*?"

"The one. The *big* one. The one that *ends things*."

Dot closed her eyes. And she *sang*.

It started as a *hum*. A low, warm, *human* hum that had nothing to do with magic and everything to do with *being alive*. It was the sound of a sister who was *scared* but *refused to be*. It was the sound of a cartoon character who had been *flattened a thousand times* and *boinged back a thousand and one*.

Wakko *joined in*. His voice was *deeper*, *rougher*, a *bass* that made the ground *vibrate*. He was *singing* the trombone. Not playing it. *Singing* it. The bent brass *rang* with his voice, and the sound was *wrong*—it was the sound of a *thing that should not make a sound* making a sound, and it was *beautiful*.

Yakko *finished it*. His voice was *cracked*—literally, the crack in his face *vibrated* with each syllable—and it was *perfect*. It was the sound of a *joke* that is also a *truth*. It was the sound of a *cartoon* that is also a *life*.

The three voices *merged*. And the song *hit* Discord.

Not as a weapon. Not as a force. As a *story*. The song was a *story*, and the story was *this*: *You are powerful. You are ancient. You are chaos. But you are in a story. And in this story, you are NOT the hero. You are the GAG. And the gag ALWAYS wins.*

Discord *screamed*. The beam of unmaking *shattered* in his hands. His form *rippled*, *flickered*, *stuttered*. The chaos energy that held him together *wavered*. For one *moment*—one single, *infinite* moment—Discord was not chaos. Discord was *afraid*.

---

## PART 7: THE FOURTH WALL

Discord *broke*.

Not physically. *Narratively*. The song had *cracked* his understanding of the world he lived in, and through that crack, he saw *out*. He saw the *frame*. He saw the *page*. He saw the *screen*. And he saw *them*—the three small, flat, *impossible* figures standing in his world, *looking at him* with the casual, *knowing* gaze of characters who have *always* been looking at the audience.

"You *see* it," Yakko said. He was *walking* toward Discord. Each step was *deliberate*. The crack in his face was *glowing* white. "You see the *frame*. You see the *wall*. And you know, deep down, in your *chaos* heart, that you *can't* break it. Because you're *in* it. You're *on the page*. And we—" he pointed at himself, "—we *are* the page."

Discord *backed away*. His feet *sank* into the dissolving ground. "No. No, no, no. I am *chaos*. I am *beyond* the story. I am the *ink* and the *paper* and the *hand that writes*—"

"You're the *ink*," Yakko corrected. "And we're the *hand*. And the *paper*. And the *reader*. And the *joke*. And the *punchline*." He was *right in front of Discord now*. He was *smaller* than Discord. A hundred times smaller. And he was *smiling*. "And you know what the punchline is?"

Discord's eyes were *wild*. "No."

"The punchline is that *you're not real*."

Yakko *punched* Discord in the nose.

It was not a powerful punch. It was a *cartoon* punch. A *boing* punch. A punch that hit with the force of a *gag*—not a physical force, but a *narrative* force. The punch *landed*, and Discord's nose *cracked*, and the crack *spread*, and the crack went *through* his face, and the crack went *through* his body, and the crack went *through* his *story*.

Discord *split*. Not in half. In *narrative*. He was split into *character* and *concept*, and the concept *dissolved*, and the character *screamed*.

---

## PART 8: THE FRACTURE

Discord was *breaking apart*. His body was *fragmenting* into pieces of *chaos*—swirling, screaming, *dying* pieces that fell from the sky like *snow*. His form was *unraveling*, the white fur and pink scales *peeling away* to reveal *nothing* beneath. Not darkness. *Nothing*. The same *nothing* that was in the crack of Yakko's face.

"Yakko..." Discord's voice was *small*. Not a roar. Not a frequency. A *whisper*. "What... what *are* you?"

Yakko looked down at the *dying* chaos creature. The crack in his face was *wider*. The white *nothing* was *spreading*. He was *losing* himself. The punch had *cost* him. A cartoon punch, delivered with *narrative force*, had *wounded the narrator*. And the narrator was *him*.

"We're a *joke*, Discord," Yakko said. And his voice was *tired*. "We've been a joke for *years*. And jokes don't *die*. They just get *told differently*."

Wakko was *crying*. His big, round eyes were *full* of tears, and the tears were *white*—the same white as the *nothing* in Yakko's face. "Yakko, your *face*—it's *spreading*—"

"I know, Wakko."

Dot was *holding Yakko's hand*. Her small, pink hand was *wrapped* around his, and she was *squeezing*. "We'll fix it," she whispered. "We'll *always* fix it. That's what *siblings* do."

Discord *looked* at them. At the *small*, *flat*, *impossible* siblings who were *holding each other* while the world *ended* around them. And something in his ancient, chaotic, *infinite* mind *shifted*.

Discord *laughed*. It was a *small* laugh. A *broken* laugh. The laugh of a *god* who is *dying* and *knows it*.

"Tell me something," Discord whispered. "When I'm *gone*... will the *joke* still be *funny*?"

Yakko *smiled*. The crack in his face *glowed*. "Oh, *buddy*. The joke's *always* funny."

---

## PART 9: THE LAST CHAOS

Discord's body *shattered*.

It was not an explosion. It was an *unmaking*. His form *dissolved* into a million pieces of *chaos*—swirling, *screaming*, *dying* fragments that *rained* down on the plain. Each fragment was a *piece* of him: a scale, a tuft of fur, a *memory*, a *feeling*, a *fear*, a *joy*. They fell like *snow*, and where they landed, the ground *bloomed*—not with flowers, but with *color*. With *sound*. With *life*.

But one fragment *remained*. One *single* piece of Discord, *floating* in the air, *spinning*, *screaming*. It was his *eye*. One eye. A *yellow* eye, *spinning*, *looking* at the three siblings with an expression that was *fear* and *wonder* and *something else*—something *new*.

"Yakko," the eye *said*. Its voice was *thin*. "The *frame*. The *wall*. You said we're *in* it. But *what's outside*?"

Yakko looked at the eye. He looked at the *nothing* spreading across his face. He looked at his *siblings*.

"Outside?" he said. "Outside is *you*, Discord. Outside is *everyone*. Outside is the *reader*. And the reader *always* gets the *last laugh*."

The eye *blinked*. And then it *dissolved*. The last piece of Discord *unmade* itself, and the plain was *quiet*. The sky was *grey*. The ground was *flat*. And the three siblings stood in the *silence*, *whole* and *broken* at the same time.

Wakko *burped*. "So... does that mean we win?"

Yakko looked at his face. The crack was *still there*. The *nothing* was *still spreading*. But it was *slower* now. *Slower*.

"Yeah, Wakko," he said. "I think we win."

## PART 10: THE PUNCHLINE

They stood in the grey silence for a long time. The plain was *empty*. The sky was *empty*. The world was *empty*. And the three siblings were *small* in it.

"Dot," he said. "You know what a *punctuation mark* is?"

"A *pause*," he said. "A *breath*. A *moment* where the *sentence* *stops* and *thinks* before it *keeps going*. And that crack?" He *smiled*. "That's my *comma*. And the *sentence* isn't *over*."

Wakko *waddled* over. He *hugged* Yakko. He *hugged* Dot. He *hugged* both of them *at the same time*, which was *impossible* given the *geometry* of the situation, but it was a *cartoon*, so it *worked*.

"Me too, big guy," Yakko said.

"Well," he said. "I think that's a wrap."

Dot *stood up*. She *dusted* off her dress. She *twirled* a strand of pink hair.

"Same time next week," Yakko confirmed.

Wakko *burped*. "I'm *still* hungry."

And the *screen* *closed*. And the *joke* *ended*. And the *punchline* *landed*.

# The Day the Universe Decided I Was the Main Character (And I Was Absolutely *Not* Okay With It)

---

My name is Hoshino Yuki, and I am, with the absolute and unshakeable certainty of a woman who has stared into the abyss of her own reflection every morning for sixteen years, *average*.

Not "average" in the way that means "moderately talented" or "slightly above the statistical median in a way that would make a parent proud at a dinner party." No. I am average in the way that means if you were to photograph the entirety of Class 2-B in a single frame, I would be the one slightly behind the front row, with my hands folded neatly in my lap, my hair—brown, unremarkable, perpetually escaping its clip at the nape of my neck—falling in a way that suggests I *tried* to look presentable but the universe had a different, lazier plan. My uniform is pressed. My shoes are polished. My face is the kind of face you forget three seconds after meeting it. I am, in the most literal and unglamorous sense, *background character energy*. I am the girl who exists so the protagonist has someone to say "Oh, Yuki, you're here too!" to. I am the NPC. I am the extra in the crowd shot. I am the one who, in a manga, would have no name tag and would be rendered in three lines of grey pencil.

I *liked* this. I *cherished* this. Being invisible was my armor, my comfort, my carefully curated little life where nothing ever happened to me and the biggest drama I ever experienced was whether the vending machine would dispense my melon soda or make me press the button four more times while a line of students formed behind me, sighing.

And then, on a Tuesday in October—the kind of Tuesday where the autumn wind had just started carrying that particular crisp, slightly melancholy scent of fallen ginkgo leaves, and the sky was that impossibly pale, washed-out blue that makes you feel like the world has been gently bleached—and then, on that *Tuesday*, the universe looked at my perfectly, beautifully *average* life and said, "Nope. Not anymore, sweetheart. You're the protagonist now. You have a *sparkle*. You have a *journey*. You have a *slime girl*."

And I wanted to die. I wanted to fold myself into a small, beige, unremarkable cube and dissolve into the carpet of the school hallway like a stain that no amount of industrial cleaner could lift.

---

It happened in the courtyard.

I had been walking to the east side of the building, where the old cherry tree stood bare and skeletal against the October sky, because that was where I ate lunch. Always. Every day. The same bench, the same corner of the courtyard where the afternoon sun hit at exactly the right angle to make the concrete glow faintly gold. I had my bento box—mild, unremarkable, packed by my mother with exactly the right amount of tamagoyaki and a single, slightly overcooked piece of grilled salmon—and I had my melon soda, and I had my *peace*.

I sat down. I opened my bento. I took a bite of the tamagoyaki. It was, as always, perfectly adequate.

And then I heard it.

A sound like someone was dropping a handful of glass marbles into a bowl of warm honey. *Tink-tink-tink-tink-tink*, but wetter, softer, with a kind of *squelch* underneath, like someone slowly pressing their thumb into a very expensive, very gelatinous stress ball. And then a *plop*. A soft, wet, *satisfying* plop, right next to my bench. Like a very large, very cold drop of something had landed on the concrete.

I looked down.

And I saw *her*.

She was—

Well. I don't have a word for what she was. I don't have a word for what was sitting on the ground beside my bench, looking up at me with two enormous, luminous, *iridescent* eyes that were the color of liquid opal, shifting between violet and gold and a pink so vivid it made my own cheeks feel embarrassed by comparison.

She was *translucent*. That's the only word that comes close, and even that doesn't do it justice. She was like looking through a pane of glass that had been made of *light itself*—you could see, faintly, the concrete beneath her, the way you can see the bottom of a very clear, very still pond. But she wasn't *clear*. She was *full* of color. Swirling, shifting, *living* color, like someone had taken a watercolor palette and dropped it into a glass of water and then *animated* the result. Pinks and blues and greens and golds and a deep, deep violet that pulsed in her core like a slow, gentle heartbeat. And *crystalline*—there were facets in her, little geometric planes of refraction that caught the October sun and threw tiny rainbows across the concrete, across my bento box, across the *inside of my eyelids* when I blinked. And *glitter*. Oh god, the *glitter*. It wasn't the flat, dead glitter of a craft store. It was *alive*, suspended in her translucent body like stars in a nebula, catching the light and throwing it back in tiny, sharp, *insane* pinpricks of color that made my eyes water. And *goopy*. She *dripped*. Slowly, languidly, a single thick strand of that prismatic, crystalline substance stretched down from her "chin" (if you could call it a chin; it was more of a *gradient*, a softening of form where the upper body simply *became* the lower body in a way that defied anatomy) and *plop* dropped onto the concrete, where it sat for a moment, shimmering, before slowly, *slowly* reabsorbing back into her with a soft, wet *shlup*.

She was about the height of my knees. She was *round* in the way that a very large, very happy water balloon is round. She had—arms? Appendages? *Extensions*?—that were more like thick, tapered tendrils of the same translucent, crystalline, glittering substance, and they were *waving*. Waving at me. One of them was raised in a little wave, and the motion was *fluid*, *liquid*, like watching someone wave through a jar of very thick, very colorful gelatin. And when she waved, little *sparks*—actual, visible, *physical* sparks of light, like the ones in a fireworks display but miniature, the size of fireflies—popped off the tip of her appendage and drifted upward, catching the wind, dissolving into nothing after a few seconds.

And she was *smiling*.

I don't know how else to describe it. Her "face"—the two enormous opal eyes, the soft upward curve where a mouth would be, the little *dimple* of color that deepened at the corners—was *smiling*. At me. At *me*, Hoshino Yuki, the girl who is the visual equivalent of beige wallpaper. She was looking at me with an expression of such *pure, uncomplicated, radiant joy* that I felt my stomach do a little flip-flop that had absolutely nothing to do with the overcooked salmon.

"Hi!" she said.

Her voice was like a music box made of glass bells being played underwater. Each word was a little *chime*, a little *tinkle*, with a faint, wet *bloop* underneath, like a very happy, very contented cat purring through a layer of warm honey.

"Hi! I like your lunch! The yellow thing! It smells like *sun*!"

I stared at her.

She stared at me.

A spark popped off her head. It drifted up, caught the light, and burst into a tiny shower of golden motes.

My brain, that magnificent, overtaxed, *average* brain that had never once in its sixteen years of existence been asked to process a sentient, translucent, crystalline, glittering, goopy, *singing* slime sitting on the concrete beside my lunch bench, performed a slow, grinding, *metallic* halt.

*What*, my brain said, in the flat, dead tone of a man watching his house burn. *What. What. What. What. What. What.*

"I—," I started.

My mouth opened. My mouth closed. My mouth opened again. A single, thin, *pathetic* sound escaped my throat. It was not a word. It was not a sentence. It was the vocal equivalent of a dial-up modem trying to connect to a server that had been decommissioned in 2003.

"*B-b-b-b-*"

She tilted her head. The motion was *liquid*, her entire upper body *flowing* to the left like a slow-motion wave, the crystalline facets in her form catching the light and throwing a new constellation of tiny rainbows across my face. A drip stretched from her left side, hung for a moment, swayed, and *plop* dropped.

"Are you okay? You're *blushing*! That's a *color*! I like your color! It's like a *peach*! A very *shy* peach!"

"I am *not* blushing," I said, and the words came out in a voice that was approximately three octaves higher than my natural register, and *cracked* on the word "not," and I could *feel* the heat flooding my cheeks, my neck, the tops of my ears, a full-body conflagration of *mortification* so intense and so *total* that I was certain I was, at that very moment, becoming a *human* heat source, that the concrete beneath my bench was going to *melt*, that the ginkgo leaves on the ground were going to *ignite*.

"I *am* blushing," she said, with the serene, unbothered confidence of a child stating that the sky is blue. She reached one of her goopy, crystalline appendages toward my face. "Let me *see*—"

"*DON'T TOUCH ME*," I shrieked, and I *flinched*, and my bento box *slid* off my lap and *clattered* onto the concrete, and the tamagoyaki *split* open, and the salmon *slid* out, and the rice *scattered* in a small, sad, white constellation across the grey ground, and I was on my *feet*, I was *backing away*, I was *stumbling*, and my heel caught the edge of the bench and I *nearly* fell, and I *did* fall, a little, a *graceful* little fall, the kind where you catch yourself with one hand on the ground and the other hand goes up in a little *flail*, and my hair *fell* over my face, and I was *crawling* backward on my hands and knees, and I was *screaming*, not with my voice, but *inside*, a long, continuous, *metallic* scream of *WHAT IS HAPPENING TO ME WHY IS THIS HAPPENING TO ME I AM AVERAGE I AM BACKGROUND I AM THE EXTRA IN THE CROWD SHOT WHY IS THERE A SLIME GIRL ON THE CONCRETE WHY IS SHE LOOKING AT ME WHY DOES SHE LIKE MY LUNCH WHY DOES SHE CALL MY BLUSH A PEACH I AM GOING TO DIE I AM GOING TO DIE I AM GOING TO DIE—*

And she *followed*.

Not *rushed*. Not *chased*. She *flowed*. Her entire body *stretched* and *poured* forward like a very large, very colorful, very *glittering* puddle, and she *reformed* a little closer to me, and then *flowed* again, and *reformed* again, and she was *pursuing* me across the courtyard with the gentle, inexorable patience of a tide, and with every *plop* she made, a little shower of sparks popped off her body and drifted upward, and the concrete *shimmered* where she'd been, and the air smelled like—

Like *rain*. Like the first drop of rain on hot asphalt in summer. Like *ozone* and *sugar* and something *electric* and *new*.

"YUKI! *YUKI*! WAIT! I JUST WANTED TO *TALK*! I LIKE YOUR *SALMON*! IT'S *CRUNCHY* ON THE OUTSIDE! I *WANT* TO *TALK* ABOUT *CRUNCH*!"

"I DON'T *WANT* TO TALK ABOUT *CRUNCH*!" I wailed, and I was on my *knees* again, and I was *crawling* toward the building, and my *face* was *on fire*, and my *uniform* was *wrinkled*, and my *hair* was a *disaster*, and I was *the most un-average thing I had ever been in my life* and I *hated* it, I *hated* it, I *hated* it—

And then I hit the wall.

I hit the *concrete wall* of the east building, and my *forehead* made a soft *thud* with it, and I *slid* down, and I was *sitting* on the ground, *backed against the wall*, *hugging my knees*, and the slime girl *plop* landed in front of me, and she was *looking up*, and she was *smiling*, and she was *sparkling*, and she said, in her little glass-bell voice, "You're *safe* now. I'm not going to *eat* you. I *promise*. I only eat *sadness* and *stagnant air* and *the feeling of being a little bit lonely on a Tuesday*. And you have *so much* of that. I can *smell* it. It smells like *old library books* and *cold tea*."

I *screamed*.

Not a *shriek*. Not a *wail*. A *scream*. A full-throated, *diaphragm-deep*, *soul-leaving-the-body* scream that I am *certain* registered on seismographs in the next prefecture.

And then—

And then the *others* came.

---

They came from *everywhere*.

From the east, from the direction of the main building, came **Tanaka Riko**, my *deskmate*, a girl with a sharp jaw and sharper opinions and a ponytail that she whipped around like a *whip* when she was angry, which was *constantly*. She was *running*, her loafers *slapping* against the concrete, her blazer *flapping*, her face a mask of *furious concern*.

"YUKI! *YUKI*! WHAT THE *HELL* ARE YOU *SCREAMING* ABOUT?!"

From the west, from the direction of the library, came **Sato Haruki**, the *class president*, a tall, *impossibly* handsome boy with a jawline that could *cut glass* and a voice that was *warm* and *low* and *exactly* the kind of voice that made girls in the *next* class *sigh* and *drop their books*. He was *running* too, which was *unlike* him, because Haruki Sato did not *run*, Haruki Sato *strode*, Haruki Sato *moved through the world with the unhurried grace of a man who knew that the world would *wait* for him, but he was *running*, and his *tie* was *loose*, and his *face* was *pale*, and he was *calling my name* in that *warm, low* voice, and I wanted to *die* in a *different* way, a *slower* way, a *more* *dignified* way.

"Yuki! Yuki, are you *all right*? What *happened*? Is someone *hurting* you?"

From *above*, from the *second-floor* balcony, came **Mizuki Aoi**, the *art club president*, a girl with *wild* hair and *paint-stained* fingers and *eyes* that were *always* *looking* at something *slightly* *behind* you, as if she were *seeing* a *sketch* of you that was *more* *interesting* than the *actual* you. She was *leaning* over the *railing*, *paintbrush* in *hand*, *mouth* *open*, *staring* at the *slime girl* with an expression of *pure, unadulterated, *insane* *joy*.

"*Oh my GOD*," Aoi whispered, and then, *louder*, "*OH MY GOD*, look at the *refraction*! Look at the *crystalline lattice* in her *left* *appendage*! It's a *hexagonal* *close-packed* *structure*! It's *BEAUTIFUL*!"

And from the *north*, from the *garden* behind the *gymnasium*, came **Fujimoto Kenji**, the *basketball* *captain*, a *mountain* of a *boy* with *forearms* like *tree trunks* and a *face* that was *permanently* *confused*, as if he were *constantly* *trying* to *solve* a *math* *problem* that *wasn't* *written* *anywhere*. He was *standing* *still*, *basketball* in *hand*, *staring* at the *slime girl*, and his *mouth* was *open*, and a *single* *droplet* of *saliva* was *hanging* from his *lower lip*, and he said, in a *voice* like a *thundercloud* *clearing*, "…Is that… a *slime*…?"

And from the *south*, from the *vending machine* *corner*, came *everyone else*. The *entire* *second-year* *class*. The *first-year* *class*. A *group* of *third-year* *girls* in *their* *senior* *blazers*. The *lunch lady*, *Ms. Ota*, *peering* *over* her *glasses*. *Two* *cherry* *blossom* *petals* *drifted* *down* from *the* *bare* *tree* and *landed* *on* *the* *slime girl's* *head*, where they *stuck*, *shimmering*, *refracting* *the* *light* *into* *tiny* *pink* *stars*.

And they were all *looking* at me.

*All* of them. *Every* single one. *Forty-seven* *pairs* of *eyes*, *plus* *two* *enormous*, *opal*, *iridescent* *pairs*, *all* *focused* on *me*, *Hoshino Yuki*, *the* *girl* who *was* *the* *visual* *equivalent* of *beige* *wallpaper*, *the* *extra* in the *crowd* *shot*, *the* *NPC* who *existed* so the *protagonist* had *someone* to *say* "Oh, Yuki, you're here too!" to.

And I was *sitting* on the *concrete*, *backed* against the *wall*, *hugging* my *knees*, *hair* *over* my *face*, *uniform* *wrinkled*, *face* *on* *fire*, *bento* *box* *scattered* *at* my *feet*, *salmon* *sliding* *toward* the *drain*, and in *front* of me, *pulsing* and *shimmering* and *dripping* *tiny* *rainbows* onto the *concrete*, was a *sentient*, *translucent*, *crystalline*, *glittering*, *goopy*, *sparkling*, *prismatic*, *iridescent*, *singing*, *smiling* *slime girl* who *liked* my *salmon* and *called* my *blush* a *peach* and *smelled* my *loneliness* like *old* *library* *books* and *cold* *tea*.

And Tanaka Riko *skidded* to a *halt* in *front* of me, *hands* on her *hips*, *ponytail* *swishing*, and *looked* *down* at me, and *looked* at the *slime girl*, and *looked* at me *again*, and her *face* went *through* *fourteen* *different* *emotions* in the *space* of *three* *seconds*, and then she *screamed*.

"YUKI *HOSHINO*! WHAT *THE* *ACTUAL* *HELL* IS *THAT*?!"

"It's *friend*," the slime girl said, *brightly*, *popping* a *spark* off her *head*. "Her *name* is *Yuki*. I *like* her. She's *warm*. And *a little bit* *sad*. And her *salmon* is *crunchy*."

"*I* *AM* *NOT* *SAD*," I *snarled* from *behind* my *hair*.

"You *are* *sad*," the slime girl said, *gently*, *tilting* her *head*, *flowing* *slightly* *toward* me. "You're *sad* in a *very* *quiet* *way*. Like a *small* *room* with *no* *windows*. I can *see* it. I can *see* *all* of it. I'm *translucent*, you *know*. I can *see* *through* *things*. I can *see* *through* *you*. And you're *very* *small* *inside*, Yuki. And *very* *quiet*. # Dvanáct lekcí

## I. Sázka

Tomáš měl v sobě něco, co lidi kolem něj trápilo. Nebyl to jen hlasitý smích, s kterým vcházel do třídy, ani to, jak Katčiným věcmi pohrdal. Byl to ten tichý, systematický způsob, jakým ji každý den trochu menšil. „Tohle umíš jen proto, že sis to nacvičila," říkal, když Katka předvedla něco, na čem pracovala týdny. „Kdybys byla normální, nemusela bys tolik cvičit." A Katka to polykala. Dny, týdny, měsíce.

Až jednoho odpoledne, když Tomáš zase přeháněl – tentokrát před celým oddělením na střední škole, kde Katčinu prezentaci označil za „dětské kreslení" – se Katka usmála. Tím chladným, tichým úsměvem, který Tomáš dosud nezažil.

„Vsadíme se," řekla.

Tomáš se zasmál. „Vsadíme se na co, Katko? Že mi uděláš čaj?"

„Že ti vymyslím činnost, kterou nezvládneš. Dvanáct lekcí. Pokud je všechny dokončíš, vyhráváš. Pokud ne – prohraješ."

„A co sázka?"

Katka se podívala na své vlasy. Dlouhé, tmavé, sahající jí k lopatкам. „Pokud prohraju, ostříháš mi je. Všechny. Na nuly."

Tomášovi se rozzářily oči. „Dobře. Jsem tvůj. A co když *já* prohraju?"

„Nic. Jen to, že přestaneš být arogantní na veřejnosti. Aspoň na týden."

Tomáš kývl, jakoby to bylo samozřejmé. „Tak si to vymysli, Katko. Jsem zvědavý, co mi vymyslíš, že by mě porazilo."

## II. Plán

Katka věděla přesně, co dělá. Nebyla to pomsta v tom krutém slova smyslu – byla to zrcadlovka. Tomáš ji trápil tím, že ji přinutil dělat věci, které ji trapily. Teď ona udělá totéž. A Tomáš, který si vsadil vlastní ego, bude muset přijít na to, co mu Katka připravila, až bude příliš pozdě.

Další den zvedla telefon.

„Dobrý den, jmenuji se Kateřina Vlková. Hledám pro svého… známého… kurz baletu. Začínajícího. Myslím, že bude potřebovat… zvláštní přístup."

Na druhém konci linky se usmála paní Margita Dvořáková, šedesátiletá baletní pedagožka s třiceti lety zkušeností a očima, které viděly každý sval, každý zbytečný pohyb.

„Zvláštní přístup? Co tím myslíte?"

„Myslím, paní Dvořáková, že tenhle chlapec bude arogantní. Bude se bránit. Bude se smát. Bude tvrdit, že to není pro něj. A já potřebuju, aby to pro něj bylo *maximálně* náročné. A maximálně… viditelné. Chci, aby se cítil přesně tak, jak se cítila já, když mi říkal, že to, co dělám, je hloupé."

Paní Dvořáková si odložila šálku čaje. „Rozumím. A co oblečení?"

„Standardní baletní. Těsné. Viditelné. Nic, co by mu zakrývalo, že je v baletním oděvu. A obuv – ne běžné baletky. Co máte nejzáludnějšího?"

„Mám pár *pointe* s dřevěnou špičkou a koženým páskem. A mám i taneční pantofle s nízkým podpatkem, které drží pata pevně, ale noha se v nich točí. A pro trestné cviky – vysoké baletky, ty staré, s dlouhým šňůrováním. Budete potřebovat i speciální punčocháče – tenké, černé, s výstřihem, a leotard. Krátký. S dlouhým rukávem, aby viděl, co má na sobě, ale nebyl v tom příliš zakrytý."

„Dokonalé," řekla Katka. „A cviky?"

Paní Dvořáková se zasmála. „Pro chlapce, který se bude bránit, arogantního a drzého? Mám pro něj pár věcí, které jsem si nechala na starší časy. Ale musím vám říct – bude to tvrdé. Ne fyzicky nebezpečné, ale…"

„Chci, aby to bylo tvrdé," přerušila Katka.

## III. První lekce

Tomáš přišel do sálu s rukama v kapsách a úsměvem, který říkal *uvidíme, co mi ta Katka vymyslí, ale určitě to bude něco hloupého*. Sál měl zrcadla od podlahy po strop, dřevěnou podlahu a tyčinky podél stěn. Uprostřed stála starší žena v černém, s vlasy spletenými do culíku, a před ní na zemi ležel balíček oblečení.

„Tomáši, vítejte. Jsem paní Dvořáková. Budu vám vést dvanáct lekcí."

Tomáš se podíval na balíček. „Tohle je… co to je?"

„Vaše uniforma. Oblečte se."

Tomáš se podíval na Katku, která stála v rohu s rukama zkříženýma. „Katko, tohle je – co to je?"

„Sázka, Tomáši. Dvanáct lekcí. Co to je, to se dozvíš, až se oblečeš."

Tomáš rozevřel balíček. Černé tenké punčocháče. Krátký leotard s dlouhým rukávem, těsný, z lesklého materiálu. A pár bílých baletních pantoflí, měkkých, s koženým páskem.

„Ne," řekl.

„Oblečte se," řekla paní Dvořáková klidně.

„Ne, já se nebudu oblékat do – do *tohoto*. To je – to je pro holky."

„Balet není pro holky, pane Tomáši. Balet je pro lidi, kteří mají tělo. A vaše tělo bude dneska cvičit. Oblečte se, nebo lekce nezačneme a sázka se počítá jako prohraná."

Tomáš se podíval na Katku. Katka se nepohnula. Jen na něj pohlédla.

Oblékl se.

Leotard mu seděl těsně, punčocháče mu obalily nohy a Tomáš cítil, jak mu v tvářích stoupá teplo. Baletní pantofle mu sedly na nohy jako rukavice. Podíval se do zrcadla a na okamžik – jen na okamžik – se v něm zrcadlil někdo, kdo se mu nelíbil.

„Tak," řekla paní Dvořáková. „První lekce. Rozhýbání. Kroužení hlavou, kroužení rameny, kroužení boky. Pomalu. S dýcháním. Začínáme."

Tomáš kroužil hlavou. Cítil se jako loutka.

## IV. Lekce – co čekalo

Paní Dvořáková měla pro Tomáše připravený program, který by i zkušeného tanečníka přinutil potit se.

**Lekce 1–3: Základy, které nejsou základní**

Nejdřív *plié* – ale ne na místě. Paní Dvořáková Tomáše přinutila dělat *plié* v polopřepadu, s jednou nohou napnutou vzad tak vysoko, jak to jeho tělo dovolí, a s rukama v *quatrième* poloze. Potom *tendu* – noha napnutá dopředu, do strany, dozadu – ale vždy s paží nataženou přes hlavu v *port de bras*, což mu trhálo ramena.

A pak *pique turn* – otočky. Jedna. Dvě. Tři. A paní Dvořáková stála vedle s metlou a každou otočku, která nebyla dokonalá, odpočítávala. „Začínáme znovu. Desetkrát."

**Lekce 4–6: Vysoké baletky a špičky**

Zde přišly *pointe* – vysoké baletky s dřevěnou špičkou. Tomáš se je pokusil obout a paní Dvořáková mu šňůrování utáhla tak pevně, že mu prsty ztuhly.

„Stojíte na špičkách. *Relevé*. Dvanáct sekund. Pak *demi-pointe*. Pak *relevé* znovu. A teď – *saut de chat*. Skok, kde se noha v letu ohýbá do *attitude* a přistáváte na špičce. Pětkrát. A teď – *fouetté*. Otočky na špičce. Dvacet."

Tomáš se po desáté otočce zhroutil na kolena. „Tohle je – tohle není – já tohle –"

„Dvacet. Začínáme znovu. A tentokrát s *port de bras*, protože vaše paže visí jako mrtvé."

**Lekce 7–9: Netradiční cviky**

Zde paní Dvořáková vytáhla z rukávu věci, které Tomáš nečekal.

*„Allegro na zemi."* Tomáš musel ležet na břiše, nohy natažené vzad, a dělat rychlé *battement* – úder nohou – zatímco paže kreslily kruhy nad hlavou. Pak *grand battement* – noha vyletující tak vysoko, jak to jde – ale z pozice na kolenou, s trupem nakloněným dozadu.

*„Adagio na tyčince – ale bez tyčinky."* Pomalé, kontrolní pohyby, *plié* přecházející do *tendu*, do *dégagé*, do *battement tendu haut* – vše v pomalém tempu, s držením každé polohy po osm úderů. „A tentokrát s očima zavřenýma. Chcete vědět, kde jste v prostoru, pane Tomáši?"

*„Turnout z boků."* Tomáše postavila k zrcadlu a přinutila ho držet *turnout* – otočení kyčlí – v *plié* po třicet sekund. Pak v *passé*. Pak v *croisé*. „Vaše kyčle jsou zamčené jako dveře. Otevřete je. Třicet sekund. Začínáme."

**Lekce 10–12: Finále**

Poslední tři lekce byly kombinací všeho. *Grand allegro* – velké skoky, *grand jeté*, *saut de chat*, *entrechat six* – ale s *port de bras* a s *turnoutem* a s *relevé* na špičce při přistání. A na závěr lekce 12: *variations*. Tomáš musel zvládnout tři kompletní variace – *adagio*, *allegro* a *pirouette* – za sebou, bez přestávky, s hudbou.

## V. Trestné cviky

Tomáš nebyl slušný. Na třetí lekci řekl paní Dvořákové: „Tohle je hloupé. Já tohle nedělám."

Paní Dvořáková se usmála. „Trest. Padesát *plié* v *croisé*, noha na špičce, paže v *quatrième*. Bez přestávky. A s úsměvem, protože se musíte učit, že disciplína není volitelná."

Tomáš se otočil. Jedna. Dvě. Tři. Čtyři. Pět. Na šesté se mu noha vykřikla. Na sedmé ztratil rovnováhu. Na osmé se zhroutil.

# Floor 47

The Rescuer's Journal said: *Sable, Drowzee. Last seen: Floor 47 of the Tower. Status: Unrescued.*

Marin had read that line eleven times before the elevator doors opened.

---

The Tower was not a dungeon in the way the others were. There were no monsters here. No traps that triggered on a wrong step, no crumbling bridges over bottomless dark. The Tower was simply *floors*. One after another, climbing or falling, each one a little darker than the last, the air a little thinner, the silence a little heavier. You could always see the exit. You could always see the light at the top, golden and warm, where the sky was and the wind was and the other Pokémon were *out there*, living.

You just couldn't climb.

Marin had been on the Rescue Team for three years. Three years of exploring, of pulling Pokémon out of the deep places, of saying *I've got you, I've got you, just hold on, we're going up, we're going up, we're going up.* Lapras were built for this. The shell on the back was not armor. It was a *place to sit*. A place for someone who was too tired to walk to rest while you carried them. That was the whole point. That was the whole *you*.

Sable had been on the team for two years.

Sable, who used to nap in the sun on the roof of the Rescue Team HQ with their eyes half-closed, humming. Sable, who had a habit of falling asleep in the middle of briefings and waking up with a smile, as if the dream had been a good one. Sable, who once carried a Furret out of a flooded cave for six floors without a single complaint, just because the Furret was shaking and Sable said, *I don't mind. I don't mind. You can rest on my back, I don't mind.*

Sable had stopped saying *I don't mind* four months ago.

Then Sable had stopped coming to briefings. Then Sable had stopped answering the comms. Then Sable had stopped *existing*, as far as the team could tell, and the only thing left was a single entry in the Journal, typed in Marin's own careful handwriting because no one else would do it:

*Floor 47. Unrescued.*

---

The elevator dropped.

Forty-seven floors. Marin counted them the way you count the seconds after a loud noise, when the world goes quiet and you're waiting to see if it will come back. *Thirty-one. Thirty-two. Thirty-three.* The air pressure changed. The light from the shaft above shrank to a coin, then a pinprick, then nothing.

Forty-seven.

The doors opened onto a room that was not a room. It was a *space*. A flat, gray, featureless space with a single bed in the center and a single window that looked out onto nothing. Not darkness. *Nothing.* The absence of a view. The absence of a sky. The absence of *outside.*

Sable was on the bed.

They were smaller than Marin remembered. Or maybe Marin had just always been big. Sable's eyes were open, but they were not *seeing*. They were looking at the middle distance, at a point just past the wall, at a place where the wall wasn't. Their paws were folded on their chest. They were breathing. That was the thing. They were still breathing.

"Sable."

No response.

"Sable, it's me. It's Marin. I'm here."

A blink. Slow. Like a creature surfacing from very deep water, where the pressure is so great that even opening your eyes is a negotiation.

"Marin." The voice was a thread. A wire so thin it might snap if you breathed on it. "You shouldn't be here. This is a *deep floor.* Your heart will take damage."

"I don't care."

"You should." Sable turned their head. Just a little. Just enough. "You've got a shell. You've got a *team.* You've got a *reason* to be up there. I don't have a reason to be up there."

"I have a reason to be *here.*"

Sable almost smiled. Almost. The way the sky almost looks like it's going to clear before the rain comes back. "You don't. You're doing a *rescue.* You're checking a box. *Sable, Drowzee. Floor 47. Status: Rescued.* And then you go back up, and you file the report, and you carry the next one, and the next one, and the next one, and you never stop, because if you stop, you have to think about the fact that you can't save everyone, and that's a floor you don't want to go to."

Marin's throat closed.

Because Sable was right. Because Sable had always been right. Because the shell on Marin's back was full of other people's weight, and they had forgotten what it felt like to be *carried*, and the only time they'd felt it in three years was the night Sable had walked into the Tower and not walked back out, and Marin had sat on the roof of HQ until the sun came up and the sun went down and the sun came up again, and no one had come to carry *them.*

"Come up," Marin said. "Get on my back. I'll carry you. I'll carry you all the way. You don't have to climb. You don't have to *do* anything. You just have to let me."

Sable was quiet for a long time.

The window that looked out onto nothing flickered. For a second, just a second, it looked like it might show something. A sky. A tree. A street. *Outside.*

Then it was nothing again.

"I tried," Sable said. "Marin. I *tried.* I was on Floor 12 and I thought, *okay, I can do this, I can go back up, I can go back to the team, I can go back to the sun on the roof.* And I climbed. And I got to Floor 8. And I looked up, and the light was *right there*, and I thought, *one more, just one more floor.* And I climbed. And I got to Floor 5. And the light was *right there.* And I turned around."

"Why?"

"Because the light was *too much.*" Sable's eyes were wet. "Because I'd been in the dark so long that the light *hurt.* And I thought, *I can't go back into that. I can't be in that. I can't be where everyone is* *okay* *and I'm not. I can't be where the sun is and I'm still* *this.* And so I turned around. And I climbed down. And I didn't stop."

Marin stepped forward. Put a paw on Sable's shoulder. The weight of it. The *warmth* of it. The whole point. The whole *you.*

"Sable. I'm here. You don't have to be okay. You don't have to be *fixed.* You just have to come up. You can come up *broken.* You can come up and sit on the roof and not hum and not smile and not *do anything,* and I will sit next to you, and the sun will be too much, and that's *fine.* We don't have to go into the light. We just have to leave the dark."

Sable looked at Marin. Really looked. The way you look at someone when you are trying to decide if what they're saying is true, and you are *so tired* of deciding, and you just want someone to *take the deciding away from you.*

"I can't," Sable whispered. "Marin. I'm so *tired.* I've been climbing for so long. I can't. I'm sorry. I'm so *sorry.*"

Marin's paw stayed on their shoulder.

The elevator behind them chimed. A soft, polite, *mechanical* sound. The doors were opening. The shaft of light from above was widening, creeping across the gray floor like a tide.

*Your heart is taking damage,* the Tower said. Not in words. In a pressure behind the sternum. A cold. A *thinning.* The way the air thins at high altitude. The way the world gets quieter and quieter until you can't hear your own heartbeat.

Marin had to go.

They *knew* they had to go. If they stayed, the floor would take them too. The dark would get into the shell, and the next time someone needed carrying, there would be no room. No *space.* The shell would be full of *this*, and they would carry it up, and up, and up, and they would never set it down, and they would be *this* forever, and the team would lose two, and the Journal would have two entries, and no one would read them because no one reads the entries for the ones who don't come back.

"Sable—"

"Go."

"I'm not leaving you here."

"You're *going up.*" Sable's voice was steady now. Calm. The calm of a person who has made a decision and the war is over and all that's left is the quiet after. "You're going up, and you're going to file the report, and you're going to say *Unrescued,* and you're going to close the Journal, and you're going to sit on the roof, and the sun is going to be *too much,* and you're going to be *angry,* and that's *fine.* You're going to be angry, and you're going to *live,* and that's the whole point. That's the whole *point.*"

The elevator was fully open now. The light was a *wall.* A golden, warm, *cruel* wall.

Marin looked at Sable.

Sable looked at the wall of light.

And Sable *turned away.*

Not in pain. Not in fear. Just... *away.* Like a flower closing at dusk. Like an eye shutting. Like a door, gently, *gently*, clicking shut.

The elevator chimed.

The doors closed.

---

The Rescuer's Journal, open on the desk in the briefing room, still had the pen in Marin's paw. The ink was wet. The entry read:

*Sable, Drowzee. Floor 47 of the Tower. Status: Unrescued.*

*Cause of non-rescue: Subject declined. Subject stated: "I can't. I'm so tired."*

*Rescuer notes: I was there. I was* ***there.*** *I had the shell. I had the* ***space.*** *I said* ***come up, come up, come up.*** *And they said* ***I can't.*** *And I had to go up without them. And I went up. And the light was right there. And it was* ***too much.***

*And I'm sorry. And I'm sorry. And I'm sorry. And I don't know how many times I have to write it for it to be enough. I don't know if it's ever going to be enough. I don't know if* ***sorry*** *is a floor you can climb out of or if it's just another room in the Tower with a window that looks out onto nothing.*

*I'm going to sit on the roof now. The sun is coming up. It's going to be too much. I'm going to let it be too much.*

*And I'm going to keep the shell empty. For a while. Just for a while. So that if someone comes, and they're shaking, and they say* ***I don't mind, I don't mind,*** *I can say* ***sit, sit, I've got you.***

*But not today. Today I'm just going to sit in the sun and be* ***too much.***

*And that's okay.*

*That's okay.*

*That's okay.*

The pen set down. The Journal closed.

On the roof of the Rescue Team HQ, a Lapras sat with their back to the sky, and the sun came up, and the light was *too much,* and they let it be, and the shell was empty, and the shell was *full,* and the sky was *right there,* and the sky was *right there,* and the sky was *right there,*

and no one came to carry them,

and no one had to,

and the sun went on,

and the sun went on,

and the sun went on.

# The Ruby's Weight

## Part One: The Vow

The morning light came through the kitchen window in a long golden blade, catching the steam rising from two mugs of coffee. Elena pressed her forehead against Mark's bare shoulder while he stood at the stove, flipping a pancake with the focused concentration of a man defusing a bomb.

"You're going to burn it," she murmured, her breath warm against his neck.

"I'm not *burning* it, I'm *caramelizing* it."

"You're caramelizing the *pan*."

He turned, and she caught the spatula before it could meet the griddle's metal lip. He kissed the top of her head. She kissed the corner of his mouth. They stood there for a moment, foreheads touching, the small domestic ritual of it so ordinary and so complete that it felt like a prayer.

"Rough day at the firm?" he asked.

"Gregory Ashworth is hosting a 'team-building dinner' on Friday." She said the name the way other people said *rotting meat*. "In the ballroom. With the *chandelier*. And he's making me sit next to him."

Mark's jaw tightened. He set the spatula down and wrapped both arms around her, pulling her against his chest. "I'll be there. I'll be *right there*."

"You'll be *there*."

"I'll be *there*, Elena. I'm not letting him get in your head. I'm not letting him get in your *space*."

She leaned back to look up at him. At thirty-four, Elena Voss was the kind of beautiful that made people look twice and then look away, as though the first glance had been an intrusion. Sharp-featured, dark-haired, with eyes the color of wet slate that could reduce a room to silence. She was also, as her colleagues quietly acknowledged, the most brilliant tax attorney in the firm's forty-year history, and she wielded that brilliance the way a surgeon wielded a scalpel—precisely, without apology, and with a certain cold delight.

And she *hated* Gregory Ashworth.

Not in the way one hates a difficult client or a tedious regulation. She hated him the way one hates a wasp that has found its way into the house—something small, iridescent, and utterly, *aggressively* alive in a space that was meant to be safe.

---

## Part Two: The Wasp

Gregory Ashworth was fifty-one, silver-templed, and possessed of the particular kind of confidence that comes from never once having been told *no* and believing, with the full conviction of the deluded, that the universe simply had not yet gotten around to it. He was the managing partner of Voss & Hartwell. He was also, by his own uninvited assertion, a "certified clinical hypnotist" with a private practice he conducted on weekends, which he mentioned at every opportunity with the pride of a man displaying a particularly gaudy tie.

He had been making passes at Elena for three years.

Not subtle ones. Not the quiet, lingering glances of a man who might, perhaps, be interested. Gregory Ashworth flirted the way a foghorn operates: loudly, persistently, and with the absolute certainty that the ship was *obligated* to hear it.

Elena remembered the incident at the office Christmas party in December, two years prior. She was in the kitchen, pouring a glass of sparkling water, when he materialized at her elbow, close enough that she could smell his cologne—something heavy, musky, expensive.

"Elena, darling, you simply *must* tell me," he said, his voice a low rumble he clearly believed was seductive, "what a woman of your... *stature*... sees in a man like Mark. He's a good boy. A *nice* boy. But nice is so very *safe*."

Elena set the glass down. She turned to face him fully. The kitchen was crowded with colleagues, but in that moment, the only two people in it were them.

"Gregory," she said, and her voice was quiet, level, and utterly without warmth. "I am going to say this once. I am married. I love my husband. You are my employer. You are also, I am told, a man who once made a 'joke' about my legs to a junior associate in a meeting room. I find you *repugnant*. I find your cologne *repugnant*. I find the fact that you are standing within my personal space *repugnant*. You will not speak to me at this party. You will not speak to me at the *office*. You will address me by my name in a professional context, or I will file a complaint with HR that will make your silver temples go *white*. Do we understand each other?"

The kitchen had gone silent. Three colleagues had frozen mid-sip.

Gregory's smile had faltered, then reassembled itself into something thinner. "You're very *intense*, Elena. I admire that. I think you're *terrified* of how attractive I find you."

"I am not terrified of anything you find, Gregory. I am *bored* of it. Now, if you'll excuse me, I'm going to go be *repugnant* to my sparkling water."

She walked out. He did not speak to her for two weeks. Then he came back, because Gregory Ashworth always came back.

There was the time he'd "accidentally" brushed his hand across hers in the elevator and said, "You know, I've been doing some *work* on a client who had a very similar... *tension*... with her husband. A little relaxation. A little *suggestion*. Worked wonders." Elena had stared at him for eleven seconds—she'd counted—before saying, "If you ever speak to me about *hypnosis* again, I will ensure that your 'private practice' is the subject of a very detailed letter to the state licensing board. And I will make it *very* detailed. I am a tax attorney, Gregory. I know how to find the *loopholes* in people."

He had not spoken to her for a month after that.

And there was the incident last spring, in the parking garage, where he'd leaned against his car and said, "You know, Elena, I think you're *holding back*. I think there's a part of you that *wants* to be... *unburdened*. I could help with that. I have a very soothing voice. I could demonstrate, if you'd like. Right here. No one's around."

She had walked to his car, opened the passenger door, and said, "Get in."

He had blinked. "What?"

"You heard me. Get in. I'm going to drive you to the office. You're going to sit in the *driver's* seat of *my* car, and I'm going to drive you to the parking spot you *should* have used, and you're going to get out, and you're going to walk to the office, and you are *never* going to speak to me in a parking garage again. Drive."

He had gotten in. She had driven. He had not spoken for the entire four-minute journey.

Mark knew all of this. He'd held her while she'd retold it, his hands in her hair, his jaw set, his eyes dark with a fury he kept carefully leashed. "I should *hit* him," he'd said once.

"You should not hit him. You should *fire* him. But you can't fire the managing partner, so you're going to have to *endure* him, and I'm going to have to *endure* him, and on Friday we're going to sit in a ballroom under a *chandelier* and he's going to *talk*, and I'm going to *not hit him*, and we are going to *survive*."

He'd kissed her forehead. "We'll survive. I promise."

---

## Part Three: The Ballroom

The Ashworth & Co. ballroom was, as Elena had predicted, an exercise in obscene excess. Crystal chandeliers the size of small cars hung from a vaulted ceiling. The tables were draped in white linen so stiff it could have served as a sail. The food was exquisite and the wine was older than Mark's firm.

Elena wore a dress of deep emerald silk, her dark hair pinned up, a single strand escaping to frame her cheek. She was, as always, the most striking woman in the room, and she was aware of it the way one is aware of a draft from a window—constantly, and with a faint irritation.

Mark sat to her left. His arm was around her waist, his hand resting on the small of her back, a steady warm weight. He leaned down and kissed her temple. "You're glowing," he whispered.

"I'm *furious*," she whispered back. "There's a difference."

Gregory Ashworth was at the head table. He wore a tuxedo that fit him with the easy confidence of a man who had never once been told his clothes didn't fit. His silver hair was swept back. He was talking to a junior partner, his hand gesturing broadly, and his eyes—Elena noticed—kept drifting to her. They *always* drifted to her. A small, proprietary flicker, as though she were a piece of furniture he'd been meaning to rearrange for years.

She caught his eye. She did not look away. She let him see the flat, cold assessment in her gaze, the one that said *I see you, I know you, and you are nothing to me.*

His smile flickered. He looked away.

*Good*, she thought. *Stay in your lane, Gregory.*

The dinner progressed. Mark talked about a tax case he was working on, his eyes bright, his hands moving as he explained. Elena listened, nodding, occasionally interjecting with a sharp observation that made him laugh. She reached across the table and squeezed his hand. He squeezed back. Small, private, *theirs*.

Then Gregory stood.

"Ladies and gentlemen," he said, his voice carrying with the practiced ease of a man who had given many toasts. "I want to propose a *little* something. A *demonstration*. A little... *entertainment*." He smiled. It was the smile of a cat that had just found a mouse. "I've been doing some... *work*... in the field of hypnotherapy. And I'd like to show you what a truly *relaxed* mind looks like. I'm looking for a volunteer. Someone who's a little... *tense*... tonight. Someone who could use a little *unburdening*."

The table went quiet.

Elena felt Mark's hand tighten on her back. She felt his gaze shift to Gregory. She felt the low, subsonic hum of his anger.

*No*, she thought. *Not me. Not tonight.*

But Gregory was already looking at her. His eyes were bright. His smile was wide. He was *pointing* at her.

"Elena," he said, and his voice was honey poured over gravel. "You look *tense*, darling. You look like a woman who's been *holding* something in all evening. Let me help you. Just a little. A little *relaxation*. You'll feel *wonderful* afterward. I promise."

The table was silent. Twenty pairs of eyes were on her.

Elena set her fork down. She picked up her wine glass. She took a slow sip. She set the glass down.

"Gregory," she said, and her voice was calm, clear, and carried to the back of the room. "I am not *tense*. I am *present*. I am sitting next to my *husband*. I am eating a *very good* scallop. And I am not your *volunteer*. I am not your *patient*. I am not your *demonstration*. You will find your little *entertainment* elsewhere, and you will *not* look at me again tonight. Do we understand each other?"

A murmur rippled through the table. Someone—Mark, she thought, though she couldn't see him—let out a low, appreciative *hmm*.

Gregory's smile did not waver. It *deepened*. "You know, Elena, I've seen that *resistance* before. The *fierce* kind. The kind where a woman is so *certain* of her own mind that she *builds a wall* around it. And you know what I've learned, in my *practice*? The wall is the most *fascinating* part. Because it means there's something *beautiful* behind it that she's *afraid* to let go of." He paused. He reached into his tuxedo jacket. "I think, Elena, that you and I are going to have a *little* conversation."

He pulled out the necklace.

The room went very, very quiet.

It was a chain of heavy gold links, thick as a man's finger, and from it hung a pendant that made the chandeliers look *tacky*. A ruby. Not a *gem*. A *ruby*. The size of a man's fist, deep and molten and *alive*, cut in a rough, ancient cabochon that caught the light and threw it back in slow, rolling waves of crimson. It was, Elena thought, with a distant, analytical part of her brain, *worth more than the building they were sitting in*.

Gregory held it up. The ruby caught the chandelier light and *blazed*.

"This," he said softly, "is a *Sikh* ruby. Fourteenth century. I've been... *borrowing* it from a collector in Jaipur. I'm going to put it on *you*, Elena. As a *gift*. A *memento*. And I'm going to let you *look* at it. Just for a moment. Just to see how *beautiful* it is. And then you're going to tell me it's the most beautiful thing you've ever seen, and we're going to have our *little* conversation, and you're going to *smile*, and everyone here is going to *applaud*, and you're going to feel *wonderful*."

He was holding it out. Extending his arm. The ruby swung gently in the air, a slow pendulum of deep red light.

Elena looked at it.

She looked at Mark.

Mark's face was a mask. His jaw was clenched so tight the muscle jumped. His hand was still on her back, but his fingers were *digging in*, white-knuckled, as though he were holding her to the earth. His eyes were on Gregory. His eyes were on the *ruby*.

"Gregory," Elena said. Her voice was steady. Her hands were steady. Her heart was *not* steady. "Put that *away*. I don't want it. I don't want *you*. I don't want your *conversation*. I am *married*. I am *devoted*. I love the man sitting next to me, and I will *not* be *demonstrated*, and I will *not* be *gifted*, and I will *not* *smile* for you. You are going to put that *rock* in your *pocket*, and you are going to *sit down*, and you are going to *eat your scallop*, and we are going to *finish this dinner*."

She said it all in one breath. Clean. Precise. *Surgical*.

The table erupted. A woman two seats down *laughed*. Mark let out a sound that was half laugh, half *roar*, and he was *proud* of her, she could tell, his whole body leaning toward her, his hand splaying across her back.

Gregory Ashworth did not sit down.

He did not put the ruby in his pocket.

He *smiled*.

"You know, Elena," he said, and his voice had changed. The honey was still there, but beneath it, something else. Something *older*. Something *patient*. "You're *very* brave. I admire that. Truly. But you're also *very* tired. You've been *fighting* me for three years. Every *meeting*. Every *parking garage*. Every *Christmas party*. And you're *tired*, Elena. I can *see* it. The tension in your *shoulders*. The way you *grip* your fork. You don't have to *fight* anymore. You just have to *look*."

He stepped forward. One step. Two. He was at the edge of the table now, close. The ruby swung gently in his hand, a slow, hypnotic arc. *Left. Right. Left. Right.*

"Just *look* at it, Elena. Just for a *moment*. You don't have to *take* it. You don't have to *smile*. You just have to *look*. And if it doesn't *fascinate* you, I'll *apologize*. I'll *apologize* to you, to *Mark*, to the *entire table*. I'll *resign*. I'll *quit*. I'll *never* speak to you again. All I'm asking is that you *look*."

The ruby swung. *Left. Right.* The light in it moved like slow, liquid blood.

Elena looked at Mark.

Mark looked at her. His eyes were *pleading*. *Please don't*. *I can't stop him*. *Please, Elena, please don't look at it*. His lips were moving. *Don't. Don't. Don't.*

She looked back at the ruby.

It was, she had to admit, *extraordinary*. The light moved through it in slow, deep waves, and there was something in the *rhythm* of its swing that tugged at the back of her mind, a small, insistent *pull*, like a thread caught in a lock.

"I'm *looking*," she said. Her voice was still steady. Still *hers*. "I'm looking, and it's a *very pretty rock*, Gregory. And now you're going to *sit down*."

"Keep looking, Elena. Just... *keep* looking. You don't have to *do* anything. You just have to *look*. And *breathe*. Just *breathe*. In... and *out*."

"I'm not *breathing* for you, Gregory. I'm *breathing* because I'm *alive* and I'm *furious* and I'm going to *leave this dinner* in approximately *four minutes* and I'm going to *file a complaint* with the *state bar* and I'm going to *make your life*—"

"Elena." His voice was softer now. *Softer*. The honey was gone. What was left was something *warm*. Something *low*. Something that sounded, God help her, almost *kind*. "You don't have to be *furious*. You don't have to *fight*. You can just... *let go*. Just for a *moment*. Look at the *light*. The light in the *stone*. It's *beautiful*, Elena. You don't have to be *brave* right now. You can just be... *tired*. You can just be *still*."

The ruby swung. *Left. Right. Left. Right.*

Elena's eyes were on it. She *hated* that her eyes were on it. She *hated* the slow, rolling waves of crimson light. She *hated* the way the rhythm of its swing seemed to match the rhythm of her own breathing, as though it were *pulling* her breath in and out, *setting* the tempo.

"I'm *not* tired," she said. But her voice was a fraction lower. A fraction *softer*. The surgical edge was still there, but it was *thinner*. "I'm *furious*. There's a *difference*. I am *furious* and I am *capable* and I am *going to leave* and you are going to *sit down*."

"You're *capable*, Elena. I *know* you're capable. I *admire* you. That's why I chose *you*. You're the *strongest* woman in this room. The *sharpest*. The most *brilliant*. And I'm not asking you to be *weak*. I'm asking you to be *still*. Just for a *moment*. Just long enough to *see*."

The ruby swung. *Left. Right.*

Elena's eyes tracked it. She *hated* it. She *hated* the way her eyelids felt *heavy*. She *hated* the way the light in the stone seemed to *pulse*, slow and deep, like a heartbeat that wasn't her own. She *hated* the way her jaw was *unclenching*, slowly, involuntarily, the muscles in her cheeks going *soft*.

"Mark," she whispered.

He was *right there*. His hand was on her back. His fingers were *tight*. His face was *close*, close enough that she could see the *fear* in his eyes, the *rage*, the *helplessness*.

"Elena," he breathed. "*Please*. Don't—"

"I'm *fine*, Mark. I'm *fine*. I'm just... *looking*."

She was not fine. She could feel it in the *weight* of her eyelids, the slow, syrupy *thickening* of her thoughts, as though her mind were being *poured* into a wider, slower container. The ruby swung. *Left. Right.* The light in it was *warm*. It was *deep*. It was *beautiful*, and she *hated* that it was beautiful, and she *hated* that the word *beautiful* was the last clear thought in her mind before the next one was *slower*, and the next one after that was *slower still*.

"Your eyes are *heavy*, Elena," Gregory said, and his voice was *so* soft now, *so* low, a murmur that seemed to come from *everywhere* and *nowhere*. "You can feel it, can't you? The *weight*. The *warmth*. Like a *blanket*. Like a *hand* on your forehead. You don't have to *hold* them open. You don't have to *fight* it. You can just... *let* them... *close*."

"I'm *not* closing my eyes," Elena said. But her voice was *different*. The edge was *gone*. The *surgical* precision was *gone*. What was left was *slower*. *Rounder*. *Softer*. "I'm *not* closing my eyes, Gregory. I am *looking* at the *rock*. And I am *furious*. And I am *not* *tired*. I am *not*—"

"You are *tired*, Elena. You've been *tired* for a *long* time. You've been *fighting* for *years*. And you're *so* *good* at it. You're *so* *brilliant* at it. But you don't have to be *brilliant* right now. You don't have to be *sharp*. You can just be *soft*. You can just be *still*. The *light* is *beautiful*. The *stone* is *beautiful*. You can just *look*. You can just *drift*."

The ruby swung. *Left. Right. Left. Right.*

Elena's eyelids were *heavy*. Not *closed*. Not *yet*. But *heavy*. The weight of them was *enormous*, as though they were made of *lead*, of *warm* lead, and the effort of keeping them open was *great*, and *exhausting*, and *pointless*.

"Mark," she whispered. Her eyes were *half* closed. The ruby was a *blur* of crimson light, a slow, rolling *pulse*. "Mark, I'm... I'm *fine*. I'm just... *tired*. I'm just... *looking*."

"Elena." Mark's voice was *cracking*. "Elena, *look at me*. *Look at me*. *Please*."

She turned her head. Slowly. *So* slowly. His face was *close*. His eyes were *wet*. His hand was *shaking* on her back.

"I'm *here*, Mark," she whispered. "I'm *here*. I love you. I'm *here*."

Her eyes were *drifting* back to the ruby. *Back* to the light. *Back* to the slow, rolling *pulse*.

"Your eyes are *closing*, Elena," Gregory said. *Gently*. *So* gently. "And that's *all right*. You don't have to *fight* it. You don't have to *hold* on. You can just... *let go*. You can just... *sleep*. It's *all right*. You're *safe*. You're *warm*. The *light* is *beautiful*. You can just... *drift*... into it..."

Elena's eyes *closed*.

The ruby swung. *Left. Right. Left. Right.*

And the room went *silent*.

Mark's hand was still on her back. His fingers were *clenched*. His face was *white*. His mouth was *open*, and no sound was coming out.

Gregory Ashworth smiled.

He was *so* proud.
